AI.result: StreamEgo achieves generalizable, unbounded real-time streaming Exo2Ego video generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: Dual-branch kinematic priors and chunk-wise autoregressive distillation enable live, high-quality exocentric-to-egocentric video translation.

title: SpatialScout-V2: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore Real-World 3D Scenes and Localize Objects?
summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SpatialScout-V2, a real-world active 3D scene exploration benchmark built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, showing that frontier VLMs achieve at most 22.52% mean IoU on object-center localization.
AI.motivation: Active 3D mapping benchmarks have largely been limited to simulation, leaving it unclear how well VLM agents explore real-world scenes and integrate partial observations.
AI.method: SpatialScout-V2 comprises 3,171 target objects across 29 categories in 100 real homes from Realsee3D, requiring agents to select viewpoints and viewing directions within an interaction budget to estimate and revise object centers, evaluated by mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage.
AI.result: Across seven frontier VLMs, six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20%, and the best model (Claude Opus 5.5) reaches only 22.52% mean IoU with 18.36% of targets exceeding 0.5 IoU.
AI.conclusion: Frontier VLMs still face major challenges in active exploration, viewpoint integration, and accurate 3D object-center localization in real residential environments.

title: FlexVSR: Continuous-Scale Super-Resolution for Streaming Video Generation
summary: Real-time streaming video generation has gained rapid momentum in live content creation and interactive media. Deploying such systems in practice requires flexible scaling factors to accommodate diverse source resolutions, target displays, and computational budgets. However, extending fixed-scale generative video super-resolution (VSR) to varying target scales poses two challenges: downsampling from a larger fixed scale incurs redundant cost, while re-optimizing the diffusion transformer (DiT) is costly and alters the shared generative prior. To address both, we propose FlexVSR, a decoupled framework for continuous-scale streaming generative VSR with supervision at only a few scales. Our key insight is that naively resampling fixed-scale latents onto a new target grid induces scale-dependent input mismatch, which can be effectively addressed through parameter-efficient, scale-aware adaptation of the latent interface without updating the DiT. To this end, FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a lightweight latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before they enter the DiT, enabling a shared frozen VSR prior to generalize across continuous scales with only 0.274M trainable parameters and an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, while introducing no additional temporal dependencies and preserving the native causal streaming protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming baselines and offline methods, and effective generalization to unseen continuous scales, filling the continuous-scale gap in real-time streaming generative VSR.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FlexVSR, a continuous-scale streaming generative video super-resolution framework that adapts a frozen DiT prior using a lightweight 0.274M-parameter latent adapter.
AI.motivation: Extending fixed-scale generative VSR to arbitrary target scales either wastes compute via downsampling or requires costly re-optimization of the diffusion transformer (DiT).
AI.method: FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a 0.274M-parameter latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before entering a frozen VSR DiT, trained with supervision at only a few scales while preserving causal streaming.
AI.result: With an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, FlexVSR achieves competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming and offline baselines, and strong generalization to unseen continuous scales.
AI.conclusion: Scale-aware adaptation at the latent interface enables continuous-scale real-time streaming generative VSR without modifying the underlying DiT prior.

title: RegionAgent: Two-Stage Preference Optimization for Regional Image Restoration
summary: Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration capabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uniform operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incomplete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using preferences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage preference learning in improving restoration quality.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RegionAgent, a VLM-based regional image restoration framework trained with two-stage step-level and trajectory-level DPO on a new regional preference dataset.
AI.motivation: Images with non-uniform coupled degradations require distinct, sequential regional restoration actions, whereas existing methods apply globally uniform operations that cause incomplete restoration or content damage.
AI.method: RegionAgent trains a VLM to select region-specific restoration actions iteratively using step-level DPO from immediate feedback followed by trajectory-level DPO from complete trajectory scores, supported by a constructed dataset of 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations, with ablations validating the two-stage preference learning.
AI.conclusion: Two-stage step- and trajectory-level preference optimization enables VLMs to plan sequential, region-aware restoration actions for complex coupled degradations.

title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
summary: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks 52 encoder-decoder combinations (4 decoders and 13 backbones) on BDD100K semantic segmentation, finding that FPN with EfficientNet-B4 performs best at 62.6% mIoU.
AI.motivation: Segmentation backbones are often chosen without systematic comparison, leaving the interaction between encoder family and decoder architecture unclear.
AI.method: The authors combine four decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet, PSPNet) with 13 backbones across six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet, EfficientNet) and train all 52 models under a unified protocol on BDD100K.
AI.result: FPN with EfficientNet-B4 achieves the best performance (62.6% mIoU, 89.8% accuracy, 0.092 loss), only two models (both FPN with EfficientNet) beat the 56.9% BDD100K benchmark, and backbone impact varies strongly by decoder (12.0 mIoU range for U-Net vs. 42.5 for FPN; EfficientNet-B4 drops to 42.6% with PSPNet).
AI.conclusion: Encoder performance in semantic segmentation is heavily dependent on the paired decoder architecture, underscoring the need for joint encoder-decoder evaluation.

title: A version of the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition for full/quad pol synthetic aperture radar data
summary: Based on the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition of reflection symmetric polarimetric SAR data we present a version for full/quad polarisation data. We demonstrate both versions on X-band F-SAR data over Vejers, Denmark. Differences between the original and our version of the decomposition occur especially for very bright man-made targets. These differences come with lower entropy for our version giving an improved focus on a more pronounced dominant scattering mechanism for these objects. Interpretation of the scattering mechanism related to the full/quad pol version of the decomposition is facilitated by means of the Cloude/Pottier $\bar{\alpha}$ angle.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition from reflection-symmetric to full/quad-polarization SAR data, yielding lower entropy and sharper dominant scattering mechanisms on bright man-made targets.
AI.motivation: The standard Cloude/van Zyl decomposition assumes reflection-symmetric polarimetric SAR data, limiting its applicability to full/quad-polarization observations.
AI.method: The authors formulate a full/quad-polarization version of the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition and interpret its scattering mechanisms using the Cloude/Pottier $\bar{\alpha}$ angle on X-band F-SAR data over Vejers, Denmark.
AI.result: Compared to the original decomposition, the full/quad-polarization version exhibits lower entropy and a more pronounced dominant scattering mechanism, particularly for bright man-made targets.
AI.conclusion: Extending the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition to full/quad-polarization data improves scattering mechanism discrimination for complex man-made targets in SAR imagery.

title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
summary: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SpecWM, a training-free speculative inference framework for streaming world models that verifies and reuses target latent velocity corrections, achieving a 1.63x speedup on WBench Navigation.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative world model methods rely on costly frame decoding and external reward scoring for verification and discard rejected drafts without providing corrections.
AI.method: SpecWM verifies draft chunks directly using the target model's latent velocity field and reuses the resulting correction via two thresholds to Accept, Refine (1-step for perceptual quality or 3-step for camera/trajectory consistency), or Reject.
AI.result: On WBench Navigation, SpecWM achieves a 1.63x speedup over the target model while improving visual quality and raising NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, and sustains quality over long rollouts on LongSpecBench.
AI.conclusion: Turning latent velocity verification into reusable multi-step refinement provides a superior quality-speed-control trade-off for streaming world models.

title: MixReact: Physics-Based Reactive Humanoid Control from Multimodal Cues via a Discrete-Continuous Mixture of Transformers
summary: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents MixReact, a unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues using a Discrete-Continuous Mixture of Transformers and a History-aware Action Transformer.
AI.motivation: Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support limited modalities and produce purely kinematic motions that suffer from physical artifacts.
AI.method: MixReact pairs a Discrete-Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT)—coupling a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention—with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for closed-loop physical execution.
AI.result: Experiments across text, audio, and video cues demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, with ablations confirming each component's contribution.
AI.conclusion: Combining discrete-continuous mixture state prediction with history-aware action execution enables physically executable, multimodal reactive humanoid control.

title: Attention Drift Regularization with Adaptive Initialization for Domain-Robust Visual Recognition
summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a pretrained source model to unlabeled target domains without source data access, yet two critical failure modes remain unaddressed. First, attention drift: source-learned attention maps shift toward spurious or background features under distribution shift, destabilizing feature representations. Second, domain-gap-agnostic initialization: applying a single fixed source model uniformly across all target domains ignores domain gap severity, causing premature overfitting to noisy pseudo-labels under large shifts. We propose DGA-CAFC to address both failures. The Counterfactual Attention-based Feature Consistency (CAFC) module enforces feature stability by minimizing the discrepancy between representations computed under learned attention and those under counterfactual-inspired normalized perturbations, thereby promoting domain-robust features independent of spurious attention shifts. The Domain-Gap Aware Source Model Selection (DGASS) module estimates domain gap severity via target prediction entropy and selects the source model variant whose confidence level best matches the estimated gap, reducing negative transfer and stabilizing pseudo-label quality. Crucially, CAFC transfers beyond SFDA: applied as a lightweight regularizer to standard domain generalization objectives without target data. Extensive experiments across SFDA and DG benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves over recent baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework. Project page is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DGA-CAFC for source-free domain adaptation and domain generalization, combining counterfactual attention feature consistency with domain-gap-aware source model selection.
AI.motivation: Source-free domain adaptation suffers from attention drift toward spurious background features under distribution shift and domain-gap-agnostic initialization that overfits to noisy pseudo-labels.
AI.method: DGA-CAFC introduces Counterfactual Attention-based Feature Consistency (CAFC) to stabilize representations under counterfactual attention perturbations, and Domain-Gap Aware Source Model Selection (DGASS) to estimate domain gap via target prediction entropy and select a matching source model variant.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across source-free domain adaptation and domain generalization benchmarks show consistent improvements over recent baselines, with CAFC also transferring as a lightweight regularizer without target data.
AI.conclusion: Regularizing attention drift and matching source model initialization to estimated domain gap substantially improves domain-robust visual recognition.

title: Beyond Covers and Titles: Evidence-First Ranking for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
summary: Short-video platforms rank new uploads before anyone has watched them, using content towers that read a video's cover, title and frames. Existing attacks on content-aware recommenders perturb pixels or features and ignore platform re-encoding, and existing defenses train against norm-bounded perturbations that neither match real edits nor preserve recommendation quality. We show with REAP, a realizable attack through {a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping and JPEG)}, that packaging edits raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points in unrelated audiences. We then observe that cold-start ranking does not need the packaging at all: a tower that sees only the video body ranks cold items best. Building on this, we propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their body, admits packaging only through a support-gated residual bounded by $\gamma$, and merges cold and warm rankings by rank percentile, yielding an exact certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts the attack gain by 81% and raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, while keeping the merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that packaging edits can manipulate cold-start video rankings by 32.0 percentile points and proposes Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which cuts attack gains by 81% on MicroLens-100K.
AI.motivation: Short-video cold-start recommenders rely on covers and titles that can be manipulated, while existing defenses ignore platform re-encoding and degrade recommendation quality.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate the realizable REAP attack through a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping, JPEG) and propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their video body, bounds packaging via a support-gated residual $\gamma$, and merges cold and warm rankings by percentile.
AI.result: REAP raises cold-video rank by 32.0 percentile points in unrelated audiences; on MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts attack gain by 81%, raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, and keeps merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.
AI.conclusion: Scoring cold-start videos primarily from body content with bounded packaging residuals provides a certified defense against packaging manipulation while improving cold-start recall.

title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design
summary: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs $1.7\times$ faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Prism, a minimalist hierarchical text detection framework using parallel lightweight heads on a single-scale backbone and geometric inclusion, running 1.7x faster than LRANet on CTW1500.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical text detectors rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy heads, resulting in bloated architectures and slow inference.
AI.method: Prism attaches parallel lightweight pixel-level regression heads to a single-scale pretrained backbone to detect words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the hierarchy using a geometric inclusion algorithm.
AI.result: Prism runs 1.7x faster than LRANet on CTW1500 with higher accuracy and surpasses OmniParser V2 by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset.
AI.conclusion: A strong pretrained single-scale backbone with lightweight pixel-level regression heads and geometric inclusion suffices for fast, state-of-the-art hierarchical text detection.

title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
summary: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates three computer vision pipelines for reading analogue pressure gauges on a curated 1,848-image dataset, finding that OpenCV with ResNet18 achieves 97.3% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Manual monitoring of analogue gauges in manufacturing introduces human error and operational inefficiency.
AI.method: The authors curate 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR) via web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation, and compare OpenCV paired with Scikit-Image, ResNet18, and VGG19.
AI.result: OpenCV with ResNet18 achieves 97.3% accuracy, substantially outperforming OpenCV with VGG19 (64.4%) and OpenCV with Scikit-Image (63.8%).
AI.conclusion: Residual learning paired with OpenCV preprocessing provides an accurate, reliable foundation for automated industrial analogue gauge digitization.

title: Tracking Objects Through Assembly and Decomposition
summary: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a prompt-free formulation for tracking objects through both decomposition and assembly, presenting the zero-shot Atlas system and the OmniST benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing state-change tracking methods require an initial object prompt and only detect decompositions, missing assembly events that start from multiple objects.
AI.method: Exploiting the insight that assembly is decomposition in reverse, Atlas constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions in a zero-shot manner to recover all object tracks and both transformation types, evaluated on the new densely annotated OmniST benchmark.
AI.result: On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing decomposition-only benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Joint forward-reverse spatiotemporal reasoning enables prompt-free tracking of both assembly and decomposition events in complex dynamic scenes.

title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
summary: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents C-LiTE, a 22M-parameter cellular foundation model for H&E histopathology trained on 60 million cell-centred crops, approaching CytoFormer's accuracy with 30x fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Tissue-patch pathology foundation models capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either narrow in scope or rely on heavy architectures and upsampling that introduces interpolation artifacts.
AI.method: C-LiTE tokenizes 64x64 px cell-centred crops at native resolution using 4x4 patch embeddings, initializes weights from a pretrained ViT-5-S via a pseudoinverse-based transformation, and pretrains self-supervised on 60 million TCGA cell crops across 19 cancer and 16 tissue types.
AI.result: Across seven public cellular classification and phenotyping datasets under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Native-resolution tokenization and large-scale cell-centred pretraining enable compact, parameter-efficient foundation models for computational pathology.

title: ResVision: Spectrum-Matched Resizing and Context-Preserving Inspection for Visual Reasoning
summary: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ResVision, combining Spectrum-Matched Resizing and Context-Preserving Inspection, to improve agentic VLM visual reasoning by 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base across 29 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agentic visual reasoning can suffer from high-frequency detail attenuation during tokenization, difficulty retrieving spatially distributed evidence, and scale/positional mismatch in isolated crops.
AI.method: ResVision introduces Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) to adaptively allocate visual tokens based on estimated image complexity, and Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) to return each inspected crop alongside the complete working view across tool turns.
AI.result: Evaluated on four frontier VLMs across 29 benchmarks, complete ResVision improves by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive complexity-based visual sampling and context-preserving crop inspection address complementary bottlenecks in multimodal agentic visual reasoning.

title: FirstCross: Convex Single-Photon 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views
summary: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.

AI.tldr: FirstCross is a network-free, convex optimization approach for few-view single-photon 3D reconstruction that cuts exposure to 1% and reconstructs an object in about one minute on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Leading neural single-photon lidar reconstruction methods like Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization and degrade in accuracy as photon flux decreases.
AI.method: FirstCross decomposes the ray-wise Poisson likelihood around the first crossing point into two tractable terms on a voxel grid: a tight convex closure using volume rendering with running-maximum transmittance to penalize surfaces in front of detected photons, and a convex upper bound for unexplained photons assuming the object is thick behind detected surface points.
AI.result: Under Transientangelo's real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across all test scenes, view counts, and flux levels, keeping three-view mean object depth error at 100x fewer photons under half of Transientangelo's all-photon error, outperforming classical fusion by 1.3-1.8x, and beating TransientNeRF by 2.8-7.7x on real room-scale captures with 1% photons.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating single-photon 3D reconstruction as a short sequence of convex problems enables fast, robust, and low-flux few-view 3D scanning without neural networks.

title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
summary: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.

AI.tldr: Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ) fits lightweight, video-specific orthogonal rotations online to adjacent KV-cache frames, enabling 2-bit KV-cache quantization in video diffusion transformers with improved generation consistency.
AI.motivation: Reusing KV-caches across denoising steps creates a memory bottleneck for long video generation, and quantizing temporally distant cache vectors causes high error due to large value ranges and video-specific channel patterns.
AI.method: TRQ groups temporally adjacent KV-cache vectors into blocks and fits an orthogonal transform (parameterized as a tree of 2-bit 2x2 planar rotations followed by a fixed shared Hadamard transform) using a globally optimal greedy fit without gradients, accelerated by fused Triton kernels.
AI.result: At 2-bit precision with matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, along with gains on other metrics.
AI.conclusion: Online, gradient-free temporal rotations effectively reduce quantization error in video diffusion KV-caches, making 2-bit cache compression practical for long video generation.

title: OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture Beyond the Camera Frame Rate
summary: For 4D reconstruction, a synchronized multi-camera rig records all views at the same timestamps and misses the motion between them. Staggered triggers spread the same frames over more timestamps. However, when the cameras along each row fire one after another, as in 4DSloMo's schedule on the N3DV rig, the row acts as one moving camera that confounds depth with motion. We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler: shifted copies of one sampling grid. From the calibration alone, OffBeat derives camera groups that fire together and their firing order. Since one group records each timestamp, a short-lived primitive can fit an error its cameras share, such as a color offset, and flicker in novel views. We show that a primitive's opacity over time weights all groups equally, for every number of groups, only if it lasts at least one camera frame interval. On Spacetime Gaussians, a minimum lifetime approximates this bound, and a closed-form smoothed box of that length satisfies it exactly, with less flicker than a Gaussian in its place at nearly equal PSNR. In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline with video diffusion on every test frame, by 3.04 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it outperforms the best synchronized method of each scene, with or without frame interpolation, by 1.98 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR, while synchronized capture is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in this frame range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation. On every N3DV scene, replacing 4DSloMo's schedule with ours raises the dynamic-region PSNR of Spacetime Gaussians, 4DSloMo without diffusion, and our reconstruction. Multi-camera rigs could follow faster motion at the same frame count by changing only when each camera fires.

AI.tldr: OffBeat models staggered multi-camera rigs as spatially distributed multicoset samplers to derive optimal firing schedules and primitive lifetime bounds, outperforming synchronized capture and 4DSloMo on 4D reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Synchronized multi-camera rigs miss inter-frame motion, while naive staggered triggers like row-by-row firing in 4DSloMo confound depth with motion and cause short-lived primitives to flicker by overfitting per-group errors.
AI.method: OffBeat derives camera firing groups and their order from calibration alone, and proves that a primitive's opacity weights all groups equally only if it lasts at least one camera frame interval, using a closed-form smoothed box of that length on Spacetime Gaussians.
AI.result: On simulated staggered N3DV capture, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline by 3.04 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR and beats the best synchronized method (with or without interpolation) by 1.98 dB between synchronized frames, while matching synchronized-plus-interpolation PSNR on PanopticSports.
AI.conclusion: Changing only camera firing schedules and enforcing minimum primitive lifetimes allows multi-camera rigs to capture faster 4D motion at the same frame count.

title: Contactless Estimation of Respiratory Frequency Using 3D-CNN on Thermal Images
summary: Monitoring physiological parameters such as respiratory rate ($f_R$) is essential for diagnosing and managing various pathological conditions. Thermal imaging offers a promising contactless alternative to traditional methods, which often rely on partially invasive sensors or obtrusive wearable systems. However, existing approaches for $f_R$ estimation from thermal signals typically require extensive pre-processing and manual or semi-automatic region-of-interest (ROI) tracking, limiting their practical applicability. This study proposes a deep learning-based method for estimating $f_R$ directly from thermal videos, eliminating the need for complex pre-processing and ROI tracking. A 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) is developed to operate on raw thermal video data. To address challenges related to small datasets, the model is trained using data augmentation and transfer learning from synthetic datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a validation $R^2$ score of approximately 0.61 on both pre-processed and raw thermal videos. By simplifying the workflow, this method holds promise for enhancing the feasibility of thermal imaging in real-world applications, such as remote healthcare and driver monitoring in automotive applications.

AI.tldr: A 3D-CNN trained with data augmentation and synthetic transfer learning estimates respiratory frequency directly from raw thermal videos without ROI tracking, achieving an R^2 score of approximately 0.61.
AI.motivation: Existing contactless respiratory rate estimation methods from thermal imaging rely on extensive pre-processing and manual or semi-automatic region-of-interest (ROI) tracking, limiting practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors develop a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) that operates directly on raw thermal video data, using data augmentation and transfer learning from synthetic datasets to overcome small-dataset limitations.
AI.result: Experimental results show the 3D-CNN achieves a validation R^2 score of approximately 0.61 on both pre-processed and raw thermal videos.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating ROI tracking and complex pre-processing simplifies thermal respiratory monitoring, making it more feasible for remote healthcare and automotive driver monitoring.

title: Fast Self-Supervised Generative CT Denoising via Few-Step Sampling
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Xingyi Yao and Zhengtao Ma contributed equally to this work. Zhennong Chen is the corresponding author
summary: Low-dose and thin-slice computed tomography (CT) images suffer from elevated noise that obscures anatomical detail, while clean references for supervised denoising are often unavailable. Although Noise2Noise permits self-supervised training from noisy pairs, direct regression tends to oversmooth fine structure. Averaging multiple independently generated samples mitigates this blur, though repeating multi-step diffusion sampling is costly. We introduce Noise2Noise with Improved Mean Flow (N2N-iMF) to accelerate this process via few-step sampling. N2N-iMF learns to generate one noisy image conditioned on its paired counterpart; at inference, independent outputs are sampled and averaged to suppress noise. We evaluated image quality and sampling efficiency on simulated thin-slice brain and low-dose abdominal CT across four sampling methods and averaging counts from 1 to 20, and validated the approach on real-world photon-counting CT (PCCT) brain scans. With ten samples per conditioning input and three network evaluations per sample, N2N-iMF achieved a mean absolute error of 2.60 HU on brain CT and 14.02 HU on abdominal CT, outperforming 50-evaluation denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) sampling (2.91 and 14.53 HU). On the same GPU, per-output generation time dropped from 7.29 to 0.43 s. Across eight PCCT cases, N2N-iMF reached a mean gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio of 1.341, versus 0.916 for Noise2Noise and 1.176 for DDIM. N2N-iMF accelerates self-supervised generative CT denoising without distillation while keeping the number of averaged outputs adjustable at inference.

AI.tldr: Noise2Noise with Improved Mean Flow (N2N-iMF) enables fast, self-supervised generative CT denoising via few-step sampling, outperforming 50-step DDIM in both image quality and speed.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised Noise2Noise regression oversmooths fine CT structures, while averaging multiple samples from multi-step diffusion models to reduce blur is computationally expensive.
AI.method: N2N-iMF learns to generate one noisy CT image conditioned on its paired noisy counterpart using Improved Mean Flow for few-step sampling, averaging multiple independent outputs at inference to suppress noise.
AI.result: With 10 samples and 3 network evaluations per sample, N2N-iMF achieves 2.60 HU MAE on brain CT and 14.02 HU on abdominal CT (versus 2.91 and 14.53 HU for 50-step DDIM), cuts per-output generation time from 7.29 s to 0.43 s, and reaches 1.341 gray-white matter CNR on real PCCT brain scans (versus 0.916 for Noise2Noise and 1.176 for DDIM).
AI.conclusion: N2N-iMF accelerates self-supervised generative CT denoising without distillation while allowing adjustable sample averaging at inference.

title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
summary: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

AI.tldr: EgoCaptioner combines a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline of 50,000 egocentric examples with GRPO-based factual and temporal rewards to achieve leading fine-grained egocentric video captioning.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal large language models often miss brief actions, confuse event order, or misinterpret wearer motion in egocentric videos, and existing caption formats poorly integrate detailed narration with precise timing.
AI.method: EgoCaptioner pairs a video-level overview with timestamped steps, trained on 50,000 coarse-to-fine annotated examples (supplemented with pose-derived motion facts when available) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rewards for factual accuracy, temporal alignment, and non-redundancy.
AI.result: Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner leads evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned QA, and temporal alignment, and outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego.
AI.conclusion: Coarse-to-fine supervision combined with complementary factual and temporal RL rewards substantially improves fine-grained, time-aligned egocentric video captioning.

title: SEEC: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Self-Supervised External-Eye Representation Learning
summary: External-eye photography captures clinically relevant periocular anatomy at low acquisition cost, yet no large-scale standardized resource exists for evaluating self-supervised external-eye representations. We introduce a 4.35-million-image Standardized External-Eye Corpus (SEEC) derived from fourteen heterogeneous public face datasets, together with a benchmark for external-eye representation learning. For evaluation, we provide held-out evaluation distributions, landmark-annotated anatomical probe sets, and clinical disease-classification experiments spanning ptosis, thyroid eye disease, and craniofacial syndromes. We evaluate representations at two complementary levels: (a) the representation level, by assessing embedding geometry across multiple data distributions, and (b) the functional level, by assessing anatomical recovery, out-of-distribution anatomical transfer, and disease classification. Our models include ResNet-101 and ViT-B encoders pretrained using InfoNCE, VICReg, and LeJEPA objectives and compared with DINOv2 and MAE. Our results indicate that representation-level and functional-level evaluations are dissociable: broader embedding-space utilization does not consistently correspond to anatomical transfer or disease-classification performance, and no single encoder is universally optimal. Domain-specific external-eye encoders outperform DINOv2 and MAE on cross-dataset anatomical transfer despite being pretrained at substantially smaller scale, while external-eye-pretrained ViT models match or outperform these general-purpose baselines on frozen disease-classification probes. We release benchmark code, evaluation scripts, and preprocessing pipelines to reproduce SEEC at this https URL

AI.tldr: SEEC is a 4.35-million-image standardized external-eye corpus and benchmark showing that domain-specific self-supervised encoders outperform general-purpose baselines on anatomical transfer and match or beat them on disease classification.
AI.motivation: External-eye photography captures clinically important periocular anatomy, but no large-scale standardized resource existed for evaluating self-supervised external-eye representations.
AI.method: The authors curate SEEC (4.35M images from 14 public face datasets) with held-out distributions, landmark probes, and disease classification (ptosis, thyroid eye disease, craniofacial syndromes), evaluating ResNet-101 and ViT-B encoders pretrained with InfoNCE, VICReg, and LeJEPA against DINOv2 and MAE.
AI.result: Representation-level embedding geometry and functional-level performance are dissociable; domain-specific encoders outperform DINOv2 and MAE on cross-dataset anatomical transfer despite smaller pretraining scale, and external-eye ViTs match or beat them on frozen disease probes.
AI.conclusion: SEEC establishes a standardized benchmark for periocular representation learning and demonstrates the value of domain-specific pretraining over general-purpose vision models.

title: GateTrace: Where Do Crowd Crossings Go Missing Under Occlusion?
summary: At large events, pedestrian tracking supports entrance and passageway counts, but totals hide which crossings were missed. In a stadium study, the system recorded about four in five clearly visible crossings but fewer than one in three mostly obscured crossings. The videos lacked trajectories annotated across frames, so we turned to MOT20, which provides pedestrian trajectories and visibility. We introduce GateTrace to locate missed crossings and assess changes to counting rules. It derives reference crossings from annotations under fixed rules, matches reports by person, direction, time and position, and traces misses through saved boxes and counting decisions. With a shared detector, ByteTrack, OC-SORT and BoT-SORT recover 38.9-46.7% of low-visibility reference crossings on development sequences, versus 98.1-99.0% at high visibility. The gap recurs on two further sequences under a protocol fixed in advance. Published outputs of MOT20-tuned BASE recover 63-78% at low visibility across both sequence groups. Losses stop at different stages across systems. Across four systems and both groups, 47-79% of low-visibility misses have no nearby output linked to the person or no possible crossing in the saved tracks. Removing later checks from BASE on development sequences leaves most misses unresolved and lowers precision against the fixed reference list from about 96% to 77%. Misses also remain among sampled reference crossings that two human annotators supported after checking the videos. GateTrace shows where crossings are lost and measures the recovery and precision costs of changing later checks. We will release the code and per-crossing records.

AI.tldr: GateTrace is a diagnostic framework that traces missed crowd crossings in MOT20 under occlusion, revealing that 47-79% of low-visibility misses lack any nearby tracker output or valid crossing track.
AI.motivation: Pedestrian tracking systems miss many obscured crossings at large events, but aggregate counts hide where and why crossings are lost across detection, tracking, and counting stages.
AI.method: GateTrace derives reference crossings from MOT20 annotations under fixed rules, matches reports by person, direction, time, and position, and traces misses through saved bounding boxes and counting decisions across ByteTrack, OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, and BASE.
AI.result: With a shared detector, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and BoT-SORT recover 38.9-46.7% of low-visibility crossings versus 98.1-99.0% at high visibility, while MOT20-tuned BASE recovers 63-78%; across all four systems, 47-79% of low-visibility misses have no nearby linked output or possible crossing in saved tracks, and removing BASE's later checks drops precision from ~96% to 77%.
AI.conclusion: GateTrace pinpoints where crowd crossings fail under occlusion and quantifies the recovery-precision trade-offs of modifying post-tracking counting rules.

title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
summary: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: ViDecide trains video diffusion models as causal step-by-step decision makers with Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), achieving an 83.8% strict success rate on multi-step reasoning and planning tasks.
AI.motivation: Video generation models frequently violate physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning because conventional training treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a sequence of decisions.
AI.method: ViDecide trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop using a decision-focused schedule, paired with Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT) that maps failed decision noise to successful continuations without policy-gradient optimization.
AI.result: Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a multi-step robot planning benchmark, ViDecide achieves an 83.8% average strict success rate, compared to 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, while generalizing to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.
AI.conclusion: Framing video generation as causal decision-making with corrective fine-tuning unlocks reliable visual reasoning and planning in video diffusion models.

title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
summary: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Edit-Ready Training (ERT) prepares vision models for LLM-driven weight-space programming by rehearsing closed-form weight edits, substantially improving LLM edit success on relabeling and error-correction tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs can directly modify neural network weights in weight-space programming, but it was unknown how dedicated network training affects the success of such edits.
AI.method: The authors introduce a benchmark of over 2,600 LLM-driven weight edits by five LLMs on CNNs and ViTs across Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS, and Entity-30, and propose Edit-Ready Training (ERT), which rehearses the direct closed-form weight edits performed by LLMs.
AI.result: Preparing networks for editing substantially raises LLM edit success where standard networks fail, and ERT achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Training networks to be edit-ready makes LLM-driven weight-space programming significantly more reliable and effective.

title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding
summary: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

AI.tldr: WeMM-Video is a family of bilingual omni-modal foundation models (2B to 35B-A3B) supporting hybrid thinking across text, image, audio, and video, setting a new open-source state of the art in omni-modal video understanding.
AI.motivation: Joint audio-visual perception and reasoning in video understanding remains a central challenge for open-source multimodal models.
AI.method: Trained on ~1.2 trillion tokens via progressive pre-training and multi-stage post-training (multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL), WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video in a hybrid-thinking architecture with both fast non-thinking and step-by-step thinking modes.
AI.result: Evaluated on over 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video-35B-A3B sets a new open-source state of the art, outperforming Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 and narrowing the gap with Gemini-3.0-Flash, while WeMM-Video-9B surpasses Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct.
AI.conclusion: WeMM-Video advances open-source omni-modal video understanding and reasoning across multiple model scales.

title: AdaPixFlow: Learning Continuous-Time 3D Dynamics Across Scenes from Sparse Multi-view Observations
summary: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Pixel Flows (AdaPixFlow) learns a cross-scene continuous-time 3D dynamics operator from sparse multi-view RGB-D observations, outperforming per-scene and competing methods on in-between and future motion prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic 3D scene methods either require slow per-scene velocity field optimization or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions that limit generalization.
AI.method: AdaPixFlow fuses multi-view RGB-D observations into a shared world-coordinate voxel grid and predicts a continuous-time 3D velocity field trained across scenes to learn generalizable motion priors without per-scene optimization.
AI.result: On held-out PhysInOne scenes, AdaPixFlow improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5% for in-between prediction and 15% for future prediction (and by 30% and 85% over per-scene velocity fields), and improves future-prediction F1 by 12% zero-shot on Spring-Gaus.
AI.conclusion: Learning a cross-scene continuous-time dynamics operator enables accurate, generalizable 3D motion prediction from sparse multi-view observations.

title: HumanCOIN: A 12,500-Hour Dataset for Human Intent in Egocentric Manipulation
comment: 41 pages, 10 figures, Project page: this https URL
summary: First-person manipulation datasets treat the observation-action pair as the atomic unit and compress the generation and execution of an action into a policy network's weights, rendering the intent state behind the action unobservable. Human motor control research shows that intent mediates between observation and action and leaves observable traces along the intent pathway from decision to effect: gaze reaches the target before the hand, muscle load builds before contact, and cortical activity precedes the motor command. To record this pathway at scale, we present HumanCOIN, a first-person manipulation dataset built around human intent: 12,500 hours across 38 scene classes with three tiers of proxies. At the output end, the L1 attention tier (10,000 h) infers gaze from headband camera video, exposing the operator's next object of attention and reach before the hand moves. Midway, the L2 exertion tier (2,000 h) records surface EMG from armbands, making load expectations readable before execution is complete. At the origin, the L3 cognition tier (500 h) records scalp EEG, giving early readouts of task decisions and monitoring. Each tier inherits all proxies from the tiers below. The dataset further provides multi-view RGB images, depth maps and point clouds, 6-DoF head and wrist pose, and step-level action and object annotations. The controlled L3 setting additionally measures gaze, hand pose and finger kinematics directly. Clock and calibration data are released with the dataset so that any read rate can be re-aligned. The three tiers cover three stations, from visual orienting to cortical preparation, making the process behind visual-action pairs available for modeling at dataset scale. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: HumanCOIN is a 12,500-hour egocentric manipulation dataset that captures three tiers of human intent proxies—gaze, surface EMG, and scalp EEG—alongside multi-view RGB-D and 6-DoF pose.
AI.motivation: Existing first-person manipulation datasets only record observation-action pairs, leaving the underlying human intent state that mediates between observation and action unobservable.
AI.method: HumanCOIN spans 12,500 hours across 38 scene classes in three hierarchical tiers: L1 attention (10,000 h, gaze inferred from headband video), L2 exertion (2,000 h, surface EMG from armbands), and L3 cognition (500 h, scalp EEG plus direct gaze and finger kinematics), all with multi-view RGB-D, 6-DoF head/wrist pose, and step-level annotations.
AI.result: The dataset provides synchronized, re-alignable multi-modal recordings from visual orienting to cortical preparation, making the full intent-to-action pathway available at dataset scale.
AI.conclusion: HumanCOIN enables large-scale modeling of human intent in egocentric manipulation beyond simple observation-action pairs.

title: Asuka-FM: A System-Architectural Co-Design Framework for Efficient Text-to-Image Pretraining on Consumer Hardware
comment: 40 pages, 19 figures, 17 tables. Project page: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
summary: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.

AI.tldr: Asuka-FM is a system-architectural co-design framework that pretrains a 206M-parameter dual-stream DiT text-to-image model from scratch on a single RTX 4090 in ~160 GPU hours for under $55.
AI.motivation: Frontier text-to-image DiTs require massive compute clusters, and training them on a single consumer GPU is bottlenecked by quadratic attention costs, JIT graph breaks from variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and frozen VAE throughput.
AI.method: Asuka-FM combines an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone, Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50%, continuous aspect-normalized RoPE with shifted square crop training for static tensor shapes, and a 10M-parameter Patch Detailer Head for pixel adaptation.
AI.result: Without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 at 512px, trained on a single consumer GPU for under $55.
AI.conclusion: Asuka-FM establishes a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic text-to-image foundation model pretraining on consumer hardware.

title: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: R2-VLA is a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented Vision-Language-Action framework that calibrates an uncertainty predictor to decide when to act autonomously or request expert help, improving task success by 9.2-11.2 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Even when retrieval-augmented VLA models retrieve relevant expert demonstrations at test time, they can fail to use them effectively, leading to task failures without a mechanism to guarantee reliability.
AI.method: R2-VLA trains an uncertainty predictor over VLA actions conditioned on retrieved demonstrations, applies a task-level risk-control procedure to calibrate the autonomy threshold to a user-specified failure risk, and continually adds expert corrections to retrieval memory.
AI.result: Across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites, R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2 to 11.2 percentage points while meeting target success rates with fewer expert requests.
AI.conclusion: Coupling retrieval-augmented test-time adaptation with calibrated risk control enables reliable, human-in-the-loop robotic manipulation.

title: Fixing the Last Mile: Failure-Aware Image Restoration with Region-Specific Guidance
summary: Recent advances in image restoration have greatly improved global image fidelity, producing visually plausible results across most regions of an image. Nevertheless, even high-quality restorations often exhibit localized failures, including artifacts in semantically important regions such as faces and text, structural inconsistencies, and texture mismatches. Although these errors typically affect only a small portion of the image, they often dominate the overall perceptual quality of the result. In this work, we propose Failure-Aware Image Restoration (FAIR) to address the "last-mile" problem in image restoration. Rather than applying one uniform generative prior over the whole image, we condition a single-pass restoration model on both where local failures are likely to occur and what corrective guidance each region requires. This region-bound conditioning enables fine-grained and controllable restoration that improves semantic accuracy and stylistic consistency in critical regions while maintaining faithful, high-quality restoration elsewhere. Our method complements existing restoration pipelines by shifting the emphasis from global fidelity to local perceptual acceptability. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach resolves common failure cases and improves perceptual quality, bridging the gap between technical accuracy and practical usability.
