AI.tldr: Failure-Aware Image Restoration (FAIR) conditions a single-pass restoration model on predicted failure locations and region-specific corrective guidance to fix localized artifacts in faces, text, and textures.
AI.motivation: Modern image restoration models achieve high global fidelity but still suffer from localized failures in semantically critical regions like faces and text that dominate human perception.
AI.method: Instead of applying a uniform generative prior globally, FAIR conditions a single-pass restoration model on both where local failures are likely to occur and what corrective guidance each region requires.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show FAIR resolves common localized failure cases and improves perceptual quality, semantic accuracy, and stylistic consistency while preserving global restoration fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Region-bound failure-aware conditioning bridges the gap between global technical accuracy and local perceptual acceptability in image restoration.

title: SHUSH: Emission-Aware Reward Design for Proactive Video Assistants
summary: Proactive video assistants must decide not only what to say, but also when to speak. Existing reinforcement-learning objectives can reward timely, correct responses without accounting for response volume, thereby encouraging unnecessary or repeated emissions. We identify this failure mode in MMDuet2, whose proactive area-under-the-curve (PAUC) reward promotes timely responses but does not price the number of emissions. We show analytically that this makes additional responses weakly penalized or effectively free, systematically encouraging over-emission. We then propose an emission-aware F1 reward for interval-valued annotations, using exclusive span--emission matching to price false emissions and missed spans. Under MMDuet2's training recipe, our policy on the visual subset of OmniPro replies 2.5x less often than MMDuet2 while raising timing F1 from 0.259 to 0.396 and content-aware F1 from 0.103 to 0.154; a more conservative variant cuts replies by 82.5% and raises precision from 0.161 to 0.418. On ProactiveVideoQA, the same reward adds replies where the baseline is nearly silent, and PAUC ranks a heavily over-emitting policy second despite near-last F1, because it is insensitive to response count. Our results indicate that proactive assistants should be trained and evaluated with objectives that price emissions.

AI.tldr: SHUSH introduces an emission-aware F1 reward for proactive video assistants that prices false emissions, cutting unnecessary replies by 2.5x while boosting timing F1 from 0.259 to 0.396 on OmniPro.
AI.motivation: Existing RL rewards like MMDuet2's proactive AUC (PAUC) reward timely responses without penalizing response volume, causing proactive video assistants to over-emit.
AI.method: The authors prove PAUC leaves extra emissions weakly penalized or free, and propose an emission-aware F1 reward for interval-valued annotations using exclusive span-emission matching to penalize both false emissions and missed spans.
AI.result: On the OmniPro visual subset under MMDuet2's recipe, SHUSH replies 2.5x less often while raising timing F1 from 0.259 to 0.396 and content-aware F1 from 0.103 to 0.154 (a conservative variant cuts replies by 82.5% and raises precision from 0.161 to 0.418), and also adds needed replies on ProactiveVideoQA.
AI.conclusion: Proactive video assistants must be trained and evaluated with emission-aware objectives that explicitly price response volume.

title: SGAR: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction via Sparse Geometry-Guided Attention
summary: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.

AI.tldr: Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) replaces dense global attention in feed-forward 3D reconstruction with learned geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention, running up to 12x faster at 1,000 views.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models rely on dense global attention across all view patches, whose quadratic cost prevents scaling to large numbers of views.
AI.method: Motivated by structure-from-motion, SGAR uses a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity so each patch token attends only to a small set of geometrically relevant tokens from other views, applicable to existing models via fine-tuning.
AI.result: SGAR is the fastest among state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse method, running up to 12x faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail.
AI.conclusion: Guiding sparse attention with learned 3D geometric proximity enables feed-forward 3D reconstruction to scale efficiently to thousand-view settings.

title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
comment: The Project Page is: this https URL. The Paper is published in ACM TOG (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026)
summary: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Direct3D-V3 is a latent-free diffusion transformer that directly models raw SDF voxel grids with manifold regularization and rendered normal supervision, yielding richer local 3D geometry.
AI.motivation: Existing native 3D generation methods compress geometry into a latent space via VAEs, introducing a reconstruction bottleneck that limits fine local detail.
AI.method: Direct3D-V3 discards the VAE and trains a DiT directly on raw SDF voxel grids, using implicit manifold regularization to suppress non-watertight surfaces, Marching Cubes with rendered normal losses for direct supervision, and auxiliary camera parameter prediction for better image alignment.
AI.result: Direct3D-V3 removes the VAE reconstruction bottleneck to produce meshes with substantially richer local detail, and extends to generative reconstruction by interleaving diffusion with normal-guided refinement.
AI.conclusion: Operating directly in the native voxel domain offers a simpler, higher-detail alternative to latent diffusion for 3D generation and reconstruction.

title: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
comment: NeurIPS 2026, Project Page: this https URL
summary: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Plan4D stitches Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and an auxiliary DPT scene-flow head to build a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos alongside dense 4D geometry.
AI.motivation: Most video world models prioritize visual aesthetics but lack explicit 4D modeling, resulting in weak physical grounding and poor geometric consistency over time, while paired action-4D training data is scarce.
AI.method: Plan4D couples the complementary priors of Depth Anything 3 and LongCat-Video via a model-stitching architecture augmented with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction, conditioned on scene context and text-specified actions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show Plan4D achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions, improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy over long horizons.
AI.conclusion: Stitching pretrained video generators with 3D reconstructors enables physically grounded, plannable 4D world models without massive paired 4D-action datasets.

title: Deterministic Temporal Embedding for Calcium Imaging Trace Extraction
summary: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.

AI.tldr: A deterministic temporal embedding framework extracts calcium imaging fluorescence traces without stochastic negative sampling or shape priors, robustly recovering irregular and touching cells.
AI.motivation: Extracting calcium-dependent fluorescence traces requires grouping pixels with coherent temporal activity, which is challenging for irregular or spatially touching cells without imposing rigid shape priors.
AI.method: Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, the method optimizes a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of dense repulsion with sparse edge compensation, then spatially decodes the latent representation.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data show robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources with efficient deterministic optimization.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic particle-mesh temporal embedding provides a reliable, shape-prior-free approach for calcium imaging trace extraction.

title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
comment: BMVC 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

AI.tldr: AURA is a causal, audio-driven streaming avatar video diffusion model that uses a rolling KV cache and two-stage distillation to stream 576p video at 20.7 fps (1.3B) and 720p at 9.7 fps (5B) on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-driven video diffusion models require dozens of denoising steps and multi-second audio look-ahead over long chunks, making them too slow and high-latency for real-time streaming avatars.
AI.method: AURA generates video chunk-by-chunk using only current-chunk audio and a rolling KV cache, trained via a two-stage distillation pipeline: trajectory alignment with chunk-wise sliding-window causal attention, followed by Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation.
AI.result: On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its bidirectional teacher (20.7 fps at 576p) and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster (9.7 fps); weights and a 30K synthetic video dataset are released.
AI.conclusion: Causal chunk-wise distillation with a rolling KV cache enables real-time, low-latency streaming talking-head generation on a single GPU.

title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning
summary: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.

AI.tldr: A pathology foundation model with attribute-aware multiple instance learning grades Barrett's esophagus dysplasia across four institutions without stain normalization, achieving 0.96 macro-AUC on a held-out test set.
AI.motivation: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers from high inter-observer variability, and prior automated systems often require site-specific stain normalization that limits multi-institutional deployment.
AI.method: Using 969 H&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions, patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identify diagnostic regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification into NDBE, low-grade, or high-grade dysplasia.
AI.result: On a held-out test set (n=130), the system achieves 0.96 macro-AUC (95% CI 0.93-0.98), 98% sensitivity and 81% specificity for binary dysplasia detection, 0.83 quadratic-weighted kappa against expert consensus, zero high-grade cases misclassified as NDBE, and consistent performance across institutions without stain normalization.
AI.conclusion: Stain-robust pathology foundation model representations can eliminate site-specific preprocessing and enable reliable multi-institutional dysplasia grading.

title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
summary: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

AI.tldr: Coda-DaVinci is a task-adaptive agentic Code2Video framework that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts 3D proxy granularity per entity, and coordinates physics simulation with visual inspection.
AI.motivation: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to control video generation, but optimal proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting strategies remain underexplored.
AI.method: Informed by controlled experiments showing coarse proxies favor natural motion while medium-grained proxies favor consistency, Coda-DaVinci adaptively chooses proxy-guided vs. direct generation, tailors entity granularity, aligns prompts with proxies, and uses a multi-agent harness with visual inspection for repairs.
AI.result: Coda-DaVinci achieves leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improves physical plausibility over direct generation, and surpasses compared Code2Video baselines in visual realism, while long-video tests reveal remaining transition stability limits.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive proxy granularity and multi-agent visual verification significantly improve controllable Code2Video generation.

title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
comment: Code and weights available at this https URL
summary: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at this https URL

AI.tldr: Depth Pro 2 is a single scalable network for both images and video that predicts native-resolution metric monocular depth, achieving sharpness, metric accuracy, and temporal consistency simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Prior monocular depth estimation methods trade off temporal consistency against boundary sharpness, with multi-frame models favoring consistency and single-frame models favoring sharpness.
AI.method: Depth Pro 2 trains a single scalable network jointly on images and video to predict dense metric depth maps at native full resolution.
AI.result: Depth Pro 2 outperforms prior work across metric accuracy, boundary sharpness, and temporal consistency simultaneously, establishing a new Pareto frontier in accuracy, quality, and runtime.
AI.conclusion: A unified, native-resolution image-and-video architecture resolves the sharpness-versus-consistency trade-off in metric monocular depth estimation.

title: ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement
summary: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. {Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

AI.tldr: ScaleWorld unifies low-resolution world prediction and one-step high-resolution refinement in a single causal video backbone using task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD).
AI.motivation: Directly generating high-resolution world videos incurs heavy compute and memory costs, while using a separate refinement model adds architectural overhead.
AI.method: For each video chunk, ScaleWorld's shared backbone first performs low-resolution prediction with a long causal history and then one-step high-resolution refinement with a short history, consolidated from specialized teachers via task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD) using local velocity matching.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ScaleWorld achieves high-quality, high-resolution world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a single causal backbone for prediction and refinement via TA-OPD enables efficient high-resolution streaming world models.

title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
comment: Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

AI.tldr: O^2LaF repurposes a single pretrained video DiT to initialize both inverse and forward dynamics models for self-supervised latent action learning, setting a new state of the art in few-shot action probing.
AI.motivation: Latent action learning recovers action supervision from unlabeled videos, but existing methods typically learn the underlying world dynamics from scratch.
AI.method: O^2LaF initializes both a feed-forward transition encoder (with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics) and a causal action-conditioned video generator (for forward dynamics) from the same pretrained video DiT, optimizing them end-to-end through a compact bottleneck.
AI.result: Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O^2LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing, improves zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments, and extends competitively to predictive priors like V-JEPA2.
AI.conclusion: Repurposing pretrained video models as shared priors for both inverse and forward dynamics offers a strong paradigm for self-supervised latent action learning.

title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

AI.tldr: Adding a fixed, input-independent set of steering vectors to frozen diffusion transformer blocks recovers 90-112% of RL post-training reward gains, showing RL post-training acts largely as activation steering.
AI.motivation: RL post-training improves text rendering and compositional accuracy in diffusion transformers, which was naturally assumed to require complex, input-dependent weight transformations.
AI.method: The authors fit a fixed set of steering vectors added to block outputs of a frozen base model (0.29M parameters on SD3.5-M vs. 18.8M for RL LoRA) to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, and also train zero-initialized steering vectors directly with online RL.
AI.result: Input-independent steering vectors recover 90.0-96.3% of reward gains across six RL-tuned image models and 89.8% and 111.9% on two video models; when trained directly with online RL on SD3.5-M, they exceed weight-based RL on OCR text rendering and PickScore.
AI.conclusion: Most of the gains from policy-gradient RL post-training in diffusion transformers come from a constant activation shift that steers existing capabilities rather than learning new input-dependent transformations.

title: Posterior Matching Distillation
summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

AI.tldr: Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD) distills diffusion models by matching exponentially tilted posterior means, enabling mode-covering, any-step generation with state-of-the-art 4-step FID on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B.
AI.motivation: Reverse-KL distribution-matching distillation methods suffer from mode-seeking bias that sacrifices sample diversity for dominant teacher modes.
AI.method: PMD supervises a stochastic any-step student by matching exponentially reweighted averages of student samples to exponentially tilted teacher posterior means (computed via a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input), which provably identifies the full conditional posterior without an auxiliary student-score network.
AI.result: On SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B, PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step distillation methods while maintaining competitive or leading prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Supervising conditional posteriors via tilted mean constraints provides a principled, mode-covering alternative to reverse-KL for few-step diffusion distillation.

title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
summary: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.

AI.tldr: Density Feedback Control (DFC) dynamically adjusts the sparsity coefficient per epoch in generator-based sparse adversarial attacks, hitting target perturbation densities in one run and improving transfer ASR.
AI.motivation: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks rely on a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to actual perturbation density shifts during training, requiring manual re-tuning and limiting transferability gains.
AI.method: DFC tightens or relaxes the sparsity coefficient at the end of each epoch based on the gap between observed hard-mask density and the target density, without altering the generator architecture or loss.
AI.result: At a 10% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within 1 percentage point of the target in a single run and improves transfer attack success rate (ASR) for two of them on CNN and Transformer targets while perturbing fewer pixels, though it yields no consistent gain for EGS-TSSA.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop density feedback eliminates manual sparsity re-tuning and improves the pixel-efficiency and transferability of generative sparse attacks.

title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback
summary: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.

AI.tldr: Inhabitant is a training-free agent framework for long-horizon 3D human-scene interaction that uses explicit spatial control and quantitative execution feedback, completing 98.7% of tasks on the new Inhabit benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents struggle with long-horizon 3D human-scene interaction (HSI) because they lack fine-grained spatial control over motion and quantitative feedback on execution failures.
AI.method: Inhabitant specifies each motion via positions, paths, and poses, measures how executed interactions deviate from intent, and iteratively revises control specifications; the authors also introduce Inhabit, a 75-task benchmark across 31 apartment layouts chaining 1-3 object goals.
AI.result: On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7% of tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, 93.3% with Claude Sonnet 5.5, and 82.7% with Gemini 4 Argon, while ablations confirm that removing spatial control causes most tasks to fail and removing quantitative feedback reduces motion precision.
AI.conclusion: Explicit spatial parameterization paired with quantitative execution feedback enables reliable, training-free long-horizon 3D human-scene interaction.

title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
summary: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

AI.tldr: MAWAM is a multi-agent world-action model that jointly denoises future views and executable actions for all robots via cross-agent attention, achieving 67.8% mean success on real-robot coordinated manipulation.
AI.motivation: Coordinated multi-robot manipulation requires predicting how each robot's actions affect the shared physical future in which teammates must act.
AI.method: Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action chunks and future-view tokens using cross-agent attention while keeping separate per-robot control interfaces.
AI.result: MAWAM achieves 67.8% mean success across three real-robot tasks (18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA) and 90.3% mean success across eight simulation tasks with up to four arms; ablations show removing cross-agent attention drops four-arm relay from 95.0% to 39.0%.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling multi-agent future views and actions with cross-agent attention substantially improves coordinated multi-robot manipulation.

title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.

AI.tldr: A new 374,000+ frame video presentation attack detection (PAD) dataset across 1-100 m and two sensor types reveals that lower-resolution mobile sensors degrade sharply beyond 50 m while DSLR maintains high accuracy.
AI.motivation: Deployed face PAD systems assume close-range (<1 m) capture and lack benchmarks covering long standoff distances, diverse environments, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion attacks.
AI.method: The authors collect 374,000+ video frames from 261 identities across five distances (1-100 m) indoors and outdoors using a DSLR and a mobile sensor with three classes (live, spoof, props), and benchmark MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50 on video clips.
AI.result: EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, 2.01% ACER) and 89-94% cross-domain accuracy; while DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof detection across all distances, the mobile sensor degrades sharply past 50 m (MobileNetV3 props accuracy drops to 55% at 75 m).
AI.conclusion: Capture distance and sensor resolution are critical, previously underexplored factors for real-world long-range video PAD.

title: GEMS: Generation and Experience Memory for Subgoal-Guided Long-Horizon World Model Planning
summary: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

AI.tldr: GEMS combines generated temporally structured subgoals with Latent Experience Memory (LEM) via a distance gate for long-horizon world model planning, beating prior baselines by up to 24.0 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Visual world models struggle on long-horizon planning because rollout errors accumulate, while standalone generated subgoals can hallucinate and memory-only subgoals are limited by experience coverage.
AI.method: GEMS generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM), using a distance gate to choose whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state.
AI.result: Across six manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves 92.8% success on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining generated subgoals with experience memory through a distance gate substantially strengthens long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
comment: 42 pages, 6 figures, 15 supplementary figures. Author's version of the article published in Science Robotics. Project page: this https URL
summary: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

AI.tldr: ROAM couples a pretrained Vision-Language Model with open-vocabulary segmentation and simulation-trained RL policies to enable kilometer-scale autonomous legged navigation in alpine and urban environments.
AI.motivation: Autonomous legged navigation in unstructured wild environments requires both high-level semantic reasoning about hazards and signs and robust low-level locomotion over diverse terrain.
AI.method: ROAM uses a VLM to assess risks, interpret signs, and assign semantic navigation costs, converts these via open-vocabulary segmentation into a real-time dense risk map, and conditions two pretrained RL policies for agile locomotion and local planning.
AI.result: Real-world experiments demonstrate kilometer-long autonomous hikes in complex alpine and urban settings with minimal intervention, including sign interpretation and safe foothold selection, while highlighting remaining VLM spatial reasoning limits.
AI.conclusion: Bridging VLM semantic reasoning with RL locomotion policies via real-time risk maps advances open-world legged robot autonomy.

title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
summary: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

AI.tldr: Tripwire-WM is a forgery-evident undetectable watermarking framework that commits image semantics into unused latent noise magnitudes, accepting 0% of imprinting forgeries on MS-COCO while reporting all of them.
AI.motivation: Existing forgery-resilient undetectable watermarks like SemBind still accept many forged images and cannot report forgery attempts, while external detectors suffer from high false-positive rates after common image processing.
AI.method: Tripwire-WM embeds a distribution-preserving commitment of the generated image's semantics into the magnitudes of initial latent noise (left unused by sign-based PRC and Gaussian Shading++ watermarks), enabling the detector to both reject mismatched forgeries and report them.
AI.result: On MS-COCO with the owner's model as surrogate, Tripwire-WM accepts 0% of imprinting forgeries (vs. up to 55.0% for SemBind) and reports 100% of them, accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries (vs. up to 46.2%), and retains >=99% genuine acceptance at 10^-6 FPR.
AI.conclusion: Committing image semantics into unused latent noise magnitudes provides provably undetectable, forgery-evident watermarking for generative image models.

title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
summary: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as this http URL and this http URL do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

AI.tldr: MKA is a 200-task benchmark evaluating multimodal knowledge agents on end-to-end professional deliverables from visually dense files, where top frontier models still score below 57% on frontier criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks rarely require genuine cross-file visual understanding—removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's GDPval score unchanged—leaving multimodal professional knowledge work untested.
AI.method: MKA comprises 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors requiring agents to synthesize visually dense files (CAD blueprints, schematics, radiographs, charts, maps) into .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html, or .png deliverables, graded by a sandboxed agentic autorater (96.2% agreement with human experts, kappa=0.91).
AI.result: Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR, using 5.7x fewer tokens) lead evaluated models, yet all models remain below 57% Climb-WSR.
AI.conclusion: MKA exposes substantial headroom for autonomous agents in visually grounded, multi-file professional knowledge work.

title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: SEANA is a drop-in SSL view-generation module that learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform to resample independent noise, improving cell-cycle classification by up to 28.6 percentage points over standard SSL.
AI.motivation: In noisy scientific imaging like microscopy, self-supervised learning encoders can exploit signal-dependent noise patterns shared across augmented views as a shortcut rather than learning semantic content.
AI.method: SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, estimates the clean signal, and resamples independent noise in VST space to generate noise-aligned SSL views without clean targets or encoder/objective changes.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic noise, SEANA consistently improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy; on real fluorescence imaging, it improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6 pp over standard SSL and 27.5 pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines.
AI.conclusion: Noise-aligned view resampling in learned VST space breaks noise shortcuts more effectively than preprocessing with denoisers.

title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs
summary: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.

AI.tldr: FG-GraphBench benchmarks fine-grained multimodal scene graph understanding across QA, captioning, and description, while FiGRA integrates continuous multimodal graph tokens into MLLMs to outperform strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing scene graph benchmarks lack coverage of fine-grained visual entities and relations, and current MLLMs do not effectively leverage graph-structured representations for fine-grained understanding.
AI.method: The authors build FG-GraphBench via a two-stage entity-grounding and relation-extraction pipeline covering FG-QA, FG-Caption, and FG-Description, and propose FiGRA, which encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens for two-stage MLLM training.
AI.result: Experiments show FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across all three FG-GraphBench tasks, demonstrating the value of preserving fine-grained entity and relation structure.
AI.conclusion: Explicit fine-grained multimodal scene graph representations substantially enhance MLLM visual understanding.

title: Stereo Visual Odometry with In-the-Loop Geometric Feed-Forward Models Towards Dense Metric Mapping
summary: We present a stereo visual odometry (SVO) framework that integrates geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) for dense depth prediction with factor-graph-based visual odometry to achieve accurate localisation and dense metric mapping. Our key idea is to exploit sparse but reliable metric geometry estimated from stereo and temporal multi-view observations to calibrate dense GFM predictions, while retaining the robustness and efficiency of model-based SVO. Rather than directly conditioning the GFM on potentially noisy stereo depth, optimised 3D landmarks are used to jointly estimate a scale-shift transformation over all keyframes within each local submap, yielding metrically consistent dense depth predictions. To balance accuracy and computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical factor-graph architecture. At the local level, sliding-window optimisation estimates high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 3D landmarks. Dense predictions are generated only for selected keyframes and registered within each submap using SE(3) Generalised ICP. Consecutive submaps are further aligned in Sim(3) using their shared geometry, allowing residual scale inconsistencies to be corrected. These intra- and inter-submap constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to produce a consistent trajectory and dense metric reconstruction. Extensive experiments on public and in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines while providing accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to failures in learned depth prediction.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical stereo visual odometry framework calibrates dense geometric feed-forward model (GFM) depth predictions using sparse multi-view 3D landmarks, achieving accurate localization and dense metric mapping.
AI.motivation: Integrating dense learned depth from geometric feed-forward models into stereo visual odometry is challenging due to scale inconsistencies and potential learned-depth failures.
AI.method: Instead of conditioning GFMs on noisy stereo depth, the framework uses sliding-window-optimized 3D landmarks to jointly estimate a scale-shift transform per local submap, aligns keyframes via SE(3) Generalized ICP, and corrects inter-submap scale drift in Sim(3) within a global factor graph.
AI.result: Experiments on public and in-house datasets show competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines alongside accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to learned-depth failures.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating dense GFM predictions with sparse geometric landmarks in a hierarchical factor graph enables robust, metrically consistent dense stereo SLAM.

title: Life-IQA+: Boosting Blind Image Quality Assessment via GCN-enhanced Layer Interaction and Flexible Hierarchical Expert Specialization
summary: Blind image quality assessment (BIQA) is essential for evaluating and optimizing visual experience. Existing BIQA methods typically aggregate features from multiple backbone stages without accounting for their unequal contributions to quality prediction. Furthermore, uniformly supervising all experts may constrain their flexibility and limit the diversity of the learned quality representations. To address these issues, we present Life-IQA+, a quality representation decoding framework that combines graph convolutional network (GCN) enhanced layer interaction and flexible hierarchical expert specialization. Specifically, the layer interaction module constructs quality queries from GCN-refined deepest-stage features and uses penultimate-stage features as keys and values, thereby enabling cross-layer representation interaction via the cross-attention mechanism. Building on these representations, we further introduce a flexible hierarchical mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising a densely activated shared expert layer and a sparsely activated routed expert layer. To enhance the representation diversity and ability of experts, we apply auxiliary classification supervision to a subset of shared experts using distortion-type labels for synthetic datasets and discretized quality-level labels for authentic datasets. Experiments on synthetic and authentic distortion benchmarks, together with controlled ablations of expert configurations and supervision strategies, show that Life-IQA+ achieves competitive prediction accuracy with a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. The code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Life-IQA+ is a blind image quality assessment decoding framework that combines GCN-enhanced cross-layer interaction with a flexible hierarchical mixture-of-experts architecture to achieve competitive accuracy and compute efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing BIQA methods aggregate multi-stage backbone features without accounting for their unequal contributions to quality prediction, and uniform supervision of experts limits representation diversity and flexibility.
AI.method: The layer interaction module builds quality queries from GCN-refined deepest-stage features and attends over penultimate-stage keys and values, followed by a hierarchical MoE with densely activated shared experts and sparsely activated routed experts, plus auxiliary distortion-type or quality-level classification supervision on a subset of shared experts.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and authentic distortion benchmarks and controlled ablations show competitive prediction accuracy with a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Combining GCN-enhanced cross-layer interaction with partially supervised hierarchical MoE experts improves quality representation decoding for BIQA.

title: Trajectory-Calibrated Merging of Embodied Policies
summary: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $\pi_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR) is a gradient-free, execution-aware model-merging framework that consolidates robot specialist policies into a single policy, achieving 77.83% success across 1,200 LIBERO evaluation episodes.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation models adapted into task specialists remain fragmented, and existing merging methods fail in closed-loop execution because parameter-space alignment is an indirect proxy for behavior and standard regression misses uncalibrated states.
AI.method: TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts across execution stages and intermediate iterative action-generation states, recomputes each block's input through already-merged blocks to handle representation shifts, fits merged weights to match experts' linear outputs, and refines the policy with a two-pass calibration using frozen specialists as teachers without changing the inference graph.
AI.result: On LIBERO, merging four pi_0.5 specialists yields 77.83% success over 1,200 episodes, outperforming FeatCal by 9.50 percentage points, RegMean by 24.17 percentage points, and direct weight averaging by 33.00 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Execution-aware, two-pass trajectory calibration enables effective gradient-free consolidation of embodied specialist policies without routing or extra training.

title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
summary: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

AI.tldr: Fitting language world models with a Bradley-Terry objective on comparative feedback can severely distort initially accurate outcome probabilities, shifting 33 to 43 percentage points onto impossible outcomes in a simulated robot push task.
AI.motivation: Comparative feedback is a practical way to train language world models that assign outcome probabilities, but it is unclear whether a Bradley-Terry objective preserves true outcome probabilities.
AI.method: The authors audit readout, response, and decision behavior on a simulated robot push task with enumerated outcome distributions, comparing Bradley-Terry training against its pre-computed optimum and a likelihood objective that knows the judge's rule.
AI.result: Starting from a model with 2.4 percentage points (pp) hazard error on unseen layouts, Bradley-Terry training moves 33 to 43 pp of probability onto outcomes not produced by any enumerated branch (around 29 pp without physically impossible events), costing about 3 pp utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions via false rejects, whereas the judge-aware likelihood learns without this shift.
AI.conclusion: The distortion stems from the Bradley-Terry objective itself rather than the comparisons, highlighting the need for judge-aware likelihood objectives when calibrating world-model probabilities.

title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
summary: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold when task and sensitive labels are associated, and introduces Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE) to preserve task utility while controlling conditional leakage.
AI.motivation: Shared medical-image embeddings can leak sensitive attributes, and standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness, which conflicts with preserving nonzero linear task signal when task and sensitive labels are correlated.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form prediction of global erasure's utility cost and propose TC-LEACE, a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of the fitting data.
AI.result: Across 85 CelebA attribute pairs on four vision foundation models and hospital chest radiographs on three foundation models (including two biomedical models), conditional leakage persists after LEACE, and TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing guardedness within task strata resolves the conflict between concept erasure and task utility in shared foundation-model embeddings.

title: MambaLIFT: Reference-Based Mechanism-Aware Attribution for VMamba
summary: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models remains challenging because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways. We introduce MambaLIFT, a reference-based, multiplier-first attribution framework for VMamba that propagates contributions through its computational graph using interaction-aware rules for selective-scan injection, recurrent memory, LayerNorm, and shared pathways. MambaLIFT decomposes the reference-relative class-logit difference, \(f_c(x)-f_c(x^0)\), by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and computational mechanism. Experiments on ImageNet-1K evaluate VMamba-T and VMamba-B, with hyperparameters selected on a calibration set and faithfulness assessed on a disjoint held-out evaluation set. MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision across audited attribution interfaces in both configurations. Under mean-colour pixel flipping, it achieves significantly higher mean faithfulness scores than MambaLRP on both configurations and the highest scores among the evaluated methods, including Integrated Gradients with matched references. Under blurred replacement, MambaLIFT is non-inferior to MambaLRP on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B, indicating that its advantage depends on the replacement protocol. Ablations on VMamba-T show that interaction allocation, temporal propagation, and pathway composition affect attribution maps. Mechanism-level analyses further show that exact relevance conservation does not imply additive effects under finite interventions: the mechanism decomposition accounts for the reference-relative logit difference but does not estimate intervention effects or establish causal validity.

AI.tldr: MambaLIFT is a reference-based, multiplier-first attribution framework for VMamba that achieves floating-point numerical conservation and higher mean faithfulness than MambaLRP under mean-colour pixel flipping on ImageNet-1K.
AI.motivation: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models is difficult because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways.
