AI.method: MambaLIFT propagates contributions through VMamba's computational graph using interaction-aware rules for selective-scan injection, recurrent memory, LayerNorm, and shared pathways, decomposing the reference-relative class-logit difference by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and mechanism.
AI.result: On ImageNet-1K with VMamba-T and VMamba-B, MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision, outperforms MambaLRP and Integrated Gradients under mean-colour pixel flipping, and is non-inferior on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B under blurred replacement.
AI.conclusion: MambaLIFT provides faithful, mechanism-aware attribution for VMamba while showing that exact relevance conservation depends on replacement protocols and does not imply causal intervention validity.

title: Extending Rademacher Complexity-Based Generalization Theory to Domain Generalization
summary: Domain generalization (DG) aims to train models on multiple source domains with distinct distributions to ensure robust performance on unseen target domains. In doing so, it elevates the concept of generalization from the traditional sample level to the distribution level. Existing theoretical frameworks introduce a domain space endowed with a meta-distribution to extend classical generalization analysis to this new setting. However, these approaches typically treat the domain space as devoid of geometry. In reality, the domain space is an inherently infinite-dimensional, nonlinear abstract space composed of probability distributions, and its complex geometric properties fundamentally determine generalization behavior. Consequently, existing geometry-free theories of domain generalization have a fundamental limitation. They lack a formal characterization of what distinguishes distribution-level generalization from sample-level generalization, leaving the inherent difficulty of generalizing across domains largely unexplained. To bridge this gap, we formalize the domain space as the Wasserstein space over the representation space. Building on the geometric properties of this space (specifically the $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$ curvature theory) we derive a novel, geometry-dependent DG error bound. By introducing an additional curvature-dependent confidence term, this bound formally disentangles the two levels of generalization effects and reveals the essential nature that domain generalization is affected by both the invariance and the curvature of the representation space. Finally, we experimentally validate the effect of curvature on domain generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the domain space as a Wasserstein space with CD(K, infinity) curvature to derive a geometry-dependent Rademacher complexity generalization bound for domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing domain generalization theories treat the domain space as geometry-free, failing to formally distinguish distribution-level generalization from sample-level generalization.
AI.method: The authors model the domain space as the Wasserstein space over the representation space and apply CD(K, infinity) curvature theory to derive a geometry-dependent error bound with a curvature-dependent confidence term.
AI.result: The derived bound formally disentangles sample-level and distribution-level generalization effects, showing that domain generalization depends on both representation invariance and representation-space curvature, which is validated experimentally.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating Wasserstein geometry and curvature into Rademacher complexity theory explains how representation geometry governs domain generalization.

title: CauSyncVLA: Causal Latent World Modeling for Asynchronous Robot Control
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.

AI.tldr: CauSyncVLA is an asynchronous dual-system controller for Vision-Language-Action policies that uses a Causal Latent World Model and Predictive Flow Warm-Starting to reach 93.8% success on LIBERO-10 at 5.04x inference throughput.
AI.motivation: Overlapping visual inference and robot execution reduces waiting in VLA policies but leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected.
AI.method: A Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history via action-sensitive distillation from a frozen expert, while Predictive Flow Warm-Starting aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training.
AI.result: On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA achieves 93.8% success at 5.04x inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and motion smoothness.
AI.conclusion: Predicting latent perceptual memory rather than pixels or physical states enables fast, smooth, and robust asynchronous VLA control.

title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
summary: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.

AI.tldr: QL-VLM is a dynamics-aware quantization and distillation framework for latent chain-of-thought reasoning in VLMs that achieves 90.43% accuracy on ScienceQA-IMG with 4-bit Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and 6.40x lower latency than explicit CoT.
AI.motivation: Latent CoT compresses textual rationales into continuous thoughts, but full-precision models remain expensive and direct 4-bit quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy.
AI.method: QL-VLM combines Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ), using nonuniform codebooks to preserve rotary-key structure for vision-language retrieval, with Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) to align continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher.
AI.result: On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM reaches 90.43% accuracy, improving over the baseline by 40.33% while using 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
AI.conclusion: Preserving retrieval and reasoning dynamics during quantization and distillation makes 4-bit latent CoT practical and accurate for VLMs.

title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting
comment: 38 pages, including supplementary material. Project page: this https URL
summary: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: ProtoCast is an interpretable weather forecasting framework that uses group-specific prototype banks and sparse mixtures of low-rank operators to adapt local features while preserving cross-variable dependencies.
AI.motivation: Neural weather forecasters keep learned patterns implicit, making them hard to interpret and prone to error when locations with different temporal evolutions receive similar forecasts.
AI.method: ProtoCast combines historical features, temporal changes, and cross-variable attention context for evolution-aware prototype matching, applies sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators per group and location before gated attention fusion, and refits prototypes every epoch with slot tracking.
AI.result: Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, and prototype deletion experiments link local feature contributions to prediction error changes.
AI.conclusion: Group-specific prototype-conditioned adaptation improves both accuracy and interpretability in data-driven weather forecasting.

title: Multiple-Camera Tracking of Rigid Objects
summary: In this paper we describe a method for tracking rigid objects using one or several cameras. The tracking process consists of aligning a 3-D model representation of an object with image contours by measuring and minimizing the image error between predicted model points and image contours. The tracker behaves like a visual servo loop where the internal and external camera parameters are updated at each new image acquisition. We study in detail the Jacobian matrix associated with this minimization process in the presence of both point-to-point and point-to-contour matches. We establish the minimal number of matches that are needed as well as the singular configurations leading to a rank-defficient Jacobian matrix. We find a mathematical link between the point-to-point and point-to-contour cases. Based on this link we show that the latter has the same kind of singularities than the former. Moreover, we study multiple camera configurations which optimize the robustness of the method in the presence of single-camera singularities, bad, noisy, or missing data. Extensive experiments done with a complex ship part and with up to three cameras validate the method. In particular we show that the tracker may well be used as a camera calibration procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a visual-servo-style multi-camera 3-D rigid object tracking method using image contours and characterizes its Jacobian singularities and minimal match requirements.
AI.motivation: Tracking rigid objects from image contours requires understanding minimal match counts, singular configurations, and how multiple cameras can overcome single-camera singularities and noisy or missing data.
AI.method: The tracker aligns a 3-D object model to image contours by minimizing point-to-contour image error, updating internal and external camera parameters per frame, while analyzing the Jacobian matrix to link point-to-point and point-to-contour singularities.
AI.result: Experiments on a complex ship part with up to three cameras validate the method's robustness and demonstrate that the tracker can also serve as a camera calibration procedure.
AI.conclusion: Linking point-to-point and point-to-contour Jacobian singularities guides multi-camera configurations that improve tracking robustness and enable calibration.

title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
summary: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

AI.tldr: AFFECT is an auxiliary training objective that teaches world models how small action perturbations change future visual observations, raising real-world DROID policy-evaluation correlation from 0.47 to 0.79.
AI.motivation: Current world models generate realistic videos but often fail to capture how small action changes alter future outcomes, limiting their usefulness for robotic policy evaluation and planning.
AI.method: AFFECT injects temporally correlated noise into actions from a task-agnostic human-teleoperation policy and trains the world model so its generated videos respond to the noise similarly to recorded videos without needing repeated executions from the same initial state.
AI.result: Across OGBench, DROID, and ALOHA-2, AFFECT increases DROID real-vs-world-model policy success correlation from 0.47 to 0.79, lowers FVD by up to 23%, and improves planning task success by up to 8.3%.
AI.conclusion: Matching action-induced visual change distributions makes world-model rollouts substantially more faithful for policy evaluation and model-based planning.

title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
summary: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

AI.tldr: UniVEP unifies endpoint and velocity prediction with consistency supervision in flow-matching robot policies, beating 16-run single-target baselines on RoboTwin with just one StarVLA run (61.36% success).
AI.motivation: Flow-matching robot policies typically use a single prediction target throughout generation, even though high-noise endpoint recovery and low-noise velocity refinement have complementary strengths.
AI.method: UniVEP jointly learns endpoint (X) and velocity (V) targets with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise decreases, requiring only one network run per step.
AI.result: On RoboTwin, UniVEP achieves 61.36% success with one StarVLA run versus 59.96% for the best 16-run single-target baseline, and with LiLa-WAM two runs beat the 16-step baseline while cutting inference latency by 77.1%.
AI.conclusion: Switching between jointly trained endpoint and velocity predictions across noise levels improves both manipulation success and inference efficiency.

title: A Practical Proprioceptive Data Collection Utility for the Unitree GO1
summary: The Unitree Go1 is a widely used platform for legged robotics research, yet collecting proprioceptive data from it is unnecessarily difficult: the Unitree SDK is sparsely documented, and ROS1 (Robot Operating System), the Go1's native middleware, is fully deprecated. We present an open-source graphical utility that enables researchers to reliably record proprioceptive data from the Go1, including joint states, IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) readings, foot force sensor data, and gyroscope measurements, without requiring ROS expertise. The tool provides a simple GUI (Graphical User Interface) for starting, stopping, and labeling recordings in real time. The contribution of this paper is the collection utility. We characterize the acquisition quality of 51 recordings collected with it, including the achieved sampling rate and repeated samples. As a secondary, deliberately modest check that the data is useful, we train a terrain classifier on it. The results are weak: a Temporal Convolutional Network reaches about 38% accuracy on held-out recordings across ten terrain classes (10% would be chance), and a window-level split that ignores recording boundaries inflates the same measurement to about 99%. We report this as a demonstration that the logged signals carry terrain information, not as a competitive classifier. The utility is designed to lower the barrier to collecting Go1 proprioceptive data without ROS.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an open-source GUI utility for recording labeled proprioceptive data from the Unitree Go1 without ROS1 and characterizes 51 collected recordings.
AI.motivation: Collecting proprioceptive data from the Unitree Go1 is difficult because the SDK is sparsely documented and its native ROS1 middleware is deprecated.
AI.method: The authors build a simple GUI to start, stop, and label real-time recordings of joint states, IMU, foot force, and gyroscope data, and evaluate data usefulness with a Temporal Convolutional Network terrain classifier.
AI.result: Across 51 recordings, the TCN achieves about 38% accuracy on held-out recordings over ten terrain classes (versus 10% chance), while a window-level split ignoring recording boundaries inflates accuracy to about 99%.
AI.conclusion: The utility lowers the barrier to ROS-free Go1 proprioceptive data collection and demonstrates that the logged signals carry terrain information.

title: Invertible Transport Between Sample-Only Distributions via Projected Characteristic Functions
summary: Many useful latent distributions can be sampled but do not have a tractable density. Such distributions may be represented by empirical collections of real-world observations or generated by scientific simulators and black-box generative models. These sample-only priors cannot be used directly in likelihood-based normalizing flows, which require evaluating the prior density. We propose Projected Characteristic-Function matching (PCF), a density-free framework for learning an invertible map between a data distribution and a prior specified only through samples. Our method aligns distributions using projected empirical characteristic functions, eliminating the need for density estimation, adversarial training, or paired observations. To address the non-uniqueness of the transport map, we introduce an optional transport regularizer that selects lower-displacement transformations while preserving endpoint alignment. We benchmark PCF on controlled transports, sample-efficiency studies, and high-dimensional alignment tasks. PCF matches the accuracy of kernel MMD on the controlled benchmark and on raw-pixel MNIST--USPS at a cost linear in the batch size, and it is more sample-efficient, achieving lower endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs across library sizes. By avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation, it reduces discrepancy memory by 29.8% and trains at batch sizes where kernel MMD exceeds GPU memory. These results show that PCF provides accurate and efficient invertible transport, particularly in sample- and memory-limited settings.

AI.tldr: Projected Characteristic-Function matching (PCF) is a density-free invertible transport framework for sample-only priors that matches kernel MMD accuracy at linear batch-size cost while reducing discrepancy memory by 29.8%.
AI.motivation: Likelihood-based normalizing flows cannot directly use sample-only priors that lack tractable densities, such as empirical collections or simulator outputs.
AI.method: PCF aligns distributions using projected empirical characteristic functions without density estimation, adversarial training, or paired observations, and includes an optional transport regularizer to select lower-displacement maps.
AI.result: On controlled transports and raw-pixel MNIST-USPS, PCF matches MMD accuracy at linear batch-size cost, achieves lower endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs, and cuts discrepancy memory by 29.8%.
AI.conclusion: PCF provides an accurate, sample-efficient, and memory-light approach for invertible transport between sample-only distributions.

title: Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function Across Architectures
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL, Interactive figures: this https URL
summary: Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this complementary form of transfer through a learn-freeze-transfer protocol, in which the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run, and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activation represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures (standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.

AI.tldr: A learn-freeze-transfer protocol shows that FAct, a five-parameter truncated Fourier activation learned in a ViT on ImageNet-1K, transfers to smaller architectures trained from scratch and improves accuracy by up to 1.71 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Transfer learning typically reuses network weights, leaving open whether a learned activation function alone can transfer and remain effective in different architectures trained from scratch.
AI.method: The authors instantiate the protocol with FAct, a five-parameter two-harmonic truncated Fourier series initialized from GELU, optimize it jointly with a ViT on ImageNet-1K, and freeze it for reuse across four smaller target architectures and four datasets.
AI.result: Reused in a ViT on ImageNet-1K, Frozen FAct improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU; across 16 architecture-dataset settings, it ranks first among 11 activations in 15 of 16 settings under a common config (up to +1.71 pp) and in 11 of 16 settings under per-activation hyperparameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: Learned activation functions can transfer useful inductive bias across vision architectures independently of the weights with which they were trained.

title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
summary: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing this http URL: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that this http URL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. this http URL thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: SKILL.PNG optimizes agent skill images in pixel space via gradient descent through frozen VLMs, outperforming frontier-LLM textual skills in 9 of 16 settings while using 64 to 256 image tokens instead of 900 to 2000 text tokens.
AI.motivation: Textual agent skills are discrete and cannot be continuously optimized, whereas gradient-based finetuning is model-specific and prevents transfer across agents.
AI.method: SKILL.PNG optimizes the pixels of a skill-like image input via gradient descent through a frozen VLM's vision encoder, supporting joint optimization over an ensemble of VLMs and hybrid text-image skills.
AI.result: Across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks, SKILL.PNG outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills in 9 of 16 settings using 64 to 256 image tokens versus roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens, and ensemble-optimized images transfer across models.
AI.conclusion: Pixel-space skill optimization combines continuous gradient-based specialization with cross-model transferability and token efficiency.

title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

AI.tldr: TacInno-VLA uses tactile innovation—contact dynamics unexplained by vision and executed actions—as a discrete auxiliary training target, reaching 87.5% simulation and 70.5% real-world manipulation success without deployment overhead.
AI.motivation: Visuo-tactile VLA models often ignore tactile inputs because much of the tactile signal is predictable from visual observations and executed actions.
AI.method: A tokenizer conditioned on visual observations and executed actions compresses future tactile changes into a discrete code, and TacInno-VLA learns to predict this code during training without adding any module at deployment.
AI.result: TacInno-VLA achieves 87.5% average success across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Supervising VLA policies with unpredictable tactile innovation effectively teaches contact-rich dynamics without extra inference modules.

title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
summary: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

AI.tldr: Awaken-HI pairs a 50,000-hour egocentric stereo video and whole-body human motion dataset (Awaken-Human) with a shared-action-expert VLA that reaches 93.75% mean success across eight humanoid tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing egocentric video datasets lack synchronized whole-body motion data needed to scale humanoid loco-manipulation learning.
AI.method: The authors build Awaken-Human (~50,000 hours, >100 skills) and train Awaken-HI, a VLA with a shared action expert that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions.
AI.result: Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error following a scaling law; after full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves 93.75% mean success across eight tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and pi_0.5.
AI.conclusion: Direct human-trajectory supervision of a shared action expert enables scalable transfer of loco-manipulation skills from humans to humanoids.

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

AI.tldr: Mind2Act World is a 30-task, 180-configuration diagnostic benchmark separating Mind, Act, and Mind2Act composition, revealing that even the strongest agent drops from 52.7% (Mind) and 39.0% (Act) to 12.0% on Mind2Act.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied benchmarks entangle cognitive reasoning and physical execution or test them separately, hiding whether failures stem from reasoning, execution, or their closed-loop composition.
AI.method: Mind2Act World evaluates 30 manipulation tasks across five domains, three difficulty levels, and two scene settings under three views (Mind, Act, and closed-loop Mind2Act) with a diagnostic harness that attributes failures to each component.
AI.result: Evaluating multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs shows single-view competence does not transfer: the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes.
AI.conclusion: Composing reasoning and physical execution through environmental feedback remains the primary open challenge in robotic manipulation.

title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
summary: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

AI.tldr: A graded provenance audit across 19 commercial video-generation APIs shows that passive attribution degrades sharply under re-encoding (83.9% to 45.3%) and only BytePlus authenticates tier claims via C2PA/GB 45438 metadata.
AI.motivation: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, creating risk that intermediaries substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips.
AI.method: The authors combine passive attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes with a survey of C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 endpoints, restricting accusations to authenticated provenance contradictions.
AI.result: Six-model container/bitstream accuracy drops from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988, and only BytePlus authenticates tier claims (187/187 deliveries), with 100/100 signed tier-swap contradictions detected and zero false flags.
AI.conclusion: Passive attribution alone is fragile under post-processing, making cryptographic provenance essential for verifiable tier and origin auditing in video APIs.

title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

AI.tldr: EditSafetyBench (5,940 image-instruction pairs) reveals a systematic text-vision safety mismatch in multimodal image editing systems, where Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1% and 81.6% of unsafe text prompts but only 24.2% and 22.4% of unsafe images with neutral instructions.
AI.motivation: Multimodal image editing safety mechanisms often rely on a single modality and fail to jointly assess risks carried by uploaded images alongside text instructions.
AI.method: The authors construct EditSafetyBench with 5,940 image-instruction pairs spanning 11 risk categories and three edit intents, and evaluate Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local.
AI.result: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1% and 81.6% of unsafe-intent text prompts but only 24.2% and 22.4% of unsafe images paired with neutral instructions; category-level sensitivity varies widely (e.g., GPT allows 70.4% of unsafe political edits vs. 34.8% for Gemini), while sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Image editing systems require safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities.

title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

AI.tldr: Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens) maps intermediate VLM states into the decoder's vocabulary space, revealing selective, task-dependent concept access and cross-modal alignment patterns consistent with Global Workspace Theory.
AI.motivation: VLM outputs do not expose how internal concept representations are selected, integrated across modalities, and used in downstream computation.
AI.method: MC-Lens uses Jacobian-based vision-encoder and language-decoder lenses to project intermediate states to a shared semantic vocabulary space, extending readout carriers to token sets and supporting counterfactual concept interventions.
AI.result: Experiments across VLM families and sizes show that multimodal concepts are readable and selectively accessed by task, counterfactual interventions alter downstream reasoning, and J-space metrics track cross-modal alignment better than hidden-state cosine while showing selective access develops later than accessibility.
AI.conclusion: MC-Lens provides an experimental framework for studying Global Workspace Theory in multimodal systems and guiding cross-modal alignment.

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

AI.tldr: PlayCraft alternates between a vision-based player agent and a crafter agent that revises games for mastery, yielding larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes than initial games and baselines.
AI.motivation: AI-generated games are often playable but not engaging because tuning them for player mastery requires extensive human playtesting.
AI.method: A vision-based player agent plays repeated episodes while recording progress, decisions, and reflections, and a crafter agent uses these reports to estimate player abilities, compare predicted performance against a target learning progression, and revise the game.
AI.result: Evaluated across three player-agent intelligence settings, PlayCraft produces larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games and outperforms baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every setting.
AI.conclusion: Iterative agent playtesting and proficiency-driven revision automate game tuning for player mastery and engagement.

title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
summary: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

AI.tldr: CodeReAct is an LLM-agentic framework for industrial maintenance that standardizes data into business objects and generates executable analysis code via a Thought-Action-Observation loop, demonstrated on multi-year chiller work orders.
AI.motivation: Industrial equipment maintenance requires complex data analysis and work-order prediction that typically depend on manual coding by data scientists.
AI.method: The CodeReAct agent interprets natural language instructions, maps industrial data into standardized business objects (BOs), and runs a Thought-Action-Observation loop that calls analytical APIs and generates executable code.
AI.result: A multi-year chiller maintenance case study shows the agent processes natural language queries to analyze work orders, detect alerts and anomalies, summarize asset status, and recommend work orders, reducing reliance on data scientists.
AI.conclusion: Recontextualizing code-generating ReAct agents around standardized business objects enables autonomous industrial maintenance analytics.

title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
summary: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.

AI.tldr: SailSearch is a human-guided workflow with two LLM agents that discovered the first CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open Market Split QOBLIB instances and built planted-XOR MIS instances where solvers fall 5 to 15 vertices short.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic research in combinatorial optimization can benefit from structured collaboration between human researchers and language-model agents.
AI.method: For Market Split, the agents designed a randomized algorithm searching across multiple lattice bases with enumeration and continued basis reduction; for maximum independent set (MIS), a generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima.
AI.result: On Market Split, the algorithm solved 130 to 133 of 156 QOBLIB instances per seed (10 seeds, 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores), including 18 of 33 previously open instances; on seven MIS instances (1,752 to 3,996 vertices), tested solvers in 8-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the certified optimum.
AI.conclusion: Human-guided dual-LLM workflows can produce competitive combinatorial optimization algorithms and hard certified benchmarks.

title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
summary: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

AI.tldr: BuggyMLE uses a Code Complexity Index (R^2 = 0.951) and controlled bug injection across 222 ML repositories to build BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite (where top solve rates drop from 95% to 9%) and fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to rival frontier models.
AI.motivation: Existing MLE benchmarks restrict agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, while standard SWE benchmarks are saturating.
AI.method: The authors define the Code Complexity Index (CCI) from ten structural features and use agents to inject controlled mutations into 222 ML repositories, creating over 6,600 variants (~260K injected lines), BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, and a three-tier training curriculum over 200 additional repositories.
AI.result: CCI predicts solve rates across eight coding benchmarks (R^2 = 0.951); on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite across 14 models, top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% with difficulty, and fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B rivals frontier models while raising SWE-bench Lite from 24% to 33% and LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.
AI.conclusion: Complexity-guided bug injection provides scalable, difficulty-graded repository-level MLE benchmarks and effective training curricula.

title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Presented as a poster at AIAS+ 2026, San Francisco, California, USA
summary: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.

AI.tldr: DSFlow is a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-workflow agent that pairs LLM-selected reusable skills with deterministic statistical diagnostic guardrails.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM agents lower the barrier to data science tools but lack the statistical control and reliability of formal diagnostic pipelines.
AI.method: DSFlow combines extensible LLM-selected skills with symbolic validation that can accept, clarify, replan, override, or fall back from proposed methods based on deterministic diagnostics, logging decisions in auditable reports.
AI.result: Regression and clustering case studies show DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct unsuitable method choices and document its reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Integrating deterministic statistical guardrails into skill-based LLM workflows bridges flexible automation and statistically sound data analysis.

title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
summary: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

AI.tldr: EverydayBench evaluates live user-facing digital work across 77 human-authored tasks, finding that the top models (Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1) tie at only 54.55% strict pass rate.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for web agents do not jointly evaluate predefined success criteria, live webpage evidence verification, and deliverable quality when multiple valid outcomes exist.
AI.method: EverydayBench spans 77 tasks across eight domains with pre-specified success criteria and combines deterministic constraint checks, live-retrieved webpage claim verification, and rubric-based deliverable scoring.
AI.result: Across 23 agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie at 54.55% strict pass rate, a GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% (low) to 45.45% (max), and task-type leaders vary across lookup, planning, comparison, and customized deliverables.
AI.conclusion: Delivering complete, well-supported outcomes for open-ended everyday digital tasks on the live web remains challenging for frontier agents.

title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.

AI.tldr: Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA) is a causal test-time compute algorithm for time series foundation models that uses rolling-origin backtests to score and average context views, reducing MASE by up to 5.9% on BOOM.
AI.motivation: Test-time compute recipes from language models do not transfer directly to time series forecasting because forecasters must remain causal and cannot use future information to score candidates.
AI.method: BGAA builds a causal verifier from each series's own history using rolling-origin backtests to score structured context views, discards views that underperform the untransformed context, and averages the surviving predictive distributions.
AI.result: BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark pair, cutting MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM (where a 313M model beats 1B and 2.5B models), though window-level oracle view selection on GIFT-Eval shows a 17-19% CRPS gap versus 0.4-1.3% deployed.
AI.conclusion: Causal backtest-gated view averaging improves TSFM accuracy at test time, with window-level view selection remaining a key open challenge.

title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
comment: 66 pages, including appendix. Code: this https URL
summary: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

AI.tldr: An AI-agent multiverse analysis of 324 empirical finance papers across 62,409 specifications reproduces 42% of signed main estimates and finds only 25% of defensible specifications retain the published sign at p < 0.10.
AI.motivation: Reusing natural experiments across many empirical finance papers raises concerns about multiple testing and publication bias, which are hard to audit manually at scale.
AI.method: AI agents rebuild data, reproduce each paper's main estimate, and re-estimate it across grids of 62,409 defensible specifications covering 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments.
AI.result: Agents reproduce 42% of signed main estimates; across defensible specifications, 25% on average keep the published sign with p < 0.10, with regression discontinuity claims more robust than difference-in-differences and higher robustness for first-order effects, larger t-statistics, available code/data, top journals, and earlier papers.
AI.conclusion: Agentic coding makes large-scale multiverse analysis feasible and quantifies how strongly published empirical finance claims depend on analytical choices.

title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
comment: This paper subsumes arXiv:2603.16744. 45 pages, including appendices
summary: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

AI.tldr: Agentic Multiverse Analysis (AMA) deploys coding agents under separation of duties to enumerate, validate, and execute specification grids, reproducing all 10 tested management studies across 1,755 estimates at tens of dollars per paper.
AI.motivation: Observational empirical analyses depend on dozens of hidden defensible analytical choices ("forks"), and human multiverse analysis is too resource-intensive for routine use.
AI.method: Informed by a 150-agent pilot showing agents mirror human fork dispersion, AMA has agents enumerate a paper's fork space, score forks against a validity rubric, run the validated grid, and cross-examine each other under strict separation of duties.
AI.result: Applied to 10 studies (1,755 specification estimates), AMA reproduces every paper's original estimates and distinguishes robust conclusions from those sensitive to undocumented analytical choices, costing hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper.
AI.conclusion: AMA provides a practical, low-cost decision-support instrument for replication policy and AI-assisted peer review.

title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
summary: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic multimodal framework fusing structured EHRs, Bio_ClinicalBERT SVD embeddings, and hybrid-RAG symbolic extraction raises 30-day diabetic readmission sensitivity by 8.28 percentage points (to 0.6667) and eliminates entity hallucinations on Hinglish notes.
AI.motivation: Most 30-day readmission models ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose LLMs parse unreliably.
AI.method: Evaluated on Diabetes 130-US Hospitals (101,766 encounters, patient-grouped 80/20 split), the framework fuses structured features, 32-component SVD-compressed Bio_ClinicalBERT embeddings, and symbolic entities from a three-stage hybrid RAG pipeline with reflective negation auditing into a cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier calibrated by Youden's J.
AI.result: On the held-out test set (n = 20,153), sensitivity rises from 0.5839 to 0.6667 (+8.28 pp), F2-score reaches 0.3824, and Brier score drops from 0.1080 to 0.0977 (at AUROC 0.6375 vs. 0.6477); on 500 code-switched notes, grounded retrieval boosts Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and cuts hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.
AI.conclusion: Grounded symbolic extraction with negation auditing enables reliable multimodal integration of code-mixed clinical notes for readmission prediction.

title: MS-Point: Multi-Modal Hierarchical Spectral Learning for Point Cloud Understanding
summary: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.

AI.tldr: MS-Point is a cross-modal point-cloud pretraining framework that aligns intermediate point features, neighborhood averages, and residuals with image features, improving transfer across classification, few-shot, and dense prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard point-image alignment pools features into global descriptors, causing different local geometric patterns to receive identical alignment signals.
AI.method: At selected encoder stages, MS-Point computes neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling, aligns each branch with visual targets, and coordinates branches via cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion across both graph encoders and point Transformers.
AI.result: Evaluations on object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning—including capacity- and computation-matched controls—show consistent transfer gains over same-backbone baselines.
AI.conclusion: Directly supervising intermediate features and local neighborhood variation yields more transferable, geometry-aware 3-D representations.

title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
summary: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

AI.tldr: Coupling a fixed language model with a general computing device makes AI agent safety undecidable in general, PSPACE-complete under finite bounds, and non-compositional across grouped agents.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents combine language models with general computing environments, raising the question of whether agent safety can be formally verified.
AI.method: The authors analyze the computability and complexity of predicting whether an agent will execute a dangerous program or its semantic equivalent, both in general and under bounded context, values, and runtime.
AI.result: Safety is undecidable in general—meaning guardrails, blacklists, whitelists, and certifications are necessarily imperfect—PSPACE-complete under finite resource bounds even with a known agent description, and non-compositional when safe agents are combined.
AI.conclusion: Formal verification cannot guarantee full safety for general computing agents, motivating practical relaxed notions of safety.

title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: this https URL.

AI.tldr: AppSci-Bench evaluates how well LLMs build and iteratively improve AI agents across seven business domains, finding that the best model (Claude Opus 5.0) achieves only a 59.1% mean-minimum score across three attempts.
AI.motivation: While many benchmarks test AI agents, few measure how well LLMs can act as Applied Scientists to elicit requirements, explore infrastructure, and build and improve agents.
AI.method: AppSci-Bench spans five new domains (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, CRM Insights) and two recast tau3-bench domains (Airline, Banking), each with a custom held-out evaluation suite.
AI.result: Across seven frontier models, Claude Opus 5.0 leads with a 59.1% mean-minimum score over 3 build attempts, achieving only 65% on requirement elicitation, while models saturate their own internal evaluations 65% of the time yet fail on held-out tasks.
AI.conclusion: Eliciting requirements and designing representative internal benchmarks remain major bottlenecks for LLMs building AI agents.

title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
