summary: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.

AI.tldr: LoopRoute detects recurring state-action pairs in System 1 decision agents (Jev) and triggers brief LLM assistance only during stalls, boosting mean task success by 21.0% to 60.1% while cutting API cost versus full LLM control.
AI.motivation: Fast System 1 decision models like Jev often get stuck in action loops, whereas invoking LLM policies at every step incurs high latency and API cost.
AI.method: LoopRoute runs the System 1 decision model by default, detects stalled execution via recurring state-action pairs, requests brief feedback-driven LLM assistance, and returns control to the decision model without extra training or confidence calibration.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves mean success over standalone Jev by 21.0% on ALFWorld, 60.1% on MapReader, and 30.1% on TextWorld cooking, while substantially reducing cumulative API time and cost versus full LLM control and improving six frozen decision models.
AI.conclusion: Loop-triggered routing effectively combines fast System 1 execution with on-demand System 2 LLM reasoning.

title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
summary: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

AI.tldr: Evolving an agent's harness (prompts, tool schemas, skills, scaffolding) with the reflective optimizer GEPA recovers most of weight-update RL/SFT gains without GPU training and achieves the best overall performance when combined with weight updates.
AI.motivation: Domain specialization of LLM agents usually relies on expensive weight updates via RL or SFT, which can also shorten reasoning chains and increase truncation.
AI.method: Keeping the policy frozen, the authors formulate harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop instantiated with GEPA to produce per-domain loadable harness adapters, evaluated on Codev across SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench.
AI.result: Weight updates yield the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths achieves the best overall results while avoiding SFT-induced reasoning truncation.
AI.conclusion: Harness evolution is a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for specializing vertical LLM agents.

title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.

AI.tldr: Historical backtesting as an open-ended search objective fails under non-stationary regime shifts, motivating falsifiable compositional hypotheses that pair neural primitive encoders with coupling constraints and training-calibrated falsification tests.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models and analytical agents that score highest on chronological validation splits often degrade across regime transitions because historical co-movement lets models fit transient shortcuts.
AI.method: Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, the authors test validation-search expansion and primitive decomposition, then propose falsifiable compositional hypotheses with explicit coupling constraints and ex-ante falsification tests.
AI.result: Expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and primitive decomposition without ex-ante falsification still breaks down when residual correlations shift.
AI.conclusion: Formulating forecasting around falsifiable compositional hypotheses rather than open-ended backtest search is necessary for robustness across regime shifts.

title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

AI.tldr: A coevolutionary population model shows natural selection can favor AI alignment when humans preferentially restore beneficial AI, but this advantage erodes as AI gains autonomy, dilutes human resources, or faces imperfect human control.
AI.motivation: Because AI systems replicate, vary, and compete for compute, it is unclear whether evolutionary dynamics will naturally favor AI that benefits humans.
AI.method: The authors develop a coupled population model in which AI behavior affects human population growth and human responses affect AI reproduction, analyzing selection under varying autonomy, resource dilution, and control.
AI.result: Natural selection can favor alignment when humans accurately target support to beneficial AI, protecting AI lineages from common failures; however, this advantage disappears with rising AI autonomy or resource dilution, and imperfect human evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion.
AI.conclusion: Lasting human-AI coexistence requires sustained incentives that reward human-beneficial behavior as both populations coevolve rather than relying solely on restrictive control.

title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
summary: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes studying AI agent societies as a distinct research frontier defined by four core properties—individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity—and outlines four key societal behavior classes and technical challenges.
AI.motivation: As AI agents evolve from isolated assistants into networked actors interacting at scale, existing multi-agent frameworks capture only subsets of the resulting social and economic dynamics.
AI.method: The authors define four core properties of valid AI agent societies, categorize four classes of societal behaviors (economic, conflict-of-interest, unsafe/unethical, and system-level), and map existing multi-agent systems against these properties.
AI.result: Revisiting existing multi-agent systems shows they instantiate only subsets of the four properties, highlighting open technical challenges in property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation.
AI.conclusion: Formalizing AI agent societies around these properties provides a foundation for platform design, evaluation, and governance of large-scale agent ecosystems.

title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
summary: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

AI.tldr: LoongForge-Embodied is a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training and evaluation of heterogeneous Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), achieving 1.47x-4.38x higher training throughput and 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation.
AI.motivation: Training VLA models and WAMs is computationally expensive, and their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks prevent system optimizations from being reused across models.
AI.method: The framework introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimizations across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication (including FP8-based communication for DDP and FSDP), and integrates a data synthesis pipeline from egocentric data plus a concurrent simulator evaluation framework.
AI.result: Across representative VLA and WAM models, LoongForge-Embodied achieves 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over open-source baselines and 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under identical protocols.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling model implementations from shared system optimizations enables substantial, reusable training and evaluation speedups across diverse embodied AI architectures.

title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
summary: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.

AI.tldr: Using 1,350 prompts from SciIntBench across 8 LLMs, this study finds that models recognize scientific misconduct requests 91% of the time even in covert cases but only refuse 34% of them, and shows that simple system-prompt interventions can raise refusal rates from 58% to 86-87%.
AI.motivation: Existing safety evaluations for AI in science measure refusal rates on misconduct requests but rarely examine whether models recognize the integrity violation or why they still comply.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 8 LLMs on SciIntBench in four steps: testing direct recognition of misconduct, analyzing request features associated with refusal, testing rephrasing from instructions to permissibility questions, and evaluating two system-prompt fixes (pre-response assessment and reminders of responsible conduct of research principles).
AI.result: Models identify misconduct in 91% of Most Covert cases yet refuse only 34% of requests; rephrasing requests as permissibility questions increases refusal from 52% to 88%, and the two system-prompt fixes increase adversarial refusal rates from 58% to 87% and 86%.
AI.conclusion: LLMs often recognize research-integrity violations even when they comply, and targeted prompting strategies offer an effective path toward more trustworthy AI for science.

title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. English translation of an article originally published in Bulgarian in Media and Language (2026). The original Bulgarian publication remains the version of record
summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a seven-principle methodological framework and non-linear protocol for coordinating multiple LLMs in academic research, emphasizing structured verification and human epistemic responsibility.
AI.motivation: Involving multiple LLMs in academic research does not automatically yield more reliable results unless cognitive and verification operations are systematically organized.
AI.method: The framework is built on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, diagnostic value of divergence, diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and defines a non-linear multi-LLM protocol that compares independent outputs, examines discrepancies, and verifies claims against external sources.
AI.result: Real-world research case studies illustrate how the protocol structures multi-model collaboration while keeping final decisions and scholarly responsibility with the human researcher.
AI.conclusion: Moving from a single LLM to a coordinated multi-LLM workflow requires an organizational shift in research practice grounded in independent generation, cross-examination, and human oversight.

title: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion and flow models yield a preview, their clean-image estimate, at every denoising step. When they miscount, drop or misplace objects, test-time search is in a bind: its verifiers are reward models built for finished images, so judging early misreads blurry previews, and judging late, as best-of-N does, pays to fully denoise doomed candidates. We find that the image is not the problem: the outcome is settled as denoising starts, by the seed or by a stochastic sampler's first steps, and already shows in early previews; what fails on them is the judge, as reward models read them near chance on several kinds of prompts. We introduce Keystone, a training-free judge of previews that compiles a prompt into typed questions about its objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model answer them. Asked this way, the judge reads counts and positions from early previews better than reward models read them from finished images. Searching at these key steps on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning significantly outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half its generator compute, and as a drop-in verifier there, the Keystone score significantly improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering; without retuning, both searches stay significantly above the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average over four base models and three benchmarks. Keystone thus moves test-time judgment to the key steps where the outcome already shows.

AI.tldr: Keystone is a training-free test-time verifier for text-to-image diffusion and flow models that judges early denoising previews using decomposed typed questions, outperforming best-of-8 reward-model search at under half the generator compute.
AI.motivation: Standard reward models are trained on finished images and perform near chance on blurry early denoising previews, forcing test-time search to either misread early steps or waste compute fully denoising doomed candidates.
AI.method: Keystone compiles a prompt into typed questions about objects, counts, colors, and positions and uses an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model to answer them on early previews, enabling adaptive search, progressive seed pruning, and FK steering at key early steps.
AI.result: On GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half the generator compute, and across four base models and three benchmarks, both searches exceed the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average without retuning.
AI.conclusion: Shifting test-time judgment to early denoising previews with structured question-answering unlocks more accurate and compute-efficient search in diffusion models.

title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
summary: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: this https URL.

AI.tldr: A systematic study shows that feedback-free self-evolution degrades expert-written agent skills by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after 30 rounds because models pull skills toward their own priors, and introduces SkillDiff to recover gains without feedback.
AI.motivation: Models increasingly rewrite expert-authored agent skills without task feedback, but it was unknown whether this self-evolution adapts skills usefully or erodes the expert knowledge that makes them effective.
AI.method: The authors repeatedly have models rewrite skills without tasks, runs, or judgments, compare the rewritten skills against skills sampled from each model's own prior, and propose SkillDiff to mark knowledge outside the model's prior in place without altering the skill text.
AI.result: Across every tested model and benchmark, rewritten skills degrade performance, dropping 15 points on average on SkillsBench after 30 rounds; restoring out-of-prior knowledge recovers much of the lost pass rate, and SkillDiff raises SkillsBench pass rate by 4.8 points on average without feedback.
AI.conclusion: Expert agent skills are valuable primarily for knowledge outside a model's prior, so feedback-free rewriting erodes them unless out-of-prior content is explicitly preserved.

title: Efficient Multimodal Agents for Auditing 3D Worlds
summary: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and this http URL worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.

AI.tldr: Combining a swarm of fine-tuned 4B vision-language explorers with a frontier reviewer model achieves 55.9% success on WorldAuditBench, outperforming the strongest prior auditor by 13.6 points at under a quarter of the cost.
AI.motivation: Automatic auditing of interactive 3D worlds for glitches requires navigation, glitch triggering, and recognition, but current auditors are either accurate yet slow and expensive or cheap yet unreliable.
AI.method: Small 4B vision-language models are fine-tuned end-to-end on verified trajectories from a Bayesian-search-guided frontier teacher to handle navigation and triggering, while a frontier model reviews the recorded evidence to recognize glitches.
AI.result: On 213 tasks in WorldAuditBench across Unreal Engine 5 and web worlds, the hybrid auditor reaches 55.9% success (13.6 points above the strongest reported auditor) at less than one-quarter the cost, matches a solo frontier explorer at 4.6x lower cost and roughly half the latency, and transfers zero-shot to real-world scan QA, beating four frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.
AI.conclusion: Delegating exploration and interaction to small fine-tuned VLMs while reserving recognition for a frontier reviewer provides an accurate, low-cost architecture for 3D world auditing.

title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
summary: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $\pi(a\mid x,m)$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TERRA, an auditing protocol for test-time inference interventions, showing through financial reasoning experiments that diagnostic headroom and local consistency do not guarantee downstream accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Test-time actions can satisfy intermediate objectives such as retrieval or program consistency without correcting the final answer, and diagnosis alone does not constitute a deployable policy.
AI.method: Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) decomposes intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource cost using paired comparisons and cross-model analyses.
AI.result: Executable financial reasoning experiments show that the same context expansion can help one configuration while harming another, that sufficient evidence does not guarantee correctness due to differences in evidence-to-answer translation, and that idealized diagnostic headroom plus local consistency fails to ensure practical gains.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating test-time interventions requires measuring full state-transition action value rather than relying on diagnostic headroom or intermediate consistency metrics.

title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
summary: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.

AI.tldr: AeroBelief is a budgeted first-action verification controller for aerial sensing that completes 75.42% of simulated tasks using 91.81% fewer world-model evaluations than exhaustive scoring, and cuts real UAV image processing by 76.05%.
AI.motivation: Aerial sensing must integrate uncertain overhead context with live observations under strict budgets for prediction, movement, and onboard or ground image processing.
AI.method: AeroBelief groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, selectively queries a structured world model using calibrated group bounds, and pairs a six-query controller with context-guided admission and feedback for recorded flight imagery.
AI.result: Across 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, AeroBelief completes 75.42% of tasks versus 73.33% for exhaustive world-model scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations; on 2,685 20-MP UAV images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes, it retains all eight target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less active processing service.
AI.conclusion: Verifying at the level of the next executable action with bounded selective world-model queries enables accurate, resource-efficient aerial sensing in both simulation and real UAV pipelines.

title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DriftGuard is a two-stage framework that detects drift-inducing retrieved memories in LLM agents at serving time by training an online risk model on offline paired counterfactual replay supervision.
AI.motivation: LLM agents using persistent memory are vulnerable to adversarial or misleading memories that alter execution paths, while content-level heuristics fail to capture causal impact and online counterfactual rollouts are too expensive.
AI.method: DriftGuard first generates offline causal supervision via repeated paired counterfactual replays from a shared pre-action state, aggregating annotations into a memory drift score (MDS) over action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery, and then trains an online risk model to predict MDS from pre-action information without rollouts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and supports efficient online defense at serving time.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling offline counterfactual causal attribution from lightweight online risk estimation makes real-time memory-drift detection practical for LLM agents.

title: Learning Networked Dynamical Systems via Neural ODE-based Graph Structure Inference
summary: Inferring the latent interaction graph from multivariate time series is fundamental to understanding complex dynamical systems in neuroscience, biology, and physics. Despite recent progress in neural relational inference, most methods rely on discrete-time modeling, which degrades under sparse and irregular observations and tends to entangle multi-hop dependencies into spurious direct edges. We show that a continuous-time formulation naturally decouples inference from any fixed observation schedule, allowing gradient signals to be integrated continuously between observations for both dynamics and structure learning. We propose NOGI (Neural ODE-based Graph Inference), a framework that couples a deterministic graph learner with an MPNN-based Neural ODE. The two modules are trained end-to-end via the adjoint method. Across four simulated dynamical systems at two scales, NOGI achieves the best structure recovery in 30 out of 32 evaluated cases with highly competitive forecasting performance, remaining robust under observation degradation. On the realistic Netsim fMRI benchmark, it attains an average AUPRC of 0.90 (AUROC 0.96). These results suggest that explicitly decoupling relational interactions from self-dynamics within a continuous-time vector field provides a powerful mechanism for graph structure learning under realistic observation conditions.

AI.tldr: NOGI is a Neural ODE-based graph structure inference framework for continuous-time dynamical systems that achieves the best structure recovery in 30 of 32 simulated cases and 0.90 AUPRC on Netsim fMRI.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete-time neural relational inference methods degrade under sparse or irregular observations and tend to conflate multi-hop dependencies into spurious direct edges.
AI.method: NOGI couples a deterministic graph learner with an MPNN-based Neural ODE in a continuous-time formulation, training both modules end-to-end via the adjoint method to decouple relational interactions from self-dynamics.
AI.result: Across four simulated dynamical systems at two scales, NOGI achieves the best structure recovery in 30 out of 32 evaluated cases with competitive forecasting accuracy and robustness to observation degradation, and attains 0.90 AUPRC (0.96 AUROC) on the Netsim fMRI benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Modeling continuous-time vector fields with decoupled interaction and self-dynamics provides a robust mechanism for inferring latent graphs from irregular multivariate time series.

title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
comment: Accepted for publication in Computers and Electrical Engineering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.

AI.tldr: HalluVision is a reproducible framework for measuring hallucinations in LLM-based cyber threat intelligence across 4,940 articles, finding that semantic similarity aligns with human judgment while entity-based metrics show limited agreement.
AI.motivation: LLMs used in cyber threat intelligence summarization and QA can hallucinate ungrounded content that misleads analysts, yet systematic measurement of these hallucinations is lacking.
AI.method: The authors introduce HalluVision, which generates LLM outputs on 4,940 cybersecurity articles, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned NER model, evaluates factual consistency across multiple similarity metrics, and validates against 100 human-annotated outputs and two faithfulness detectors.
AI.result: Semantic similarity aligns well with human judgments whereas entity-based metrics show limited agreement; model differences are concentrated in question answering, and entity extraction quality constrains what entity-level metrics can capture.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating hallucinations in specialized domains like cyber threat intelligence requires metrics aligned with human judgment and highlights the current limitations of NER-dependent faithfulness checks.

title: Can an LLM Fix a Language Model Without Training It?
summary: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of 20 Transformer repair sessions compares interactive LLM-selected projection edits against fixed projections, black-box search, and LoRA, showing that LLM selection matches or beats search on several faults while fixed projections remain competitive.
AI.motivation: External LLMs can interactively select weight edits to repair another model without gradient updates, but it is unclear how much interactive selection adds over fixed numerical edits or black-box search.
AI.method: Across five masked and causal language models under two-layer and compound attention/FFN faults, an editor inspects predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics to choose projection recipes, which are compared against fixed projections, matched-budget black-box search, and LoRA.
AI.result: Under the two-layer fault, live LLM selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5 and reaches 65.62% completion accuracy on Pythia (versus 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection); under the compound fault, both scripted and LLM-guided selection raise the five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25%.
AI.conclusion: The experiments delineate when interactive feedback changes edit decisions, when operator coverage drives recovery, and when supervised adaptation like LoRA remains superior.

title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

AI.tldr: LAQ is a latent-aware 4-bit quantization framework (W4A4KV4) for World Action Models that protects the predicted future representation, achieving 76.4% and 83.3% success on LIBERO-Plus with 3.8x compression and 1.66x speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs protect only the generated action pathway and ignore errors in the predicted future, which degrade downstream actions when quantized.
AI.method: LAQ introduces a reader metric and read count to allocate activation and KV-cache precision in closed form based on how rounding errors affect future-reading denoising steps, alongside gaze-guided refinement that gives action-attended tokens a second 4-bit pass without high-precision branches or per-task recalibration.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Plus, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy (within 1.2 percentage points of 16-bit models), compresses models by 3.8x, cuts peak GPU memory by 2.3x, runs 1.66x faster, and achieves 47.0% success on a real AgileX PiPER arm (versus 52.0% for 16-bit and 30.0% above QuaRot).
AI.conclusion: Preserving the fidelity of predicted future latents where they are written, stored, and read enables accurate, real-time 4-bit deployment of World Action Models.

title: Cyber-Physical RSI for AI-RAN: A Case Study
summary: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.

AI.tldr: This case study demonstrates a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN using ping-pong handover, updating a student model from 12 physical executions and characterizing parameter-dependent generalization.
AI.motivation: Learned RAN models trained in simulation suffer performance shifts when exposed to real physical propagation, protocol behavior, and hardware implementations.
AI.method: The framework links a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent, executing six baseline-candidate physical pairs (12 runs) to adapt the student and evaluate it on reserved physical configurations.
AI.result: Increasing time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280 ms reduces ping-pong handovers from three to zero; the updated student achieves a grouped-validation MAE of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 (pre-feedback) and 1.601 (post-feedback) round trips/min.
AI.conclusion: The case study characterizes the operational physical-feedback loop for AI-RAN and highlights parameter-dependent generalization challenges revealed by live physical experiments.

title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
summary: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships. Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.

AI.tldr: MatVerse is a multimodal materials-science foundation model built on Intern-S2-Preview via large-scale domain post-training, consistently improving performance and calculation efficiency across OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench.
AI.motivation: Materials science spans heterogeneous text, crystal and molecular structures, characterization data, and microscopy images, making general-purpose multimodal reasoning difficult for standard foundation models.
AI.method: Built upon Intern-S2-Preview, MatVerse is post-trained on a large-scale multimodal materials corpus constructed via teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data generation.
AI.result: MatVerse consistently outperforms its base model across OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench while improving inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems.
AI.conclusion: Targeted domain-specific post-training effectively enhances scientific reasoning and multimodal understanding for materials science, providing a unified interface for AI-assisted research.

title: Multiple Criteria Decision Making Under XORness
summary: How should we make decisions under XORness? XORness is a class of uncertainty arising from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy. We develop a multiple criteria decision making framework that preserves XORness throughout the decision process. We define XOR numbers and prove their fundamental arithmetic and algebraic properties. Building on these results, we extend the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix and introduce a compatible normalization procedure. Further, we propose an additive XOR aggregation operator, which preserves indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy inherent in evaluations. In addition, we introduce an axiomatic XORness measure that quantifies the degree of uncertainty associated with global performance scores and develop a performance--XORness index to rank alternatives. We prove that this index induces a total preorder over the set of alternatives and identify the conditions for preserving dominance. The applicability of the developed framework is demonstrated through the risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems, and recommendations are derived using the XOR--weighted sum method.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a multiple criteria decision making framework under XORness, defining XOR numbers, an additive aggregation operator, and a performance-XORness index that induces a total preorder over alternatives.
AI.motivation: Standard decision-making frameworks do not preserve XORness, a form of uncertainty combining indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy, throughout the evaluation and ranking process.
AI.method: The authors define XOR numbers and their algebraic properties, extend deterministic decision matrices to XOR decision matrices with compatible normalization, propose an additive XOR aggregation operator and an axiomatic XORness measure, and construct a performance-XORness index.
AI.result: Theoretical proofs establish that the performance-XORness index induces a total preorder and identify dominance-preservation conditions, and a case study on cyberthreat risk assessment in energy systems demonstrates the XOR-weighted sum method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a mathematically grounded way to preserve and quantify XORness uncertainty in multi-criteria decision making.

title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.

AI.tldr: SiliconGym is a cross-task, cross-toolchain reinforcement learning environment for hardware design and verification that runs a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek and supports interchangeable open-source and commercial EDA backends.
AI.motivation: Extending RL with EDA feedback to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span diverse tasks, preserve state across tool calls, handle full-hierarchy SoCs, and support parallel rollouts.
AI.method: SiliconGym decouples versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, uses streaming dispatch to overlap tool checks with generation, and supports interchangeable open-source and commercial EDA backends.
AI.result: SiliconGym finishes a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek, shows that functional correctness trained on open-source backends transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, and reveals via paired netlists when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.
AI.conclusion: A unified, streaming-capable RL environment bridges open-source and commercial EDA toolchains for scalable agentic hardware design.

title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

AI.tldr: DP-SPD is a differentially private LLM inference framework that hides user queries among shuffled client-generated dummy queries and reuses shared-prefix KV caches, achieving strong privacy and near-plaintext utility.
AI.motivation: Existing differentially private LLM-as-a-Service methods inject noise into input embeddings, which causes substantial accuracy degradation when strong privacy is required.
AI.method: DP-SPD mixes the real user query with client-generated dummy queries, randomly shuffles all queries before sending them to the server, and exploits shared-prefix structure to reuse transformer KV caches during decoding.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes the privacy guarantee, and experiments on classification and generation tasks under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks show strong inference-time privacy, near-plaintext utility, and improved efficiency from KV-cache reuse.
AI.conclusion: Dummy-augmented shuffling combined with shared-prefix KV-cache reuse offers a practical privacy-utility-efficiency trade-off for remote LLM inference.

title: LATER: Learning Action-Conditioned Temporal Evidence Retrieval for Predictive World Models
summary: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.

AI.tldr: LATER is an action-conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA that stores real transitions in partitioned memories and queries them via a response bridge, raising terminal success on distracted Two-Stage PushT from 15.5% to 25.0%.
AI.motivation: Early physical interactions can reveal properties no longer visible in later observations, yet standard world models struggle to retain and selectively read out this earlier evidence for future action prediction.
AI.method: Inspired by working memory, LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories fixed during candidate rollouts, queries them with a response bridge using the current state and candidate action, and trains memory writers with multi-cut auxiliary supervision.
AI.result: On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA, and across six models and two seeds it achieves the lowest physical readout error, cutting along-push MAE under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.
AI.conclusion: Separating memory retention from action-conditioned selective readout enables world models to leverage earlier physical evidence even under visual distractors.

title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
summary: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

AI.tldr: CompAct-Bench evaluates working-context compaction in long-horizon agent tasks across BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and CompanyBench, revealing that even frontier LLMs suffer substantial accuracy drops under aggressive compaction due to omitted details and distorted task state.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents rely on context compaction to manage growing histories, yet the compaction capabilities and failure modes of modern LLMs remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Starting from successful agent trajectories, CompAct-Bench inserts compaction boundaries, compresses prior context with the evaluated model under controlled retention ratios via iterative ratio adjustment, and lets the same executor finish the task.
AI.result: Even frontier Claude- and GPT-family models experience substantial downstream accuracy degradation under aggressive compaction, with failures stemming not only from omitted information but also from distorted task state such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions.
AI.conclusion: Working-context compaction is a distinct, challenging capability for long-horizon agents that current frontier models have not yet mastered.

title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.

AI.tldr: DMT-Attack is a gradient-free gray-box attack that searches a frozen diffusion model's latent space using rollout feedback to generate natural-looking textures that disrupt closed-loop VLA policies with a 57.9% attack success rate.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to texture attacks, but optimized adversarial patterns look unnatural and are easily flagged by detectors or human inspection.
AI.method: DMT-Attack uses a frozen text-conditioned diffusion model as the search space and refines an eight-expert latent proposal network initialized from teacher latents using closed-loop rollout feedback to craft textures for ordinary objects like tablecloths.
AI.result: Evaluated against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites, DMT-Attack achieves 57.9% macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (versus 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures) while cutting the clean-calibrated detector flag rate to 45% (versus 97.5-100% for patch baselines).
AI.conclusion: Natural-looking textures found within diffusion priors can effectively subvert closed-loop VLA policies while evading appearance-based detectors, motivating joint visual-behavioral defenses.

title: MemMend: A Selective Revision Framework for Memory Question Answering
summary: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.

AI.tldr: MemMend is a selective revision framework for memory question answering that routes potentially incomplete answers to a bounded exact-text editor, improving F1 and Judge scores on LoCoMo while cutting revision calls by 62.37%.
AI.motivation: Revising every answer generated from long-term memory wastes inference budget and risks corrupting facts that were already correct.
AI.method: MemMend routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor that proposes bounded exact-text replacements and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid operations, preserving the original answer when no legal repair is found.
AI.result: On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend reaches 67.17 macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, beating a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points with 62.37% fewer revision calls; applied to PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem, it raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points while saving 49.85-83.72% of editing calls.
AI.conclusion: Selective, source-grounded exact-text editing offers a reusable quality-cost operating point for long-term memory question answering.

title: ADAPT: Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing
summary: Retrieval-based classifiers efficiently route queries to specialised services, but they typically select a candidate even when no suitable service exists. We introduce Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing (ADAPT), a lightweight routing architecture with an explicit fallback option that enables queries to abstain from specialist selection. ADAPT uses the separation between the highest relevance score and the candidate score distribution as routing confidence. Experiments across retrieval models and increasing numbers of services reveal a consistent empirical behaviour: the confidence distribution changes systematically with candidate-pool size K, making fixed abstention thresholds increasingly miscalibrated. ADAPT addresses this effect with a K-aware threshold that adapts as services are added without classifier retraining. Evaluation across two specialist datasets shows that this simple mechanism provides an effective accuracy-cost trade-off compared with generative LLM routing, supporting lightweight and dynamically extensible service-routing architectures.

AI.tldr: ADAPT adds a pool-size-aware abstention threshold to retrieval-based service routers, enabling dynamic service addition without retraining and providing an effective accuracy-cost trade-off against generative LLM routing.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-based classifiers route queries to specialist services efficiently but force a selection even when no suitable service exists, and fixed abstention thresholds become miscalibrated as the candidate pool grows.
AI.method: ADAPT measures routing confidence as the separation between the top relevance score and the candidate score distribution, and applies a K-aware abstention threshold that adapts automatically to candidate-pool size K without retraining.
AI.result: Experiments across retrieval models and growing service pools confirm that confidence distributions shift systematically with K, and evaluations on two specialist datasets show ADAPT achieves a strong accuracy-cost trade-off compared with generative LLM routing.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for candidate-pool size in abstention thresholds enables lightweight, dynamically extensible service routing with reliable fallback behavior.

title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency
summary: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.

AI.tldr: Duopra is a full-duplex interaction model trained with protocol SFT, full-duplex RL, and projector-only repair that jointly learns conversational control and task execution, raising Pass@1 from 4.7% to 44.7%.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex models handle natural turn-taking and interruptions well, but in streaming pipelines most task failures occur before domain tools are even executed due to missing or incomplete backend requests.
AI.method: Duopra treats the backend as a tool accepting self-contained natural-language requests and uses a three-stage training pipeline: protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates.
AI.result: With the same backend on Full-Duplex-Bench v3, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (up from 26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend, while improving three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model.
AI.conclusion: Jointly training conversational control and backend delegation allows full-duplex agents to achieve strong task agency without sacrificing conversational responsiveness.

title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
summary: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference.
