TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.

AI.tldr: This study diagnoses widespread rationale hallucination in multimodal safety guards and introduces Tool-Contrastive Grounding RL (TCG-RL), which substantially reduces hallucinated rationales while preserving safety prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multimodal safety guards increasingly output rationales alongside safety labels, yet it is largely unknown whether those rationales are visually grounded or factually faithful.
AI.method: The authors categorize rationale hallucination into visual rationale hallucination and safety attribution hallucination, analyze Think-with-Image tool-use failures, and propose TCG-RL, which rewards visual tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference.
AI.result: Across rationale-generation methods, VLM backbones, and safety datasets, rationale hallucination is widespread and does not reliably shrink with higher accuracy or larger scale; TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation hides ungrounded safety explanations, and contrastive tool-use rewards are needed to make multimodal safety guards both accurate and verifiably grounded.

title: Inject Where It Matters: Objective-Dependent Feature Control in Rectified-Flow Image Editing
comment: Accepted as a poster at the Principles of Generative Modeling (PriGM) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Many prompt-driven FLUX editing methods rely on injecting source features into target-conditioned generation, creating an inherent trade-off between source preservation and the desired edit. We address this problem by controlling where source features are injected and which transformer blocks are used. First, we introduce adaptive masks that spatially gate feature injection using differences between source- and target-conditioned block outputs at matched inversion states. Second, we use REINFORCE to select Top-K injection blocks under different preservation-editability objectives. The selected blocks are fixed at inference and require no online search. On PIE-Bench with FLUX.1-dev, spatial masking controls the alignment-preservation trade-off. On 60 validation examples, a learned nine-block set gives lower whole-image LPIPS than the 18-block RF-Edit set within the same masked pipeline, with slightly lower alignment. Among 50 random nine-block sets, it has the lowest LPIPS but not the highest reward. Separate objective sweeps reveal different block preferences for preservation and alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper controls spatial and block-level feature injection in rectified-flow FLUX image editing using adaptive masks and REINFORCE block selection, achieving lower whole-image LPIPS than an 18-block baseline using only 9 blocks.
AI.motivation: Prompt-driven FLUX editing methods inject source features into target generation, creating a trade-off between preserving the source image and achieving the desired edit.
AI.method: The authors introduce adaptive spatial masks derived from differences between source- and target-conditioned block outputs at matched inversion states, and use REINFORCE to select a fixed Top-K set of transformer injection blocks under different preservation-editability objectives.
AI.result: On PIE-Bench with FLUX.1-dev, spatial masking governs the alignment-preservation trade-off; on 60 validation examples, a learned 9-block set yields lower whole-image LPIPS than the 18-block RF-Edit set (with slightly lower alignment) and achieves the lowest LPIPS among 50 random 9-block sets.
AI.conclusion: Objective-dependent block selection and spatial masking provide fine-grained control over preservation versus editability in rectified-flow image editing without online search.

title: Self-Replicating Language Models
comment: About 64 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Under review at Artificial Life
summary: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether LLMs can self-replicate and undergo Darwinian evolution across genome emission, weight mutation, and sample-based teaching, finding small LMs can evolve in narrow niches while flagship teaching-based replication remains infeasible.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether LLMs and LLM-based agents satisfy the Darwinian definition of life clarifies whether they can adapt autonomously through evolution.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three self-replication modes: emitting a genome to train offspring, copying and mutating weights, and teaching a child from generated samples.
AI.result: Small language models can replicate and adapt to narrow niches under selection, though selection also drives mutation rates toward zero, limiting further evolution; flagship LLMs can write replicators, but teaching-based replication by large LLMs remains technically and economically infeasible.
AI.conclusion: While small language models exhibit basic Darwinian replication and adaptation, current large-scale self-replication via teaching is constrained by cost, feasibility, and collapsing mutation rates.

title: Whose Risks Count? What 1,901 AI Incidents Reveal About Corporate Disclosures
summary: AI systems can harm people, yet the AI actors that provide or deploy them are rarely obliged to disclose these risks. US securities regulation is an exception. Companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose their material risks, including those of their AI systems, in filings that carry liability for misstatement. Materiality, however, is defined by what a reasonable investor would consider important, so harms to third parties enter disclosure only insofar as they become financial risks for the company. We test whether AI harms do so by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half belong to a risk type that the AI actor never disclosed, and this share varies with the kind of harm. Filings disclose the risk types of 67\% of system failures but only 2\% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2\% of incidents. Securities disclosure thus records the risks that AI actors face rather than the harms that people subject to AI bear. Public authorities that hold AI actors accountable for such harms could make them financially material. We release DISC, the Disclosure--Incident Securities Corpus, to support this work.

AI.tldr: Matching 1,901 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors reveals that half of incidents involve risk types never disclosed by the company, with filings covering 67% of system failures but only 2% of social system harms.
AI.motivation: AI systems can harm third parties, yet it is unclear whether US securities materiality rules compel companies to disclose these harms in SEC filings.
AI.method: The authors construct DISC (Disclosure-Incident Securities Corpus) by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings across 328 AI actors by risk type, analyzing 1,901 incidents with both pre- and post-incident filings.
AI.result: Half of the 1,901 incidents belong to a risk type never disclosed by the AI actor; filings disclose risk types for 67% of system failures but only 2% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2% of incidents.
AI.conclusion: Current securities disclosure captures financial risks to AI actors rather than harms borne by the public, suggesting that regulatory accountability is needed to make third-party harms financially material.

title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
summary: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

AI.tldr: HabitusMem models user memory as revisable assistant beliefs with evidence, scope, and status rather than raw interaction history, achieving state-of-the-art results on PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems retrieve raw interaction history without indicating whether a user preference is still current or where it applies, causing personalized agents to act on outdated or misapplied preferences.
AI.method: Inspired by Bourdieu's habitus, HabitusMem trains a memory writer that maintains text-record beliefs about a latent user preference state—including evidence, scope, and status—for a frozen agent, incorporating learned request conditioning and auxiliary training tasks.
AI.result: Across two agent families, HabitusMem outperforms existing memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0, with ablations showing learned request conditioning drives answering gains and auxiliary tasks improve tool use.
AI.conclusion: Representing memory as structured, revisable beliefs over latent user preferences enables more accurate personalization than retrieving raw dialogue history.

title: Decoupled Knowledge Retrieval and Compact Memory Enable Reliable Lifelong Model Editing
summary: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.

AI.tldr: BiSpace is a lifelong LLM editing framework that decouples semantic query routing from sparse internal knowledge injection, shrinking per-edit storage to 10.2% and improving Overall Performance by over 23% on sequences up to 16K edits.
AI.motivation: Memory-based lifelong model editors keep base weights frozen, but linearly growing storage and degrading retrieval accuracy limit their scalability over long edit sequences.
AI.method: BiSpace separates memory retrieval and knowledge injection into two representation spaces, routing queries in an external semantic space while injecting knowledge into the LLM's internal representation space via sparse, storage-efficient updates.
AI.result: BiSpace reduces per-entry storage to about 10.2% of the original size, remains resilient up to 16K sequential edits, and improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods on a challenging benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling retrieval and injection spaces makes memory-based lifelong model editing scalable and reliable at thousands of edits.

title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
summary: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.

AI.tldr: StarTV-Agent combines process-level RL and weakness-driven demonstrations with fast/slow workflow reuse for traffic scenario understanding, improving performance by up to 8.0% while cutting token usage by up to 52.1%.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented VLMs for traffic understanding suffer from sparse terminal rewards during training and high repeated planning costs across similar tasks at inference.
AI.method: StarTV-Agent uses Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) and Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) during training, and pairs a fast path—Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) with label-free feedback—against a slow ReAct path at inference.
AI.result: Across three traffic scenario benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
AI.conclusion: Combining process-aware policy learning with adaptive workflow reuse yields both higher accuracy and substantial token savings in tool-augmented VLM agents.

title: Coherent belief and opinion propagation produces more echo chambers: corrected version
summary: The occurrence of echo chambers is a well-known phenomenon in social networks. Echo chambers are groups of agents satisfying three properties: homogeneity, i.e., sharing the same opinion, segregation, i.e., listening primarily to agents of the same group, and reinforcement, i.e., increasing opinion similarity over time. Opinion dynamics models have been used to explain how echo chambers occur through agents updating their opinions. However, social network users also exchange beliefs supporting their opinions. Here, we aim at identifying the effect of propagating beliefs together with opinions on the formation of echo chambers. For that purpose, we complement an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations. Beliefs and opinions are also maintained coherent guided by values that agents share. We introduce measures, applying to either beliefs and opinions, to identify echo chambers based on the three properties. This model is used to simulate opinion and belief propagation with varying initial conditions and agent tolerance for different opinions/beliefs. Results confirm the occurrence of echo chambers observed in previous opinion dynamics studies in a different setting and with a stricter measure. They also demonstrate the occurrence of echo chambers with belief propagation. Finally, they show that connecting opinions to beliefs and maintaining their coherence increases the number of belief echo chambers, but that they involve a reduced number of agents.

AI.tldr: Extending opinion dynamics with belief merging and value-guided coherence shows that propagating beliefs alongside opinions increases the number of belief echo chambers while reducing the number of agents in each.
AI.motivation: Standard opinion dynamics models explain echo chambers through opinion updates alone, overlooking how social network users also exchange supporting beliefs.
AI.method: The authors augment an opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations, enforce coherence between beliefs and opinions via shared values, and define strict three-property measures (homogeneity, segregation, reinforcement) to simulate varying initial conditions and tolerances.
AI.result: Simulations confirm opinion echo chambers under stricter measures, demonstrate belief echo chambers, and show that maintaining opinion-belief coherence produces more belief echo chambers containing fewer agents each.
AI.conclusion: Coupling belief propagation with opinion dynamics fragments social networks into smaller, more numerous belief echo chambers.

title: Trustworthy Geospatial AI Workflows: Reproducible Maritime Analytics and Forecasting on Open-Source AIS Data
summary: Publicly available geospatial data provide increasing opportuni- ties for data-driven maritime analytics and predictive modelling. However, their availability does not necessarily imply that the underlying observations are equally suitable for downstream AI applications. Properties of the data source and observation pro- cess, including provenance, reporting regularity, spatial coverage, observation density, and missingness, can affect how geospatial data are interpreted, processed, and ultimately used by predictive models. At the same time, trustworthy geospatial AI requires ana- lytical workflows in which these processing decisions can be made explicit and reproduced. This paper presents a reproducible mar- itime geospatial AI workflow built around damast, an open-source data-processing and machine-learning library developed at Simula Research Laboratory. Using AIS observations from multiple public data providers as a case study, we demonstrate metadata-aware validation, reusable processing pipelines, maritime trajectory con- struction, and reproducible machine-learning experimentation. The predictive stage is model-agnostic and is instantiated in this study using a Transformer-based vessel-trajectory forecasting model. Building on these implemented capabilities, we further outline an envisioned extension toward trustworthiness-aware geospatial AI. The extension introduces explicit characterization of source- and data-level properties and their relationship with downstream model performance. This distinguishes capabilities demonstrated in the current workflow from trustworthiness-oriented components identified for future development. Overall, the study demonstrates how reproducible open-source infrastructure can provide a practi- cal foundation for developing more transparent and trustworthy geospatial AI workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible maritime geospatial AI workflow built on the open-source damast library using multi-provider AIS data and Transformer forecasting, and outlines an extension for source-level trustworthiness characterization.
AI.motivation: Publicly available geospatial data vary widely in provenance, reporting regularity, coverage, density, and missingness, requiring transparent, reproducible pipelines to ensure reliable downstream AI modeling.
AI.method: Using open-source AIS observations from multiple providers, the authors implement metadata-aware validation, reusable processing pipelines, trajectory construction, and a model-agnostic forecasting stage instantiated with a Transformer, while outlining future trustworthiness extensions.
AI.result: The study demonstrates an end-to-end reproducible maritime analytics and vessel-trajectory forecasting workflow in damast and distinguishes implemented capabilities from proposed source- and data-level trustworthiness metrics.
AI.conclusion: Open-source infrastructure with explicit metadata validation provides a practical foundation for transparent and trustworthy geospatial AI workflows.

title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
summary: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

AI.tldr: Meta-RTL evolves agent harnesses for RTL optimization using EDA feedback while keeping the base LLM and budgets fixed, reducing WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% on development designs and 20.5%/14.0% on unseen IC-RTL designs.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for RTL optimization rely on hand-engineered search procedures rather than systematically discovered harnesses.
AI.method: Meta-RTL evolves executable RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop using EDA feedback under fixed model, EDA flow, and per-design budget constraints, and characterizes three resulting search mechanisms via ablations.
AI.result: Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs (with area reductions on 70%) and transfers without further evolution to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, cutting WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and synthesized area by 12.6%.
AI.conclusion: Automated harness evolution is an effective way to improve LLM-based RTL optimization and generalize across unseen hardware designs.

title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Code and results available from the corresponding author on request
summary: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible, explainable ML workflow for solar PV power forecasting tested on a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, achieving 11.6% nRMSE and showing that input features matter more than model choice while SHAP reflects model rather than physical properties.
AI.motivation: Published solar PV forecasting results are often difficult to compare or trust due to random data splits, missing baselines, and uncalibrated feature attributions.
AI.method: The authors review ML families for PV forecasting, build a reproducible workflow combining automated model search, conformal calibration, and SHAP explainability, and evaluate it over a full test year on a 16.32 kWp plant using 4 km NWP forecasts.
AI.result: The best models reach 11.6% nRMSE (roughly half the error of smart persistence), conformal calibration raises 80% prediction-interval coverage from 64.5% to 81.7%, input feature selection impacts accuracy far more than algorithm choice, and SHAP rankings shift when correlated inputs are removed.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous temporal validation, conformal calibration, and cautious interpretation of feature attributions are essential for trustworthy, deployable solar PV forecasting.

title: The Price of an Explanation: What Demanding Verifiable Artifacts Costs, and What It Buys Back
comment: 8 main pages, 3 main figures. 19 pages total. Accepted in NeurIPS 2026 AI4Science Workshop
summary: Generative models produce many candidate solutions but provide no intrinsic signal by which to rank them. One mitigation is to demand a \emph{verifiable artifact}: a program that can be executed against the available evidence. A common concern is that requiring executable verification incurs costs in both solution quality and computational budget. We measure these two costs on the $120$-task ARC-AGI-2 evaluation set. Demanding a verifiable artifact from an LLM reduced the score from $93$ to $68$ of $120$ tasks ($77\%$ to $57\%$). Of those $25$ tasks, $21$ were reached by no program-producing configuration we ran, at any budget, by sampling or by search; yet for $27$ of the $28$ tasks that only the answer-only arm solved, some program arm held a program that reproduced every demonstration and still failed the test. The bottleneck is obtaining an explanation that \emph{generalizes}, not finding one. A short evolutionary search over two already-sampled programs, at no additional model cost, beats best-of-$2$ sampled code by $9.2 \pm 1.4$ tasks, and over a single sampled program beats $1$-shot sampling by $9.9 \pm 1.3$. Moreover, because a program can be checked against the training examples, any program-producing protocol can terminate early once a task is explained: under the same stopping rule, best-of-$n$ sampling declines up to $38\%$ of its budget and the evolved arm up to $49\%$, whereas an answer-only baseline cannot terminate early. Applying the same methodology to decoder synthesis for quantum error correction yields interpretable decoders evaluated against a certified panel of published decoders on held-out exam shots.

AI.tldr: Demanding executable programs from an LLM on ARC-AGI-2 drops accuracy from 77% to 57% because programs fail to generalize to test cases, though evolutionary search over two sampled programs improves over best-of-2 by 9.2 tasks and enables early stopping.
AI.motivation: Requiring verifiable executable artifacts provides a ranking signal for generative models, but its costs in solution quality and compute budget are not well quantified.
AI.method: The authors evaluate answer-only versus program-producing LLM arms on the 120-task ARC-AGI-2 set and quantum error correction decoder synthesis, testing evolutionary search over sampled programs and early termination on training examples.
AI.result: Requiring a verifiable program lowers solved tasks from 93 to 68 of 120 (77% to 57%), with 27 of 28 answer-only-exclusive tasks having a program that passed all demonstrations yet failed the test; evolutionary search over two sampled programs beats best-of-2 by 9.2 +/- 1.4 tasks at no extra model cost, while early stopping cuts budget by up to 38% (best-of-n) and 49% (evolved).
AI.conclusion: The main bottleneck in program-based reasoning is generalization rather than demonstration fitting, though cheap evolutionary search and early stopping recover substantial efficiency.

title: From Cases to Criteria: Reusing Evaluation Knowledge for Task-Specific Rubric Generation
summary: Query-specific rubrics make LLM evaluation more fine-grained and transparent, and generating high-quality rubrics requires both identifying the target query's evaluation scope and specifying concrete checks. Historical rubrics provide reusable evaluation experiences, yet existing approaches reuse either complete query-rubric cases or aggregated criteria and dimensions without explicitly connecting recurring evaluation requirements to their criterion-level evidence and source-query context. This can preserve irrelevant task details or lose the broader evaluation structure. In this paper, we introduce RubricDuo, which organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph linking evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries, where reusable evaluation requirements across queries are abstracted by shared concepts. Given a target query, RubricDuo first combines concepts relevant to the target query with retrieved historical cases to draft a rubric with broad coverage. It then revisits each draft criterion, retrieves concept-linked historical criteria and their source queries, and adapts applicable evidence to refine the criterion. Experiments on RubricBench and HealthBench demonstrate that RubricDuo achieves the overall best performance among the evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging.

AI.tldr: RubricDuo organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph to draft and refine query-specific evaluation rubrics, achieving the best alignment with human rubrics and downstream LLM judging on RubricBench and HealthBench.
AI.motivation: Existing rubric-generation methods reuse either whole query-rubric cases or aggregated criteria without linking recurring evaluation requirements to criterion-level evidence and source-query context.
AI.method: RubricDuo builds a Rubric Knowledge Graph connecting evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries, drafts a rubric from relevant concepts and retrieved cases, and refines each criterion using concept-linked historical criteria and source queries.
AI.result: On RubricBench and HealthBench, RubricDuo achieves the best overall performance among evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Structuring historical rubrics as a concept-linked knowledge graph enables more faithful and transferable task-specific rubric generation.

title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
summary: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an end-to-end validation pipeline for self-hosted agentic LLM serving, showing that trace replay reproduces per-session load within 1.18x (versus 4.98x for live re-runs) and revealing throughput gaps on MoE models.
AI.motivation: Enterprises migrating agentic workloads from closed APIs to open-weight deployments need accurate lifecycle-wide validation, as ad hoc evaluation tools are rarely checked for fidelity.
AI.method: The authors build an open-source end-to-end validation pipeline, compare captured-trace replay, live re-runs, and synthetic workloads using vLLM code-coverage analysis, and conduct a case study deploying four large MoE models on llm-d.
AI.result: At the 95th percentile, trace replay stays within 1.18x of recorded input tokens compared with 4.98x for live re-runs; live, replayed, and synthetic workloads exercise complementary vLLM Python paths; and target MoE models reach roughly half the optimal concurrency and 60% of the throughput on captured workloads versus public traces.
AI.conclusion: Combining trace replay with complementary workload validation exposes real-world serving bottlenecks that public traces miss during enterprise LLM platform rollouts.

title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.

AI.tldr: ROAM-GRPO augments GRPO by routing well-solved problems to an off-mode track that mines and self-distills verified distinct reasoning strategies, increasing peak pass@16 by 4.7% on MATH lvl5.
AI.motivation: SFT paired with RLVR often collapses LLM policies into a single low-diversity reasoning mode, causing repeated samples to look identical and limiting pass@k gains.
AI.method: ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training, prompts the model to generate distinct solution strategies on an off-mode track, verifies logical validity and distinctness with an LLM judge, and self-distills those strategies back into the policy.
AI.result: Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of MATH lvl5, ROAM-GRPO increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and increases correct embedding cosine distance by roughly 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly mining and self-distilling verified alternative strategies counteracts policy collapse in RLVR and improves reasoning diversity.

title: GaussTrans: A Gaussian Interface Framework for Multi-Layer Refractive Transport
summary: We investigate surface modeling of multi-transparent interfaces to achieve accurate light transmission. The interplay of errors in geometric structure, light paths, and observation results during the reconstruction of transparent media with a high number of layers makes this a challenging problem. Some existing techniques address the reconstruction of transparent scenes by reducing the number of layers or simplifying light paths; however, this limits their direct applicability to high-order transparent scenes. We propose GaussTrans, a compact framework for light transport in high-order transparent scenes, consisting of three components: Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection. Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces use a hybrid approach combining Gauss surfaces and fields to reconstruct different interfaces. Transport-Coupled Refinement reduces coupling errors by evaluating the entire light path. Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection combines primitive support regions to reduce errors in the intersection of interfaces and rays. In experiments on datasets such as RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher accuracy with relatively low spatial storage requirements.

AI.tldr: GaussTrans is a compact framework for multi-layer refractive light transport that combines Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection to improve accuracy with low storage.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing scenes with many transparent layers suffers from coupled errors in geometry, light paths, and observations, which prior methods avoid only by limiting layer counts or simplifying light paths.
AI.method: GaussTrans integrates Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces to represent multiple interfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement to optimize over entire light paths, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection using primitive support regions to reduce ray-interface intersection errors.
AI.result: On datasets including RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher reconstruction accuracy while maintaining relatively low spatial storage requirements.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling hybrid surfaces and full-path refractive transport enables accurate, storage-efficient reconstruction of high-order transparent scenes.

title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027), with technical appendices. 10 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables
summary: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts are highly sensitive to the fiber-orientation field supplied to the material model. In conventional workflows, that field comes from resin-flow analysis, which requires molding-specialist support and takes about 25 hours of work per part. We previously proposed a surrogate model that addresses this bottleneck by predicting the orientation field in about 3 minutes. This paper reports the implementation, validation, and operational design that turned the model into an engineering tool for Honda design workflows. We present staged validation from 2D plates to production parts, evaluation against a predefined engineering angular-error criterion, and the expert review that approved design use in March 2025; the system has since been transferred to the crash-safety group and is in initial, limited use in directed fracture-prediction scenarios. The developed system combines injection-gate setting support for cases in which gates are unknown (90% gate-count accuracy, mean position error 11% of flow length), voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and report generation in a single GUI. The complete orientation-preparation workflow takes about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the conventional 25-hour flow-analysis route, and can be run directly by crash CAE engineers without molding-specialist support. As evidence of practical impact, component-level crash analysis using the predicted orientation field reduced the absolute peak-force error from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%, while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region. The deployment lesson is that a surrogate model alone is not enough for practical adoption: gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and shareable reporting are what make the model usable as a design tool.

AI.tldr: This paper turns an AI surrogate model for fiber-orientation prediction into a production engineering tool for Honda crash CAE workflows, cutting orientation preparation time by 99.6% from 25 hours to about 0.1 hours.
AI.motivation: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts depend heavily on fiber-orientation fields from resin-flow analysis, which conventionally requires molding-specialist support and roughly 25 hours per part.
AI.method: The authors integrate injection-gate setting support, voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and shareable report generation into a single GUI, alongside staged validation from 2D plates to production parts.
AI.result: Gate-setting support achieves 90% gate-count accuracy and 11% mean position error of flow length; component-level crash analysis cuts absolute peak-force error from 19.0% (isotropic baseline) to 11.4% while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region, and the system received design-use approval in March 2025.
AI.conclusion: A surrogate model alone is insufficient for industrial adoption; surrounding workflow automation such as gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and reporting makes it usable as a design tool.

title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
summary: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

AI.tldr: An LLM agent (GPT-6 Astra) redesigns a magnesium stent across roughly 1,650 CAD parameters within a 15-simulation budget, reducing peak strain objective by 32% and outperforming the industrial shape optimizer Tosca.
AI.motivation: Simulation-driven engineering design requires few nonlinear finite-element solves, high-dimensional CAD parameterizations, and coordinated proportional redesigns rather than local surface polishing, whereas existing optimizers satisfy at most two of these three conditions.
AI.method: GPT-6 Astra directly edits a 1,650-value CAD geometry parameterization of a magnesium stent over 15 simulations, where each proposal is built in CAD, meshed, simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and its full results are read by the LLM.
AI.result: Within 15 simulations, GPT-6 Astra lowers the high-percentile bend strain objective by 32% compared to a 10% improvement from Tosca; an earlier 25%-lower design verified in an independent full-deployment model shows 14% less strain and 63% less damage at its most damaged spot at full expansion.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose LLMs can combine learned engineering knowledge with simulation feedback to adjust over a thousand CAD parameters and achieve valid, substantial design improvements.

title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
summary: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.

AI.tldr: System-One RSI couples a fast online OODA decision loop with an offline team of reasoning agents to build external muscle memory for sub-second interactive control without expert demonstrations or parallel simulation.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models offer strong multimodal understanding but are too slow for sub-second control, while fast decision models lack the fine-grained task experience that prompting and few-shot examples fail to provide.
AI.method: An online inner loop maps visual observations and task questions to structured judgments via a decision model and converts them into timed actions via a decision tree, while an offline outer loop of reasoning agents revises prompts, trees, and model parameters from captured interaction records.
AI.result: Using a 27B decision model, mean Snake score rises from 1.30 to 7.35, median completion time in Zenless Zone Zero drops by 8.4%, and in Black Myth: Wukong the evasive policy reaches 11x the survival time of a stationary reference while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7%.
AI.conclusion: Separating fast online execution from offline recursive self-improvement enables interactive agents to acquire fine-grained control skills from a small number of real episodes.

title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
summary: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a stratified conditional distributional testing framework to localize where artificial agents diverge from human play, uncovering mode-specific bot divergence in a commercial match-3 game.
AI.motivation: Evaluating whether agents behave like humans requires comparing entire behavioral distributions across contexts rather than average outcomes, as session-level win/loss metrics offer little signal beyond mean comparisons.
AI.method: The authors compute nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells and discover subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play, focusing on process-level metrics such as move efficiency.
AI.result: Applied to a commercial match-3 game, the framework reveals that a playtesting bot diverges substantially from humans in certain game modes while showing no detectable divergence in others, patterns invisible to aggregate metrics.
AI.conclusion: Conditional distributional testing on process-level metrics provides actionable localization of human-agent behavioral differences, and the implementation is released as open source.

title: ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding
summary: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: ForeSeek is a foresight-driven video agent for long-form video understanding that replaces reactive clip retrieval with predictive exploration, achieving competitive or superior accuracy with 2.5x to 4.4x fewer observed frames.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based video agents rely on reactive retrieval driven by local saliency without a global temporal plan, creating a major efficiency and reasoning bottleneck on long videos.
AI.method: ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, refines its search using failed expectations as backtracking signals, and is trained via a two-stage framework for foresight-guided reasoning and decision making.
AI.result: Across five long-video benchmarks, ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency-accuracy trade-off, matching or surpassing the strongest search-based agent while observing 2.5 to 4.4 times fewer frames.
AI.conclusion: Transforming long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration substantially reduces frame consumption without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Serialization Tax in Shared-Latent Exchangeable Decisions
summary: Accurate item probabilities can produce inaccurate group-level decisions. A system may score each item separately, yet act on whether enough hidden items succeed: show a slate, defer a panel decision, or inspect a batch. When items share an uncertain latent state, independent marginalization preserves means but removes dependence from the aggregate posterior. We call this error the serialization tax. For binary items sharing one success rate, classical convex-order comparisons give a more dispersed exact count law than any independent completion with the same total mean. We quantify variance and total-variation gaps, derive threshold separation under margin conditions, and connect posterior approximation to decision regret. Separate results cover non-binary outcomes, heterogeneous items, and sufficient posterior resolution. TaxScore identifies large hidden blocks with unresolved uncertainty near a decision boundary for routing to richer posterior heads. On pre-specified, hidden-target-free MovieLens 1M/10M audits, existing shared-latent heads improve high-score negative log-likelihood (NLL)/utility from 0.673/0.696 to 0.629/0.723 and from 0.670/0.691 to 0.639/0.715. Routing gives 0.006--0.012 full-population utility gains, with matched controls identifying their sources. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the serialization tax—error caused by independent item marginalization in shared-latent group decisions—and introduces TaxScore routing to improve MovieLens 1M/10M utility and NLL.
AI.motivation: Systems that score items independently and then make group-level decisions (such as showing a slate or deferring a panel) lose dependence in the aggregate posterior when items share an uncertain latent state.
AI.method: The authors quantify variance, total-variation gaps, threshold separation, and decision regret via convex-order comparisons, and propose TaxScore to route large hidden blocks with unresolved boundary uncertainty to richer posterior heads.
AI.result: On MovieLens 1M and 10M audits, shared-latent heads improve high-score NLL/utility from 0.673/0.696 to 0.629/0.723 and from 0.670/0.691 to 0.639/0.715, while TaxScore routing yields 0.006 to 0.012 full-population utility gains.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for shared-latent posterior dependence and routing uncertain boundary blocks to richer heads mitigates the serialization tax in group-level decisions.

title: SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-Glasses Pipelines
comment: 10 pages; research framework and analytical limits; no empirical efficacy results. Includes an author reflection in Korean in Appendix C
summary: Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM). Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space, and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework, not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.

AI.tldr: SEOYUN is a research framework, threat model, and evaluation protocol for designing refusal-inducing examination documents that reduce the usefulness of unauthorized VLM queries from camera-equipped glasses.
AI.motivation: Camera-equipped glasses can turn exam pages into VLM queries, and while device detection addresses possession, there is no structured threat model or evaluation protocol for whether exam documents themselves can induce model abstention.
AI.method: The authors formalize reverse jailbreaking (inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal), distinguish refusal from answer leakage, derive sampling comparisons under camera assumptions, and separate digital, simulated, and physical evaluation inputs with a CSAT candidate corpus.
AI.result: The paper prepares a local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness, but explicitly reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results in this version.
AI.conclusion: SEOYUN establishes a rigorous threat model, analytical limits, and evaluation protocol for refusal-inducing exam documents rather than a validated defense.

title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
summary: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of over five million Hugging Face records finds that explicit mentions of the EU AI Act remain rare (over 1,500 records) and focus mostly on assigning compliance responsibility rather than explaining how compliance is achieved.
AI.motivation: Although the EU AI Act's obligations for general-purpose AI providers and transparency have taken effect and affect public model-sharing platforms like Hugging Face, little is known about how practitioners respond in practice.
AI.method: The authors collected over five million repository cards, discussions, and commits across Models, Datasets, and Spaces on Hugging Face, identified over 1,500 records explicitly mentioning the AI Act, and manually coded them using a primarily closed coding approach.
AI.result: Explicit AI Act mentions are rare across all repository types; repository cards mainly assert compliance or shift responsibility to downstream users, discussions report alleged violations, and commits update supporting compliance artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners currently focus on who is responsible rather than how to comply, indicating a need for platform-level automated checks, documentation templates, and clearer regulatory guidance.

title: Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated Biologically Plausible Network
summary: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.

AI.tldr: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks trained with eligibility propagation (e-prop) achieve a 100% survival rate on the Unitree H1-2 humanoid—matching backpropagation through time—whereas fixed reservoirs and reward-modulated STDP plateau much lower.
AI.motivation: While artificial spiking neural networks can mimic biological neural cultures, it remains open whether they can control full-size humanoid locomotion while retaining both biological plausibility and robust performance.
AI.method: The authors distill an RL expert policy via dataset aggregation into spiking networks trained under four schemes ordered by biological faithfulness: fixed reservoir with linear readout, reward-modulated STDP, eligibility propagation (e-prop), and backpropagation through time (BPTT).
AI.result: E-prop reaches a 100% survival rate matching BPTT and demonstrates brief bipedal stepping on the H1-2 humanoid, whereas the fixed reservoir and reward-modulated STDP plateau at roughly 43.7% and 11% survival, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Eligibility propagation bridges biological plausibility and robust humanoid locomotion control, while more biologically faithful local rules still lag significantly in performance.

title: Pareto-Optimal and Strategyproof Data-Sharing Between Competitors
summary: We study data-sharing among firms competing in the same market through the quality of their predictive models. We model firms' profit through two main components, precision and market share, where the former depends on the firm's own number of datapoints and the latter depends on the endowments of all firms. We characterize Pareto-optimal contracts as those in which at least one firm receives all of the other firms' datapoints. We then propose a parametric family of data-sharing contracts and show that, under any of them, the relative market shares of all firms remain constant, eliminating the negative effect of sharing data with competitors and equalizing all firms' gains relative to the no-sharing scenario. We further show that one contract within this family satisfies both Pareto-optimality and strategyproofness against firms attempting to under-declare the size of their initial endowment. Finally, using a real-world dataset, we empirically test the gain in profit for all firms under the contract described above, and show that data-sharing is particularly beneficial when the machine learning task is harder or when firms' initial endowments are closer to homogeneous.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes Pareto-optimal and strategyproof data-sharing contracts among competing firms, showing that a parametric contract family keeps relative market shares constant and equalizes profit gains.
AI.motivation: Firms competing in the same market through predictive model quality face a tension between gaining precision from shared data and losing market share to competitors.
AI.method: Modeling firm profit via precision (own datapoints) and market share (all firms' endowments), the authors characterize Pareto-optimal contracts where at least one firm receives all data and propose a parametric contract family that preserves relative market shares.
AI.result: One contract in the proposed family satisfies both Pareto-optimality and strategyproofness against under-declaring initial endowments; empirical tests on a real-world dataset show data-sharing yields larger profit gains when the ML task is harder or endowments are more homogeneous.
AI.conclusion: Properly designed contracts eliminate the competitive downside of sharing data with rivals and incentivize truthful endowment reporting.

title: SenseAlign: Learning Decision-Aligned Predictive Representations for Active Urban Sensing with UAVs
summary: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: SenseAlign is an RL framework for active urban sensing with UAVs that aligns a partially observed student's latent representations with a privileged teacher's decisions, outperforming baselines on Barcelona's 1,570-segment road network.
AI.motivation: Active urban sensing with drone fleets requires simultaneously modeling complex spatio-temporal traffic dynamics and making decisions under partial observations, which prior work rarely addresses jointly.
AI.method: SenseAlign trains a privileged teacher RL agent with future ground-truth traffic, then trains a student agent with an auxiliary traffic-prediction branch by matching its action distributions to the teacher's under predicted versus ground-truth future traffic, incurring zero inference overhead.
AI.result: On a real road network of central Barcelona with 1,570 road segments, SenseAlign consistently outperforms baselines across multiple utility formulations.
AI.conclusion: Shaping predictive latent representations to align with privileged decision-making improves partially observed UAV fleet coordination without adding inference-time cost.

title: Sage-Evolve-Preview:Adaptive Observation for Post-Training Self-Improvement
summary: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Observation (AdaObs) dynamically refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks when post-training recursive self-improvement plateaus, raising mean anchor scores from 66.4 to 73.7.
AI.motivation: Post-training recursive self-improvement loops typically observe only a fixed anchor benchmark's aggregate score, causing progress to stall and exploration to repeat once anchor-only feedback stops revealing actionable gaps.
AI.method: AdaObs keeps the anchor objective fixed while a controller adapts active observations at plateaus by refining diagnostic granularity, escalating difficulty, and adding related tasks, fusing validated increments back into training.
AI.result: Across eight anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from 66.4 to 73.7 under a matched data budget, outperforming the FixedObs baseline, and improves the seven-task average on PostTrainBench across two agent backends.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the observation harness rather than relying solely on a fixed anchor score is a key mechanism for sustaining post-training recursive self-improvement.

title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
summary: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.

AI.tldr: The FrontierOR Challenge benchmarks agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for operations research problems, where current one-shot LLMs match Gurobi on only 39% of large instances.
AI.motivation: Operations research relies on weeks of specialist algorithm engineering per problem, and it remains open whether LLM agents can automatically design optimization algorithms that scale to realistic instances.
AI.method: The challenge releases 60 of 180 audited problems in Stage 1 (weekly rounds of 15 across six domains and five formulation types) and unseen problems in Stage 2, ranking Main (sandboxed open-source) and Self-hosted tracks by feasibility-checked objective ratios against a frozen reference.
AI.result: In FrontierOR's one-shot baseline evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi (within 1% objective and no slower) on only 39% of large instances.
AI.conclusion: The FrontierOR Challenge provides a standardized, multi-problem testbed to drive progress in scalable agentic algorithm design for operations research.

title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
summary: Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing remains challenging because experimental datasets are limited and process-property relationships vary across materials and operating conditions. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) govern process stability and defect formation. Conventional ML models typically use dimensional process parameters, which represent laser-material interactions only implicitly and may limit cross-material transfer. This study evaluates whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, combining laser processing conditions with material thermophysical properties, improve melt pool prediction over raw process parameters. We systematically benchmark seven models: four classical ML methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2). Experiments span 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets, covering regression of melt pool width and depth and classification of melting modes. Dimensionless features yield comparable or superior predictive performance in most settings, with the largest gains in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). Tabular foundation models generally achieve stronger classification performance than classical baselines, particularly for multi-material datasets. These findings indicate that combining physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular models can improve data-efficient melt pool modeling and support more transferable process-window identification in LPBF.

AI.tldr: Combining physics-informed dimensionless features (normalized enthalpy and Peclet number) with pretrained tabular foundation models improves cross-material melt pool geometry prediction (up to R^2 = 0.96 for depth) and melting-mode classification in laser powder bed fusion.
AI.motivation: Experimental datasets in laser powder bed fusion are limited, and conventional ML models using raw dimensional parameters struggle to generalize across materials and operating conditions.
AI.method: The authors benchmark four classical ML models (GP, SVM, RF, XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, TabICLv2) using normalized enthalpy and Peclet number versus raw parameters across 316L, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets.
AI.result: Dimensionless features match or outperform raw parameters in most settings, achieving the largest gain in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96), while tabular foundation models generally outperform classical baselines on multi-material melting-mode classification.
AI.conclusion: Pairing physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular foundation models enables more data-efficient and transferable process-window modeling in additive manufacturing.

title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
summary: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption.
