The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.

AI.tldr: This paper updates the fosf fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic reasoner with similarity-based reasoning and a translation engine that compiles ontology-rewritten OSF queries into standard SPARQL for flexible RDF query answering.
AI.motivation: Standard SPARQL queries over RDF knowledge graphs fail to return relevant approximate answers when queries are inconsistent with the underlying ontology.
AI.method: The updated fosf reasoner extends OSF logic with a similarity relation among sorts, normalizes fuzzy OSF constraints using sort definitions and feature declarations, and translates the rewritten OSF terms into standard SPARQL.
AI.result: The system compiles similarity-aware, ontology-rewritten OSF queries into standard SPARQL, enabling approximate query answering over RDF knowledge graphs.
AI.conclusion: Integrating sort similarity and fuzzy constraint normalization into OSF-to-SPARQL translation allows flexible, ontology-aware retrieval even when exact matches fail.

title: Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
summary: Textual recommendations generated by large language models (LLMs) can be difficult to inspect. This paper introduces \emph{Client Exits}, a lightweight mechanism for enriching LLM responses while separating semantic intent from client-specific presentation. The model inserts predefined, machine-interpretable markers into its output, and the receiving client decides whether and how to realize the corresponding enrichments. This allows supplementary information to be presented as graphics, text, speech, or other modalities without prescribing a concrete interface. We implement a prototype combining a finetuned Qwen model with a modified LibreChat client. Using the Question--Option--Criteria (QOC) approach including three XML-based client exits. We evaluate two QOC-oriented model variants trained on essentially the same examples, with client-exit annotations added for one variant. Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response. An LLM judge, informed about the mechanism without being instructed to favor it, prefers this model's answers in 66\% of the comparisons. These results demonstrate successful marker generation on the evaluated test set and support the feasibility of client-controlled enrichment.

AI.tldr: Client Exits is a lightweight mechanism where an LLM embeds machine-interpretable XML markers in its output so the client can render supplementary enrichments, earning 66% preference from an LLM judge.
AI.motivation: Textual recommendations from LLMs are often difficult to inspect, and coupling presentation directly into the model output limits how clients can display supplementary information across modalities.
AI.method: The authors finetune a Qwen model to insert three XML-based Question-Option-Criteria (QOC) client-exit markers into responses, paired with a modified LibreChat client that realizes the enrichments.
AI.result: Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response, and an informed LLM judge prefers its answers over a matched baseline in 66% of comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Separating semantic intent from client-side presentation via structured exit markers is a feasible way to improve LLM transparency and adaptability.

title: Actor-Predictor Architecture for Reinforcement Learning with Formal Specification Objectives
summary: One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks. It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as $(a^n b^n)$, for which finite-automaton-based approaches are not applicable.

AI.tldr: Actor-Predictor learns a surrogate representation of formal specification progress without constructing an automaton, outperforming automaton-based RL baselines on LTL tasks and handling non-regular specifications.
AI.motivation: Enforcing temporal safety constraints in RL typically requires converting logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping, which becomes intractable for large specifications and cannot handle non-regular logic.
AI.method: A predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification later, feeding its learned features as auxiliary inputs to an actor optimized with GRPO and RWR.
AI.result: Theoretically, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state under sufficient predictive accuracy; empirically, on grid world and Isaac Lab robotic tasks, Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL tasks and succeeds on non-regular specifications like (a^n b^n).
AI.conclusion: Learning specification-progress predictors bypasses automaton construction bottlenecks and extends formal-specification RL to non-regular constraints.

title: Rigel-Ladon: An Option-Count Law for a One-Pass Decision Encoder, Tested on Held-Out Option Counts and Held-Out Schemas
summary: Laya is a small neural network that reads a text, a question and K written options, and returns one probability per option in a single pass. We ask how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether that can be predicted. We score nested option sets (every K-option question contains the smaller ones) on four question pools, for the released model (Base) and our fine-tune (FT), and score every item against each single rival. FT trained on one 12-option topic question (in-family); a 12-option HR (department-routing) question is out-of-family. Logit accuracy (the log of correct over incorrect answers) is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88. Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 (a log-linear rule: 1.6 and 6.7). Taking the slope from the topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy on HR predicts its other K within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base). On a 35-label pool of five schemas the law fails (5 to 11 points). Independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected: the gold-versus-rival log-odds shifts by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per doubling of K, yet pairwise answers reproduce K-way accuracy within 4.7 points. Order averaging (averaging over several orderings of the options), shortlists, a temperature law and calibrated prediction sets did not transfer (FT's 90% sets cover 84% on HR). 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held. Caveats: one model family and LLM-labelled synthetic text.

AI.tldr: Rigel-Ladon establishes a linear law between logit accuracy and log(K-1) for the Laya one-pass decision encoder as option count K grows from 2 to 35, predicting held-out K within 0.3 to 1.2 points on single-schema pools.
AI.motivation: A one-pass decision encoder scores K written options in a single forward pass, but how its accuracy degrades as K increases and whether that scaling is predictable across schemas remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Laya (Base and fine-tuned FT) on nested option sets from K=2 to 35 across four question pools and single-rival pairs, testing a linear law in logit accuracy versus log(K-1), order averaging, shortlists, and calibrated prediction sets.
AI.result: Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 points, and predicts out-of-family HR accuracy within 0.3 (FT) and 0.7 (Base) points using only 2-option HR accuracy, though it fails on a 35-label multi-schema pool (5 to 11 points) and independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected.
AI.conclusion: Option-count scaling in one-pass decision encoders follows a predictable logit-log law within single schemas, though calibration and multi-schema generalization remain limited.

title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
comment: Accepted at the 20th International Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning (NeSy 2026). Conference version: this https URL
summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

AI.tldr: ClosureBench isolates how LLMs handle missing information under OWA, CWA, and LCWA across 960 instances, showing that high overall accuracy (up to 99.86%) can mask large failures (down to 18.23% core switch accuracy) when closure rules change.
AI.motivation: LLM agents frequently reason over incomplete records, but existing evaluations conflate general reasoning with whether agents follow the stated closure assumption (treating missing facts as unknown versus false).
AI.method: ClosureBench tests every base scenario under Open World (OWA), Closed World (CWA), and Local Closed World (LCWA) assumptions—varying only the missing-information rule—and requires correct answers across all variants, alongside agent extensions.
AI.result: Across 960 instances, models achieve 71.18% to 99.86% overall accuracy, but core switch accuracy on instances whose gold label changes with the closure contract spans 18.23% to 99.31%, with major errors under LCWA.
AI.conclusion: Agent benchmarks must explicitly test adherence to closure assumptions when information is absent rather than relying on aggregate accuracy over existing facts.

title: Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?
summary: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, for one architecture.

AI.tldr: Sirius-Tiamat evaluates how far the 421M-parameter Laya one-pass decision encoder can be compressed before its decisions flip, finding that 6-bit grouped rounding flips fewer decisions than layer deletion at equal stored size.
AI.motivation: Compressing one-pass decision encoders reduces memory and compute, but practitioners need to know how quantization, pruning, and distillation affect decision stability and confidence calibration both in-family and out-of-family.
AI.method: The authors measure decision flips relative to fp32 and expected calibration error (ECE) across 1,221 in-family synthetic items, 273 unseen-schema items, and 800 out-of-family items (ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag) under bf16, 6-bit rounding, int8, layer deletion, early exit, and distillation.
AI.result: bf16 flips 0.2% in-family and 2.2% out-of-family decisions, 6-bit grouped rounding flips 1.3% and 5.9%, and deleting 6 layers flips 0.9% and 9.1% while raising ECE from 5.9% to 39.2% (restored to 3.6% via label-free temperature scaling); dynamic int8 flips 30% of decisions.
AI.conclusion: At equal stored size, grouped rounding preserves decisions better than layer deletion, and simple temperature recalibration fixes pruning-induced miscalibration.

title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Transitioning from Pre-training to Post-training
summary: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.

AI.tldr: Edit-based training supervises LLMs only on minimal textual corrections at the first point of failure in their own sampled trajectories, improving ReasonIF instruction following on Qwen3-32B while preserving untargeted skills.
AI.motivation: Full-trajectory SFT overconstrains model outputs by forcing imitation of entire demonstrations, while trajectory-level RL provides weak credit assignment without pinpointing where reasoning fails.
AI.method: An editor identifies the first failure point in a model's sampled completion under a given criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span; the model is then supervised exclusively on these edited spans, either offline or online.
AI.result: Instantiated on Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark, edit-based training substantially improves reasoning-instruction compliance compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level RL baselines while largely preserving performance on untargeted tasks.
AI.conclusion: Localizing supervision to minimal failure-point edits is an effective, less disruptive alternative to full-trajectory SFT and coarse RL for shaping LLM reasoning.

title: DeepQuest: From Knowledge Gaps to Scientific Discovery in Alzheimer's Disease
summary: Automating experiments does not necessarily advance scientific understanding. Research agents must identify meaningful knowledge gaps, determine what available data can resolve, and assess whether their findings advance existing knowledge. We introduce DeepQuest, a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease research. DeepQuest transforms unresolved questions from domain reviews into traceable, testable hypotheses and prioritizes them through data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking. It couples iterative experimentation with two-level auditing that separates experimental reliability from knowledge contribution relative to two frozen literature corpora. On OASIS-3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses and outperforms the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three language-model reviewers. The full framework achieves an audit-assessed scientific finding rate of 95.24%, outperforming both general-purpose executors and domain-specific research agents. This scientific finding rate remains stable across literature corpora and evaluator model families. Representative findings concern neuropsychiatric symptoms and dementia risk, longitudinal amyloid spatial stability, and neocortical tau-associated clinical impairment, with key associations supported in independent ADNI and AIBL cohorts. These results show how aligning knowledge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing can turn automated research into traceable, evidence-supported scientific discovery. Our source code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: DeepQuest is a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease that generates 42 feasible hypotheses on OASIS-3 and achieves a 95.24% audit-assessed scientific finding rate.
AI.motivation: Automating experiments alone does not advance science unless agents can identify meaningful knowledge gaps, screen data feasibility, and audit whether results genuinely contribute to existing literature.
AI.method: DeepQuest converts unresolved questions from domain reviews into traceable hypotheses, prioritizes them via data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking, and couples iterative experimentation with two-level auditing against two frozen literature corpora.
AI.result: On OASIS-3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses, outperforms baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three LLM reviewers, and reaches a 95.24% scientific finding rate, with key neuropsychiatric, amyloid, and tau associations supported in ADNI and AIBL cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Aligning knowledge-gap discovery, data feasibility, and literature-grounded auditing turns automated experimentation into traceable scientific findings.

title: Context as a Resource
comment: 27 pages, including appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

AI.tldr: ClonAct is a routerless context-virtualization architecture for concurrent personal-agent tasks that lifts true-conflict repository merges from 33.3% to 63.3% while using 45.9% fewer prompt tokens.
AI.motivation: Funneling concurrent tasks into one linear LLM session causes cross-topic constraint bleed and stalling, whereas router-ticket hierarchies suffer from lossy prose handoffs, routing overhead, and blind merges.
AI.method: ClonAct virtualizes context blocks directly using a non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk.
AI.result: Across three multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, the trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges from 33.3% to 63.3% with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens, and under continuous surge streams ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timeouts.
AI.conclusion: Routerless context virtualization avoids the overhead and merge failures of hierarchical agent routing while sustaining high throughput on concurrent streams.

title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

AI.tldr: Deployment lessons from IBM's self-distilled agent memory pipeline on AppWorld show that optimal memory size depends on the model: strong models (DeepSeek-V3.2) benefit from all 191 guidelines (+9.5 points), whereas weaker models (gpt-oss-120b) perform better with a small selected subset (~29 guidelines).
AI.motivation: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks repeat procedural mistakes, but it is unclear how many distilled guidelines an agent should receive at inference time and what failure modes arise in production.
AI.method: The open-source altk-evolve pipeline (deployed in IBM's CUGA and watsonx Orchestrate) mines short lessons from agent trajectories, consolidates them into provenance-tracked guidelines, and supplies either all guidelines or a selected subset at inference on AppWorld.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 task-completion and +16.1 scenario-completion points using all 191 guidelines, while gpt-oss-120b rises from 39.9% to 51.2% with all 199 guidelines but reaches 55.4% with a selected subset of about 29; the authors also document backfiring guidelines, dropped provenance, swallowed API errors, and baseline confounds.
AI.conclusion: The right amount of agent memory is a property of the model's capacity rather than the memory itself, requiring selective retrieval for weaker models and careful production auditing.

title: World Models Favor Learned Priors over Visual Evidence
summary: World models are increasingly used to simulate physical interactions, but training a separate model for each environment limits scalability. Cross-environment prediction requires identifying the current physical rule, which appearance alone may not reveal. We therefore study visual calibration: using object motion and interactions in a short video as direct evidence to infer the current rule and predict motion under that rule from a different initial state. However, differences in data availability across physical conditions can yield a long-tailed training distribution, biasing models toward common rules even when evidence supports rare ones. To study this challenge, we introduce TailWorld, which evaluates the transfer of demonstrated rules across initial states while independently controlling training imbalance and calibration informativeness. The benchmark compares predictions with two reference futures from the same prediction initial state, one following the demonstrated rule and the other a common rule, to measure prediction bias toward common dynamics. We further propose Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT), which learns how different rules affect object motion, infers the current rule from calibration interactions, and applies it to prediction from a new initial state. RIFT explicitly controls the influence of training frequency on rule inference, allowing sufficiently informative observational evidence to support rare rules. Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across varying training imbalances and distribution shifts, with gains in predicting rare dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the TailWorld benchmark and Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT) to counter world models' bias toward common physical rules over rare ones supported by visual calibration evidence.
AI.motivation: Cross-environment world models must infer the active physical rule from short calibration videos, but long-tailed training distributions bias models toward common rules even when visual evidence supports a rare rule.
AI.method: TailWorld evaluates rule transfer across initial states while controlling training imbalance and calibration informativeness; RIFT learns how rules govern object motion and explicitly controls training-frequency influence during rule inference.
AI.result: Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across varying training imbalances and distribution shifts, with notable gains on rare physical dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decoupling prior training frequency from visual rule inference enables world models to generalize to rare physical laws when observational evidence is informative.

title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
summary: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

AI.tldr: ZeroVLN is a slow-fast vision-language navigation framework that achieves strong VLN-CE performance with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain by using a semantic tool-calling interface and closed-loop RL.
AI.motivation: Conventional VLN methods fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation data to predict geometric goals, which substantially alters base weights and degrades general visual capabilities.
AI.method: ZeroVLN equips an un-fine-tuned VLM brain with a semantic tool-calling interface to send natural-language movement decisions to an action expert, adapts the action expert, and jointly optimizes both via closed-loop agentic RL.
AI.result: Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE benchmarks while inducing minimal weight changes and largely preserving general VLM capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling high-level semantic navigation decisions from low-level continuous execution via tool calling and closed-loop RL eliminates the need for navigation SFT on the VLM brain.

title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items, responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do not.

AI.tldr: Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA) uses attribute-labeled CoT traces from LLMs to make Q-matrix construction inspectable, revealing assignment disagreements and examinee-fit differences missed by matrix-level overlap.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specs, but evaluating only the final matrices leaves individual item-attribute assignments opaque.
AI.method: RTA prompts LLMs to produce attribute-labeled chain-of-thought reasoning steps and analyzes those traces to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each item-attribute assignment alongside expert review.
AI.result: Across four LLMs on 11 fraction subtraction items (536 examinees, 100 replications), CoT-derived Q-matrices achieve 0.809 mean overlap with the reference (versus 0.877 for direct generation) with higher variance, while trace inspection exposes item-type coding and labeling-rule disagreements.
AI.conclusion: RTA provides diagnostic, inspectable evidence for Q-matrix validation that aggregate matrix-agreement and fit metrics cannot capture.

title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
summary: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

AI.tldr: Seer guides small on-device deep-research agents at inference time using offline-trained, shared tool-response simulator and value estimator models, boosting GAIA accuracy from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.motivation: Privacy and local control favor running small deep-research agents on-device, but inference-time search via real tool execution is costly, self-evaluation is weak, and model-specific guidance requires repeated adaptation.
AI.method: Trained offline on a shared corpus of real research trajectories, a reusable tool-response simulator and a discounted-correctness value estimator evaluate candidate actions locally, executing only the selected action in the real environment.
AI.result: Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves small agents—raising GAIA accuracy from 13.6% to 41.7% (Qwen3.5-4B) and 22.3% to 50.5% (Qwen3.5-9B)—without executing discarded candidates.
AI.conclusion: Reusable offline-trained world and value models can substantially strengthen small local research agents through extra local computation without extra real tool calls.

title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
summary: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).

AI.tldr: This paper compiles exact multi-digit arithmetic and Boolean circuits directly into pretrained LLM weights with zero training examples or runtime hooks, achieving 99.17%–100% 6-digit arithmetic accuracy on Granite 4.2 3B and Qwen 3.5 4B.
AI.motivation: Pretrained language models remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters.
AI.method: The authors combine two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, cross-token scale cancellation via Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and GatedDeltaNet shifts, and norm-compensated width extension with Base-1000 BPE emission and differential tied unembeddings.
AI.result: A 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4–8 digit signed {+,-,x} circuits, 3-literal Boolean (100%), and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits; on 6-digit arithmetic (BF16), Granite 4.2 3B and Qwen 3.5 4B reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with FP32 sidecar) and 98%–100% mid-sentence resumption, beating LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%) while passing 14/14 >2K-token Tango splits.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form, zero-gradient circuit grafting embeds exact deterministic computation into pretrained weights while bounding normalization drift and preserving natural-language competence.

title: Monte Carlo Pass Search for Setpieces
summary: Set pieces produce about a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG), yet they are usually evaluated by what happened next. We present Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) for set pieces, which treats a corner or a lofted free kick as a distribution over plausible executions and plausible futures instead of a single realised event. From the pre-kick state, MCPS proposes counterfactual deliveries and counterfactual set-ups (where the attackers stand at the kick), plays each out many times in a world model (3D ball physics, a generative model of all 22 players, the keeper's come-or-stay decision and a Player-to-Touch model) and scores every future with a value model. On 249 deliveries from 30 Serie A 2025/26 matches, with every model applied only to matches it never saw, the best available delivery is worth 0.0085 xG more than the one kicked (+28 %), mainly because it reaches an attacker before the keeper. Searching where the attackers stand as well adds +0.0027 xG with the observed ball and +0.0033 on top of the best ball; designing their runs too adds +0.0007 more. We show how to keep such a search honest, and estimate how much more data each component needs before a club could rely on it.

AI.tldr: Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) models set-piece deliveries and attacker setups as distributions over counterfactual executions in a learned world model, finding available Serie A deliveries worth +0.0085 xG (+28%) over the actual kicks.
AI.motivation: Set pieces generate roughly a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG), yet standard evaluations judge them only by the single realized outcome rather than counterfactual alternatives.
AI.method: From the pre-kick state, MCPS proposes counterfactual deliveries and attacker setups, simulates futures using 3D ball physics, a 22-player generative model, keeper come-or-stay, and Player-to-Touch models, and scores each future with a value model.
AI.result: On 249 deliveries from 30 held-out Serie A 2025/26 matches, the best available delivery yields +0.0085 xG (+28%) over the kicked ball, optimizing attacker starting positions adds +0.0027 to +0.0033 xG, and designing runs adds +0.0007 xG.
AI.conclusion: World-model-based counterfactual search quantifies unrealized set-piece value and highlights data requirements for club-level deployment.

title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
summary: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: FLUID is a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and building flexible multimodal task-guidance agents grounded in human-human WTaG and HoloAssist data, achieving the best balance of correctness, precision, timing, and latency.
AI.motivation: Existing task-guidance benchmarks treat synthesized dialogues as rigid single-reference targets for what to say and when, missing the natural flexibility of real-time guidance where multiple timings or silence can be appropriate.
AI.method: Using natural human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility to both evaluate flexible guidance and train a real-time guidance agent.
AI.result: The FLUID agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, though avoiding speech overlap remains an area for improvement.
AI.conclusion: Grounding evaluation and agent design in evidence-based timing flexibility moves situated task guidance closer to natural human-AI interaction.

title: LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits
summary: Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.

AI.tldr: ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen) separates true intersectional interactions from independent single-attribute effects using an additive baseline and Freedman-Lane null, cutting false subgroup flags from 66.1 to 0.09 per synthetic dataset.
AI.motivation: Standard intersectional LLM audits flag subgroups that exceed each individual attribute alone, a condition that independent additive attributes already satisfy, leading to widespread false positives.
AI.method: ADDIS fits an additive model over all identity attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD), and tests significance against a Freedman-Lane permutation null; the authors also build IndiPersona (10,000 Indian personas across six attributes) to audit 13 open LLMs.
AI.result: On 150 synthetic null datasets, the standard criterion flags 66.1 false subgroups on average versus 0.09 for ADDIS, while ADDIS recovers 84% of planted interactions (versus 32%); on IndiPersona, ADDIS flags 3.0% of 738 subgroups versus 7.1% for the standard criterion, consistently identifying gender identity x sexual orientation and (via counterfactuals) caste x class interactions.
AI.conclusion: Much of what standard audits label as intersectional bias stems from additive single-attribute effects, making an additive baseline essential to isolate genuine interactions.

title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
summary: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.

AI.tldr: Testing label-free persona and knowledge directions for LLM lie detection up to 70B scale shows they often track reply wording on identical-word knowledge lies, though their sum outperforms supervised probes on Liars' Bench.
AI.motivation: Linear probes for LLM lie detection rarely transfer across lie types, and label-free role-play directions remain untested at 70B scale and on knowledge lies where lies and honest denials share identical wording.
AI.method: The authors expand a persona bank with knowledge-denying roles, construct a knowledge direction contrasting answerable versus unanswerable questions followed by scripted denials, and evaluate middle-layer directions on Liars' Bench and Gender-Secret across four models including Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct.
AI.result: The persona direction beats single-dataset probes on three of four models (failing on Qwen) and beats random-persona directions on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct; on identical-word knowledge lies, persona directions stay near the random-direction band while the knowledge direction separates lies on two models (narrowly on a third), and their sum beats a supervised probe on all four models on Liars' Bench.
AI.conclusion: Label-free persona and knowledge directions offer complementary signals for cross-domain lie ranking, though wording confounds remain a key limitation on identical-word denials.

title: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
summary: When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model--backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses.

AI.tldr: MM-SystemOneBias benchmarks 13 multimodal models across 5,323 instances and six paired interventions, showing that System-One decision models are more stable than their backbones under formatting and distraction changes but less responsive to correct external cues.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal behavior separately, leaving no unified protocol to compare multimodal decision models against their backbones on practical judgment tasks.
AI.method: MM-SystemOneBias evaluates 13 models on 5,323 instances from nine datasets and 11 scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image-text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale.
AI.result: Across seven matched decision-model/backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs (and option-order in six), lose less accuracy under incorrect external judgments (all seven) and conflicting descriptions (six), but gain less from correct external judgments (six); unchanged decisions still show 4.56 to 11.55 percentage-point probability shifts.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal decision models trade sensitivity to helpful external cues for greater robustness against interface perturbations and misleading inputs, while probability shifts reveal hidden sensitivity beyond accuracy.

title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images
summary: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.

AI.tldr: ProtoDiffusion is a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE that encodes multi-layer RGBA designs into HW+N tokens instead of NHW, achieving 66.41 FID and 19.1x faster text-to-design generation than a cascade baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-layer graphic design models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, causing representation size to scale with cumulative layer extent.
AI.method: ProtoVAE encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer, which ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises conditioned on image or text (with optional bounding boxes) while automatically determining layer count and layout.
AI.result: ProtoVAE reaches 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops; on LayerD, image-to-design achieves 0.040 RGB L1 with boxes (0.057 without) and 0.850 alpha soft IoU; text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID (versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein]), 0.860 text accuracy, and 19.1x speedup over a generation-then-decomposition cascade.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a single spatial prototype with per-layer candidate tokens enables compact, fast, and flexible multi-layer graphic design generation.

title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027)
summary: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely ($R^2 > 0.99$) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.

AI.tldr: Trace2ST uses an LLM generate-replay-feedback loop to recover executable IEC 61131-3 Structured Text PLC programs from I/O traces alone, reproducing 43 of 47 benchmark programs exactly and achieving 94% scan agreement on unseen inputs.
AI.motivation: Industrial PLCs often run legacy programs whose source code is lost, while their continuous I/O logs remain available, raising the question of whether LLMs can recover and verify executable Structured Text from traces.
AI.method: An LLM generates a candidate ST program from a compressed trace summary, which is replayed scan-by-scan against the recording with mismatching trace segments fed back for up to three revisions, validated against two open-source PLC runtimes.
AI.result: Across 47 third-party programs, Trace2ST reproduces 43 traces exactly and agrees on 94% of scans for unseen inputs (rising from 0.80 to 0.98 on adversarial inputs when branch-targeting traces are added, versus 0.40 for automata learning); on a water-treatment testbed, recovered laws achieve R^2 > 0.99 and expose an actuator attack.
AI.conclusion: Iterative replay-guided LLM synthesis recovers structured, generalizable PLC control logic from I/O traces far more effectively than classical automata learning.

title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
summary: Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not). However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well. Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Montúfar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

AI.tldr: This tutorial paper reviews universal approximation theorems for neural networks and explains why depth provides exponentially greater expressivity than width, while noting that approximation theory alone does not guarantee training or generalization.
AI.motivation: Understanding the mathematical foundations of neural networks requires clarifying both what universal approximation theorems establish and what they leave unanswered regarding efficiency, optimization, and generalization.
AI.method: The authors survey classical universal approximation results (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik, Leshno), Barron's quantitative Fourier-norm bounds, and Montúfar's linear-region analysis comparing deep versus shallow architectures.
AI.result: Non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, Barron's bounds quantify approximation rates for bounded Fourier-norm functions, and Montúfar's results show that the number of linear regions grows exponentially with depth.
AI.conclusion: Depth is fundamentally more expressive than width for a fixed parameter budget, providing a mathematical justification for deep learning alongside the open challenges of optimization and finite-data generalization.

title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
summary: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

AI.tldr: An empirical study on the APT dataset evaluates four feature-reduction techniques across five classifiers under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks, finding that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information most consistently improve robustness.
AI.motivation: Feature reduction is widely used to cut dimensionality and overfitting, yet its impact on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack types remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors test SVM, decision tree, random forest, MLP, and k-NN on the APT dataset under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks, comparing PCA, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information using accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score.
AI.result: Permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally deliver the most consistent robustness improvements across classifiers and attacks, whereas PCA and recursive feature elimination show more variable effects.
AI.conclusion: Selecting features via permutation importance or mutual information offers a more reliable defense-oriented preprocessing strategy than variance-based or wrapper-based reduction.

title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
summary: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the weak sample compression conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size O(d^2 log^2 d) for every binary concept class of VC dimension d.
AI.motivation: Floyd and Warmuth's 1995 sample compression conjecture asks whether every VC-dimension-d class admits an O(d) compression scheme, and even the weaker polynomial-in-d conjecture had remained open since Moran and Yehudayoff's 2016 exponential-in-d bound.
AI.method: The authors construct an explicit sample compression scheme whose size scales near-quadratically with the VC dimension d.
AI.result: Every binary concept class of VC dimension d admits a sample compression scheme of size O(d^2 log^2 d), improving exponentially over the prior d-only bound.
AI.conclusion: Proving a near-quadratic sample compression bound settles the polynomial sample compression conjecture for all VC classes.

title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
summary: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.

AI.tldr: DVBench is the first end-to-end benchmark for real-world UVM hardware design verification agents across 95 tasks, where the best frontier agent (Codex & GPT-6 Astra) achieves only a 21.05% overall success rate.
AI.motivation: Existing hardware design verification benchmarks evaluate decoupled subtasks rather than the full end-to-end Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) workflow required in real-world chip development.
AI.method: DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, evaluating intermediate artifacts (feature lists, test plans, reference models) and final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection.
AI.result: Evaluating frontier LLMs (such as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode), the top-performing combination (Codex & GPT-6 Astra) achieves only 21.05% overall success.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end UVM design verification remains a major challenge for current LLM agents, highlighting substantial room for improvement in complex hardware verification workflows.

title: CRAFT: Constrained Route planning with Adaptive Framework and Template-based code generation
summary: Everyday routing requests are rarely a point-to-point shortest path. A driver may need to visit stops, sometimes in a fixed order, under time budgets or distance limits, and perhaps recharge their EV car along the way. Each combination is a distinct routing problem that classically requires its own algorithm, so no fixed solver covers the space of queries users may ask. This paper presents CRAFT, which takes a constrained routing query as free text and returns a route that satisfies the user's requirements on a real road network. An LLM parses the query and generates four search functions, which a generic graph-search engine executes on the road network. We formalize the underlying problem as State-Expanded RCSP (SE-RCSP), which extends resource-constrained shortest paths (RCSP) with non-additive state such as node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking. We evaluate CRAFT on 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, analyzing correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic POI filtering.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is a constrained route-planning framework that uses an LLM to translate free-text routing queries into search functions executed by a generic graph-search engine on road networks.
AI.motivation: Real-world routing requests involve diverse combinations of stops, ordering, budgets, and EV charging, which no fixed classical solver can cover.
AI.method: The authors formalize State-Expanded RCSP (SE-RCSP) to handle non-additive states like node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking, and use an LLM to parse natural-language queries into four search functions for a generic graph-search engine.
AI.result: CRAFT is evaluated on 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, analyzing correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic POI filtering.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM-based template code generation with a formal state-expanded graph search engine enables flexible constrained route planning from free-text queries.

title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Preregistered study with a negative confirmatory result. Code and protocol records: this https URL
summary: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: this https URL

AI.tldr: Before the Choice is an evidential framework for studying prospective representations in language models, which finds no evidence of prospective simulation in an initial symbolic-environment test case.
AI.motivation: Observable decisions reveal selected actions but do not identify which unchosen alternatives were internally represented, requiring stronger evidential distinctions for AI welfare research.
AI.method: The framework distinguishes future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance across four experimental contrasts, tested via low-rank probes on unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments.
AI.result: A preregistered probe on 293 admissible pairs achieved 0.020 paired accuracy versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline, and late-key decoding in matched worlds remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18 across 141 families) despite passing positive controls.
AI.conclusion: The results neither identify prospective simulation nor prove its absence, demonstrating that identifiability, sensitivity, and dependence-aware null models must constrain decodability inferences.

title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MADJEPA is a multi-stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for medical anomaly detection that learns normality from healthy patient images alone.
AI.motivation: Medical anomaly detection must rely on unlabeled healthy data, and standard self-supervised world models like I-JEPA can over-generalize to abnormal data when used alone.
AI.method: The pipeline combines three stages: (1) I-JEPA training on normal data, (2) target encoder distillation to curb over-generalization to anomalies, and (3) pseudo-anomaly classification to calibrate a tight boundary around the normal manifold.
AI.result: Evaluated on six medical imaging datasets (including MRI, OCT, X-ray, and histopathology), MADJEPA achieves competitive performance, ranking first on three datasets, with ablations confirming each stage's necessity.
AI.conclusion: A multi-stage JEPA training pipeline effectively adapts world-model representations for robust medical anomaly detection.

title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
summary: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require.
