We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: VG-Steer is a test-time policy steering method that corrects frozen robot policies under out-of-distribution shifts using visual-geometric abstractions from LVMs and VLMs.
AI.motivation: End-to-end robot policies overfit and fail under distribution shifts, while existing test-time adaptation methods either rely on implicit learned signals or only provide coarse spatial corrections.
AI.method: VG-Steer transfers nuanced motion from successful in-distribution rollouts along object-relational distance pairs, using LVMs and VLMs to combine task-relevant entities and distance projections into a visual-geometric guidance signal.
AI.result: In simulation, it corrects flow-matching policies under pose and goal shifts; on a real robot, it more than doubles cable-placement success one grid step outside training positions and steers single-task policies toward unseen objects while nearly eliminating object confusion.
AI.conclusion: Explicit visual-geometric abstractions from foundation models enable effective, nuanced test-time adaptation of frozen robot policies.

title: From FAIR to AWARE: Data Readiness for Agentic AI in the Earth Sciences
comment: 34 pages (27 main text, 7 Supplementary Information), 1 figure, 1 table, 2 boxes
summary: Artificial intelligence in the Earth sciences is beginning to act: prototype agents already search archives, run simulations and draft analyses. Scientific data were curated for researchers who bring expert judgement; an autonomous agent cannot be assumed to supply it. Data can satisfy the FAIR principles and still mislead a machine acting alone. We propose that Earth-science data become AWARE (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled), an agent-specific requirements layer that extends FAIR, within a three-part agenda: AWARE data, bounded tools, layered validation. The ingredients exist across community infrastructure. We outline a staged, measurable path to adoption, intended to reduce silent error.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the AWARE data-readiness layer to extend FAIR principles for autonomous AI agents operating in the Earth sciences.
AI.motivation: Scientific data curated for human experts with domain judgement can mislead autonomous AI agents even when the data satisfies FAIR principles.
AI.method: The authors define AWARE (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled) as an agent-specific requirements layer within a three-part agenda of AWARE data, bounded tools, and layered validation.
AI.result: The paper outlines a staged, measurable adoption path built on existing community infrastructure to reduce silent errors by autonomous agents.
AI.conclusion: Extending FAIR to AWARE data readiness is necessary to make Earth-science archives safe and reliable for agentic AI.

title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
summary: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a parametric memory management system for LLMs that stores facts in a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter with temporal decay and uses a learned policy to retain, update, or forget user memories.
AI.motivation: Existing parametric memory methods mirror continual learning by retaining all information indefinitely, whereas real memory systems must reinforce recurring facts, update changed beliefs, and let transient details fade.
AI.method: The substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter using k-hot rank combinations with independent temporal decay, paired with a lightweight learned controller that decides what to remember, how deeply, and for how long.
AI.result: On a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with changing beliefs, the learned policy balances recall and abstention to reach 86% of oracle performance, outperforming CL and RAG baselines that default to one behavior.
AI.conclusion: Combining a decay-capable LoRA substrate with a learned lifecycle controller establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory in model weights.

title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
summary: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

AI.tldr: PLANTA is an ontology-mediated planning framework that jointly plans task actions and architectural reconfigurations for self-adaptive autonomous robots.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots must adapt both task plans and architectural configurations to changing conditions, but these decisions are interdependent and cannot be planned in isolation.
AI.method: PLANTA represents architectural alternatives and requirements in the Web Ontology Language and task actions in PDDL, automatically integrating them for joint satisficing planning and runtime replanning.
AI.result: Evaluated in underwater inspection and ground navigation scenarios, PLANTA demonstrates feasible runtime co-adaptation with lower planning time and memory consumption than optimal-policy generation while maintaining similar plan quality.
AI.conclusion: Integrating ontology-based architecture models with PDDL task planning enables efficient joint task and architecture co-adaptation for robots.

title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
summary: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.

AI.tldr: FI-ITEP is an in-training embedding pruning method for large-scale recommendation models that uses feature importance to set per-table pruning ratios, reducing memory and GPU costs without hurting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard in-training embedding pruning (ITEP) uses size-based heuristics for per-table pruning ratios, which can degrade recommendation accuracy.
AI.method: FI-ITEP computes feature importance (FI) with minimal overhead and assigns higher pruning ratios to embedding tables associated with less important features.
AI.result: Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP reduces total memory by 20-40% while matching or improving accuracy over percentile-based ITEP, cutting GPU trainers (e.g., from 112 to 80) and saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per launch, with trends reproduced on DLRM (Criteo 1TB).
AI.conclusion: Guiding in-training embedding pruning with feature importance delivers substantial memory and compute savings in production recommendation systems.

title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
summary: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

AI.tldr: ReLay is a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers reusable generator programs from analog layouts and evolves its library as layouts accumulate.
AI.motivation: Analog layout generators are limited by handcrafted libraries, as designer knowledge in completed layouts remains implicit in geometry and hard to reuse across process design kits (PDKs).
AI.method: ReLay translates existing layouts into generator code, promotes recurring constructions into library functions, and provides a benchmark of 1,050 hand-drawn layouts across 27 circuit families and three open-source PDKs.
AI.result: Learned library functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls on held-out layouts, and frontier LLM agents using ReLay generate new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation with comparable completion and electrical quality.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional layout-code translation and library evolution enable reusable, process-portable analog design and more cost-effective LLM-driven layout generation.

title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
summary: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.

AI.tldr: This study audits an LLM-agent workflow for post-quantum cryptographic FPGA hardware, finding that module-level tests and undirected reviews miss flaws that require independent mutants, scoped reviews, and formal checks.
AI.motivation: When LLM agents generate both RTL and its validating tests or reviews, self-generated evidence is insufficient to guarantee trustworthy cryptographic hardware.
AI.method: The authors apply a seven-stage verification-gated workflow to port an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a Zynq UltraScale+ card, then audit it with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks.
AI.result: The accelerator is byte-exact on-board and passes 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases and 484 ML-DSA known answers, but existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 netlist mutants; module-scoped review catches known flaws in 54/54 sessions (vs. 3/6 and 1/6 for whole-design review), while formal checks catch all planted custody flaws that scoped review detects in only 3/20 sessions.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy agentic hardware design requires author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM reviews, and formal checks for custody invariants.

title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
summary: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.

AI.tldr: FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that uses explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops to produce synthesis-ready FPGA hardware.
AI.motivation: Successful C/C++ compilation does not ensure correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS).
AI.method: FPGA-GEN encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules into explicit task contracts with bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions.
AI.result: On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task pass 407/425 (95.8%) public testbenches; in a conversion campaign, it admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation and Vivado synthesis/fit, and in TensorCore screening its selected candidate cuts CSynth cycles by 73.7% and LUTs by 14.6% (with 26.7% more DSPs).
AI.conclusion: Contract-driven agentic workflows with bounded HLS tool feedback reliably generate correct and hardware-efficient RTL from C/C++.

title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

AI.tldr: Dune is a zeroth-order optimizer for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) test-time adaptation that reduces gradient estimation variance by combining online historical error regression with current perturbation observations.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation-based test-time adaptation is too memory-heavy for resource-constrained robots, while standard zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from noisy gradients that stall or degrade long-horizon updates.
AI.method: Dune trains a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor on past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates to reduce variance without backpropagation or extra forward passes.
AI.result: Experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots show that Dune achieves higher success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
AI.conclusion: Coupling historical error regression with zeroth-order updates stabilizes low-memory test-time adaptation for VLA models.

title: SGLayout: Schema-Guided Closed-Loop Refinement for LLM-Driven Parameterized Layout Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: SGLayout is a schema-guided closed-loop framework that refines LLM-generated parameterized layouts by back-projecting geometric and rule violations onto specific code targets.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack spatial awareness for one-shot parameterized layout generation, and existing geometric evaluations cannot be directly mapped back to actionable code-level fixes.
AI.method: Upon code execution, SGLayout builds a structured schema linking code instances to geometric attributes, evaluates intent compliance (structural checks and vision-language assessment) and rule compliance (DRC), and projects violations back to exact code targets for iterative repair.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks in GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate compared to 50.89% for the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional code-to-geometry schema linking enables targeted, surgical repair in LLM-driven parameterized layout generation.

title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
summary: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).

AI.tldr: ChainAgent is a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers chainable vulnerabilities and functional gadgets in PHP web applications using an evolving exploit graph.
AI.motivation: Existing vulnerability scanners analyze flaws in isolation while attack planners assume known components, missing vulnerabilities whose security relevance only emerges within an exploit chain.
AI.method: Informed by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent models vulnerabilities and functional gadgets via preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects, searching backward from unmet preconditions and forward from discovered capabilities.
AI.result: Across 15 PHP applications and three LLM backends, ChainAgent achieves 42.02-44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4x more correct dependency edges than Codex; on 30 real-world PHP apps, it finds 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains (9 achieving RCE).
AI.conclusion: Guiding LLM source-code inspection with an evolving exploit graph and object-centered chaining knowledge substantially improves automated discovery of multi-step web exploits.

title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
comment: 10 pages. Accepted at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026). Project page: this https URL
summary: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical reinforcement learning pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, showing superior sample efficiency and performance over flat RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Sequential tasks benefit from composing separately trained skills, but complete demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines need systematic comparison against flat RL baselines.
AI.method: In navigation, parameterized skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manual high-level plans; in manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment, and lifting are trained sequentially by initializing downstream skills from predecessor rollouts, with frozen Pick and Lift skills reused for stacking via a new Place skill.
AI.result: The hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms flat DQN in unseen navigation layouts with fewer interactions, and in manipulation it requires fewer steps than flat SAC with lower cross-seed variance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstration-free skill composition provides a sample-efficient and low-variance alternative to flat reinforcement learning for navigation and manipulation.

title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
summary: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a four-level executable validation protocol to test whether LLM-generated HVAC digital twin specifications are both syntactically valid and physically accurate.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-generated digital twin specifications stop at parse success or simulation convergence, failing to catch models that converge to physically wrong steady states.
AI.method: The protocol checks static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence against a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by +/-20% sizing perturbations, tested across eight LLMs and 14 HVAC topologies.
AI.result: Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6-100% of trials and converged in at least 80.0%, but achieved behavioral equivalence in only 50.0-98.6%, with roughly half of failures converging to wrong steady states (mostly in desiccant rotor systems); pass rates varied by under 5 percentage points across description authors.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific physical validation levels, especially for hard-to-model components like desiccant rotors, are essential when generating executable digital twins with LLMs.

title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
comment: 26 pages, 11 figures, including appendix. Code: this https URL
summary: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

AI.tldr: WeightCode is a Weight-Space Programming framework that uses a frozen LLM to write executable programs that directly install new capabilities into trained neural networks without gradient-based training.
AI.motivation: Extending trained neural networks with explicit task knowledge remains difficult without costly gradient-based fine-tuning or risking catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: A frozen LLM generates executable weight programs that read and modify a network's weights directly using task knowledge, installing independent computations into the target network.
AI.result: Weight programs enable unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success) while preserving prior skills; on ImageNet, four programs yield 8.84-17.62 point net gains over eight fine-tuning baselines, retain 83-110% of gains across five independent ViTs, and compose additively with 5.23-14.50 point contrast-robustness gains.
AI.conclusion: Weight-Space Programming provides a reusable, gradient-free route to installing and accumulating capabilities directly in neural network weights.

title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
summary: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: AIstatLab presents a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet pipeline for BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3 brain-tumor segmentation using consensus pseudo-labeling, nested-region objectives, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter.
AI.motivation: Brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities requires robust training across shared ET, TC, and WT regions and effective use of unlabeled data.
AI.method: Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers generated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases, retaining 983 via fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-agreement screening to train with 1,351 annotated cases using a nested-region objective and four-expert bottleneck adapter.
AI.result: The final five-fold ResEnc-M submission achieved a mean DSC of 0.834, mean NSD of 0.510, and Acalc of 0.6720 on the validation server, with component gains being modest, region-dependent, and clearest on ET.
AI.conclusion: Quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labeling and expert bottleneck adaptation support competitive heterogeneous brain-tumor segmentation.

title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
summary: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $\Theta(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $\Sigma_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that planning width remains NP-hard to approximate within sublinear factors even when the unique optimal plan is supplied.
AI.motivation: Iterative-width search runs in polynomial time for bounded tuple-chain width, but whether knowing an optimal plan makes planning width easier to approximate was an open question.
AI.method: The authors characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states and construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a unique optimal plan, single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions.
AI.result: Distinguishing width 1 from Theta(N) is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width; no polynomial-time algorithm achieves one-sided approximation o(N) or symmetric o(sqrt(N)) unless P=NP, and threshold testing is coNP-complete for fixed k >= 1 and Sigma_2^P-complete for input k, though a greedy algorithm achieves a logarithmic approximation on explicit state graphs.
AI.conclusion: Supplying an optimal plan does not remove the computational hardness of certifying or closely approximating small planning width.

title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
summary: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-based framework for joint speech-scene generation that models distinct, temporally aligned speech and environmental audio token streams from mixed recordings.
AI.motivation: Existing speech-scene generators collapse speech and environment into a single mixed representation and rely on simulated mixtures, failing to capture their distinct acoustics and real-world interactions.
AI.method: A source-aware neural audio codec extracts aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both streams in an interleaved manner conditioned on scene descriptions and speech content.
AI.result: Experiments show improved speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing methods, with consistent gains from adapting to in-the-wild mixed recordings without isolated sources.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved LLM modeling of distinct source-aware token streams enables coherent, high-quality speech-scene generation and real-world adaptation.

title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
summary: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.

AI.tldr: Whole-page policy improvement is a generative re-ranking method that decomposes a page-level objective into per-position training targets to optimize item selection and ordering jointly.
AI.motivation: Existing generative re-ranking methods either apply a uniform page-level signal to every position or imitate static pre-built target pages, failing to capture how items compete and complement each other.
AI.method: The proposed local page-level objective splits into one training target per position, comparing candidate items at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to.
AI.result: On KuaiRand-1K, RL4RS-SeqSlate, and an industrial logged-page dataset, the method outperforms evaluated generative re-ranking baselines, and on a synthetic benchmark with a known optimum it comes closest to the optimal page.
AI.conclusion: Per-position targets derived from complete-page scores enable generative rankers to make better whole-page decisions.

title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
summary: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.

AI.tldr: CoachSI is a self-improvement method for generalist robot policies where a frozen VLM coaches the policy in language by naming the next atomic step, and successful rollouts are relabeled for fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills well but fail on long-horizon composition, and self-training on their own rollouts stays within their existing distribution.
AI.method: A frozen off-the-shelf VLM watches camera images and outputs only the next atomic instruction (never actions); successful coached rollouts are hindsight-relabeled with the original task instruction to fine-tune the policy with its action backbone frozen.
AI.result: Naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x on stalled states, and fine-tuning boosts unassisted long-horizon success in unseen scenes from 47.4% to 59.3% (56.8% with camera-only coaching), beating human-demo and self-collected baselines by 9.8 and 7.3 points at equal data budgets.
AI.conclusion: Language coaching from a frozen VLM teaches robot policies what step comes next without altering their underlying atomic action skills.

title: Towards Autoregressive Neural Network Parameter Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently established a new paradigm in machine learning, demonstrating exceptional zero-shot generalization and complex reasoning capabilities. Concurrently, neural network parameter generation has emerged as a promising avenue for rapid task adaptation and model synthesis. Existing weight generation techniques, however, struggle to jointly learn the distribution of diverse models, to encode heterogeneous architectures within a single generator, and to generalize out of distribution. We therefore ask whether pretrained parameters can be encoded into a discrete domain so that the zero-shot generalization LLMs exhibit in text generation can be transferred to weight generation. Following this view, we propose an LLM-inspired approach, Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (IGPG), that formulates network parameter generation as an autoregressive modeling problem. We first quantize pretrained weights with a VQ-VAE, then train a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator over the resulting tokens. At inference, the generated weight tokens are mapped back to parameter space by the VQ-VAE decoder. We evaluate the framework across in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer, and cross-architecture settings. The proposed method achieves competitive performance in in-distribution generation and provides useful parameter initializations for held-out datasets and architectural configurations, improving downstream performance over random initialization after adaptation. These results suggest that discrete autoregressive modeling provides a promising framework for learning and transferring structure across collections of pretrained neural network parameters.

AI.tldr: Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (IGPG) formulates neural network weight generation as discrete autoregressive modeling over VQ-VAE-quantized parameter tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing weight generators struggle to jointly model diverse distributions, handle heterogeneous architectures, and generalize out of distribution.
AI.method: IGPG quantizes pretrained network weights into discrete tokens using a VQ-VAE, trains a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator over those tokens, and decodes generated tokens back into parameter space at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated across in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer, and cross-architecture settings, IGPG achieves competitive in-distribution performance and provides parameter initializations that outperform random initialization on held-out datasets and architectures after adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Discrete autoregressive modeling over quantized weights offers a promising paradigm for transferring structure across pretrained neural networks.

title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
summary: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.

AI.tldr: FlashX is a CBA-based NAND flash architecture that accelerates experience retrieval for Diffusion Transformer-based embodied agents, improving both task success and inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: Warm-starting DiT denoising with retrieved experiences helps VLA and WAM agents generalize to OOD environments, but scaling experience banks creates storage, bandwidth, and search bottlenecks on edge hardware.
AI.method: FlashX uses CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA) NAND flash with interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines for parallel pSLC key search alongside dense TLC latent storage, paired with proprioception-aware clustering for incremental acquisition.
AI.result: Across VLA and WAM workloads, experience reuse improves task success by up to 12.24%p (dense) and 7.43%p (compute-efficient), while FlashX delivers 2.57x higher search throughput than prior NAND search architectures, 9.7x search reduction via clustering, 1.29-3.95x end-to-end speedup, and 1.12-2.34x energy efficiency over SSD retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing CBA NAND flash with Compute-in-Flash and proprioception-aware clustering enables scalable, energy-efficient experience reuse for embodied AI.

title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
summary: Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities. Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions. Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap. Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis across heterogeneous cohorts.

AI.tldr: HIT-Fuse is a hierarchical tensor fusion framework that integrates six multi-omics and digital pathomics modalities, reconstructs missing modalities, and provides traceable biological attributions for cancer prognosis.
AI.motivation: Precision oncology needs multi-modal integration of molecular and pathology data, but existing fusion models often lack biologically grounded interpretability and cannot handle missing modalities.
AI.method: HIT-Fuse compresses six modalities (CNV, DNA methylation, RNA-seq, miRNA, RPPA, ViT pathomics) with autoencoders, applies two-stage CP tensor decomposition, reconstructs missing latent modalities from clinical covariates and observed omics, and traces attributions mathematically.
AI.result: Across four TCGA cohorts, HIT-Fuse identifies subgroups with significant survival stratification, boosts glioma weighted F1 by 56.4% via cohort expansion, and achieves 71-92% miRTarBase support for decoded miRNAs and 77-84% DepMap coverage for selected genes.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical tensor fusion with missing-modality reconstruction and mathematical traceback enables scalable, biologically interpretable multi-omics cancer prognosis.

title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

AI.tldr: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning (DFRL) post-trains LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as the RL reward.
AI.motivation: When LLM predictions feed into downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not guarantee lower decision costs.
AI.method: DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize induced decision regret without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, using heuristic warm-starting and randomized exact reward correction to reduce expensive exact solves.
AI.result: DFRL outperforms prediction-loss baselines on three synthetic optimization problems and accelerates early learning on knapsack; on H&M inventory planning, reasoning before predicting reduces regret by 31.4% over SFT and 12.4% over the strongest conventional forecasting baseline.
AI.conclusion: Post-training LLMs directly on downstream decision regret aligns predictions with optimization outcomes while keeping exact-solve overhead manageable.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
summary: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

AI.tldr: Tether is a runtime security framework that executes agent actions in an ephemeral sandbox, infers system-call semantics, and enforces formally verified stateful policies written in Lean 4.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agent monitors lack provable guarantees, while stateless policy layers miss multi-step data flows and hidden execution side-effects inside scripts.
AI.method: Tether runs each proposed action in an isolated sandbox to infer abstract semantics from system calls and enforces stateful information-flow, access, and network policies written in an embedded Lean 4 DSL that verifies global security invariants.
AI.result: Evaluated on realistic coding-agent benchmarks with a single shared policy across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while keeping the benign false-positive rate under 5%.
AI.conclusion: Combining sandboxed system-call semantic inference with Lean-verified stateful policies provides provable, low-overhead runtime security for autonomous agents.

title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
comment: Extended version of a paper submitted to ESANN 2027
summary: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.

AI.tldr: This paper derives structural stability bounds for GINs and single-head GATv1 under deterministic edge perturbations and compares them against a perturbation-independent output diameter bound.
AI.motivation: Graph neural network stability bounds are rarely benchmarked against the trivial baseline of bounding the maximum distance between any two outputs regardless of the graph.
AI.method: The authors derive structural stability bounds for GINs and single-head GATv1 under non-small deterministic edge perturbations and characterize when these bounds are tighter than the diameter bound.
AI.result: For GINs, the stability bound is tighter under a condition linking perturbation size, depth, and maximum degree—holding widely on Cora but failing beyond a few layers on MUTAG—whereas for GATv1 the structural bound is never tighter than the diameter bound.
AI.conclusion: Degree-based structural stability bounds can be informative for shallow GINs on high-degree graphs but are vacuous for GATv1, motivating attention-mass-based analyses.

title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
summary: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

AI.tldr: This large-scale empirical study of 120,918 bug reports across 101 open-source projects characterizes how AI involvement in bug reporting and maintenance has evolved from 2024 to 2026.
AI.motivation: AI-generated bug reports have been criticized for unreliable claims, yet some maintainers view AI use positively, requiring empirical evidence on what makes AI-involved reports valid and how maintainers respond.
AI.method: The authors analyze 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects (January 2024 to September 2026), tracing AI involvement across discovery, reporting, validation, and resolution, and test practical reporting guidelines on 53 AI-discovered bug submissions.
AI.result: AI-involved reports have grown more complete and valid over time, with AI use in reproduction and diagnosis (unlike report writing) correlating with higher validity; maintainers spend more effort on AI-assisted human-discovered bugs than AI-discovered ones, and following the authors' verification-focused guidelines yielded a 69.81% acceptance rate across 53 reports.
AI.conclusion: Emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability turns AI-generated bug findings into actionable, maintainer-accepted reports.

title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
summary: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.

AI.tldr: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary hybrid GEMM unit with two PE variants (Splice-BP and Splice-LUT) that substantially reduces tile energy and improves throughput for AI inference accelerators.
AI.motivation: Conventional binary systolic arrays incur high energy and accumulation latency during low-order-bit processing in quantized CNN and LLM inference.
AI.method: Splice-Core minimizes low-order accumulation latency while preserving value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits, implemented via bit-plane (Splice-BP) and single-cycle shared-weight-multiple (Splice-LUT) processing elements.
AI.result: Across 26 INT4 CNN and LLM workloads in 45nm, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT cut geometric-mean tile energy by 77.4% and 76.4% with 14% and 9% smaller post-P&R area than a binary systolic array; Splice-LUT also boosts throughput by 44.4% and reduces EDP by 6.13x, while W8A8 workloads see 77.3-88.1% energy savings.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid temporal-unary/binary GEMM architectures offer major energy, area, and EDP improvements for quantized AI inference accelerators.

title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
summary: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.

AI.tldr: FedDIA is a federated reinforcement learning aggregation method that weights robot clients by their local policy improvement over the global model amplified by inferred environment difficulty.
AI.motivation: Standard federated RL aggregation (uniform averaging or return-weighting) suffers from the plateau problem, where clients in easy environments achieve high returns and dominate updates despite no longer learning.
AI.method: FedDIA scores each client by how much local training improves upon the received global model, scaled by environment difficulty inferred directly from the global model's own performance without environment descriptions.
AI.result: On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA achieves a 75.5% mean success rate across training and held-out environments versus 68.7% for the strongest federated baseline, maintaining its lead under transfer to warehouse/living-space layouts and with a defective client.
AI.conclusion: Weighting federated RL updates by relative improvement and inferred difficulty overcomes the plateau problem in heterogeneous robot fleets.

title: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics
comment: The tool DARSY and all benchmarks are available at this https URL
summary: This paper presents DARSY: a software tool for abstraction-based verification and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions. DARSY requires only a simulator of the system and a Lipschitz bound on its dynamics, and needs no knowledge of dynamics or noise distributions. The tool is fully automated and constructs a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions, whose probability intervals are obtained via statistical techniques and Lipschitz reasoning. Robust dynamic programming on this IMDP then yields a policy together with a lower bound on the probability that the unknown system satisfies a desired specification. This lower bound holds with a user-specified confidence; that is, it is probably approximately correct (PAC). The tool is implemented in Python and supports general Lipschitz-continuous system dynamics and specifications expressed in syntactically co-safe LTL (scLTL), which includes reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety specifications as special cases. Beyond standard IMDPs, DARSY implements a two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction that also bounds the probability of transitioning to aggregated state blocks, yielding smaller abstraction errors than IMDP abstractions and, as a result, tighter satisfaction guarantees. We demonstrate DARSY's broad applicability across a variety of benchmarks and specifications.

AI.tldr: DARSY is an automated Python tool for data-driven abstraction and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions.
AI.motivation: Formal verification and policy synthesis for stochastic systems typically require known dynamics or noise models, which are often unavailable in practice.
AI.method: Using only a simulator and a Lipschitz bound, DARSY samples transitions to build a finite interval MDP (IMDP) or a tighter two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction, then applies robust dynamic programming to synthesize policies for scLTL specifications with PAC lower bounds.
AI.result: Demonstrated across multiple benchmarks and specifications, the 2IMDP abstraction achieves smaller abstraction errors and tighter satisfaction probability guarantees than standard IMDP abstractions.
AI.conclusion: DARSY provides a practical, automated tool for PAC-guaranteed policy synthesis in unknown Lipschitz-continuous stochastic systems.

title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
summary: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.

AI.tldr: A^2-VLA is an agentic affordance-discovery framework that adapts Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to unseen tools by constructing, testing, and reusing geometric affordance skills in simulation.
AI.motivation: Transferring manipulation skills across tools with different shapes requires understanding task-relevant geometric affordances and verifying how new tools support them.
AI.method: Given teleoperated source-tool demos, an embodied agent reconstructs scenes in simulation, discovers and refines functional-region affordance-extraction skills through autonomous experiments, stores them in a skill library, and feeds encoded features to a pi_0.5 backbone.
AI.result: A^2-VLA achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting and improves real-robot task success by 30.7 percentage points over pi_0.5 across three tool-use tasks.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous simulation-based affordance discovery and skill accumulation enable effective zero-shot tool adaptation in VLA policies.

title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
summary: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

AI.tldr: GRODE-RTL is an anchor-centric dependency representation that maps single-clock-stage netlist fan-in cones back to editable RTL source lines to improve LLM-based repair of non-local faults.
