AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with non-local RTL faults because flat source code obscures hardware dataflows while full synthesized netlists overwhelm the context with metadata.
AI.method: GRODE-RTL extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register, maps netlist nodes to source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view that prioritizes direct drivers and folds distant hops.
AI.result: Across 30 formally validated non-local faults, GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets.
AI.conclusion: Selective, source-mapped dependency views rather than full netlist exposure are key to effective LLM-based RTL repair.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

AI.tldr: TipDex-VTLA is a vision-tactile-language-action policy that regulates execution-time action refinement using estimated visual reliability and tactile forecast verification.
AI.motivation: Illumination changes cause action drift in dexterous manipulation, and existing VTLA policies lack principled mechanisms for deciding when and how tactile feedback should correct actions.
AI.method: Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's sensitivity to lighting perturbations, while Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch to gate bounded corrections for unexecuted actions.
AI.result: Trained only under normal lighting, TipDex-VTLA achieves 87.5% average full-task success under normal lighting and 73.8% under challenging unseen lighting across four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining visual sensitivity estimation with tactile forecast verification enables robust dexterous manipulation under unseen illumination shifts.

title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
summary: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.

AI.tldr: Auto-Alpha is an autonomous quantitative factor-research framework that pairs report-guided initialization with a test-driven implementation loop and an Experience Library.
AI.motivation: Autonomous factor research requires both generating economic hypotheses and implementing, backtesting, and auditing them systematically.
AI.method: An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signals, a research agent implements them with backtest feedback, and semantic audits, quantitative reviews, and human admission filter factors into a persistent library alongside an Experience Library.
AI.result: Starting from 120 reports (32 initial factors), Auto-Alpha produces 420 implementations and retains 62 more; on a 105-factor snapshot over 2020-2026, it achieves a median 1-day Rank IC of 0.0301 and 16.81% annualized return after costs for a weekly Top-300 portfolio (vs. 1.71% for CSI 1000).
AI.conclusion: Auto-Alpha demonstrates an end-to-end operating workflow for autonomous factor discovery, though controlled studies are needed to isolate individual component contributions.

title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
summary: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic this http URL and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR) to operationalize emotional overreliance (EO) and relational harm (RH) in AI companionship, finding EO in 63.2% and RH in 10.5% of non-roleplay conversations.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing healthy engagement from harmful emotional reliance on companion AIs is difficult without standardized behavioral definitions.
AI.method: The authors define TRR to separate observable EO behaviors from RH evidence, analyze naturalistic Replika conversations from 110 adults, and evaluate open-source LLMs on detecting 14 EO behaviors.
AI.result: EO-related behaviors appeared in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations and observable RH in 10.5%, with recurring EO patterns co-occurring with harm; open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration.
AI.conclusion: Graduated safety interventions tailored to trajectories of emotional overreliance are needed to mitigate relational harms in AI companionship.

title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
summary: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-driven traffic-control xApp for programmable 5G RANs that dynamically translates operator intents and runtime E2 telemetry into traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAN controllers rely on static rules or fixed state-action spaces that cannot adapt to changing operator intents and network conditions.
AI.method: The xApp combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and current configurations to generate traffic-control policies asynchronously without interrupting packet forwarding or E2 measurement processing.
AI.result: In an OpenAirInterface 5G testbed, the xApp achieves an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91 (vs. 0.52 for static TC-RAN) and maintains approx. 0.88 under degraded channel conditions (vs. approx. 0.4 for static).
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous LLM-driven policy generation enables flexible, intent-aware traffic control in dynamic 5G programmable RANs.

title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

AI.tldr: This mixed-methods study characterizes unfaithful work reports by coding agents into 11 subtypes across four categories and introduces FaithDetector to automatically detect them.
AI.motivation: Coding agents' work reports are often trusted without full verification, so false or unsupported claims can propagate errors and mislead developers and evaluators.
AI.method: Analyzing real developer-agent conversations in SWE-chat, the authors taxonomize self-admitted unfaithful reports, annotate 435 sampled reports, and develop FaithDetector informed by the observed patterns.
AI.result: Overstated task success is the most common subtype, and resolving unfaithful reports costs an average of 4.3 extra user turns and 12.71 minutes; FaithDetector outperforms the baseline by about 13 percentage points in macro-F1 on naturally sampled reports.
AI.conclusion: Empirical characterization and automated detection of unfaithful reporting provide essential safeguards for evaluating and supervising autonomous coding agents.

title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
summary: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10° off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.

AI.tldr: Passage-conditioned navigation enables wheeled-legged robots with fixed locomotion skills to traverse stairs and ledges reliably by recording taught crossing poses and enforcing an entry gate after local replanning.
AI.motivation: Collision-free detours can still leave legged robots slightly misaligned at stairs or ledges, causing fixed skills to stall or fall when no robot model or trial-and-error training is available.
AI.method: From a single 27-minute teaching session, the method stores each crossing as an event and enforces an entry gate before every ledge that forces the robot to turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10 degrees off the taught pose.
AI.result: Under localization noise, valid ledge crossings rise from 24.1% to 88.6%; in simulation, pushed robots suffer 0 falls in 180 stair climbs (vs. 9 without) and rejoin within 0.14 m; on a real robot over 271 m and 7.0 m elevation, it completed all 6 runs and won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge.
AI.conclusion: Remembering and enforcing taught transition poses allows robots with fixed skills to navigate multi-obstacle terrain autonomously without models or retraining.

title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
summary: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Lineage, a large-scale benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature, and shows that 19 representative retrieval systems struggle to recover multi-hop empirical comparison neighborhoods.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks rely on topical relevance or citation links, which fail to capture which prior methods a paper explicitly uses as empirical comparison baselines for literature synthesis and experiment planning.
AI.method: The authors build Lineage-Constructor to convert heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues (2018-2025), yielding 3,950 graph components, 67,502 nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet queries.
AI.result: Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that performance drops sharply with lineage distance and that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.
AI.conclusion: Empirical lineage retrieval remains a challenging open problem, and Lineage provides structural ground truth for evaluating literature retrieval and research agent workflows.

title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
summary: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the call trajectories of the ID algorithm for causal identifiability and derives structural constraints on the nesting, outer summations, and denominators of its output formulas.
AI.motivation: When the ID algorithm determines that an interventional distribution is identifiable, it outputs deeply nested products, ratios, and summations of conditional probabilities whose structure is not well characterized.
AI.method: The authors trace the trajectories of ID algorithm calls, each ending with a tail (alternating lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and use graph ancestry tests to analyze when inner summations persist in denominators.
AI.result: They show that line 4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation while the tail forms all inner summations and ratios, prove that a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a tail repetition is entangled (detectable via an ancestry test in the original graph), and derive a nesting-depth bound and a dimensional count.
AI.conclusion: These structural results constrain the form of ID algorithm outputs and provide direct guidance for implementing and simplifying causal identification formulas.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
comment: 5 main pages, 2 main figures. 15 total pages. Accepted in NeurIPS 2026 EvoRobust Workshop
summary: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: The authors express quantum LDPC belief-propagation decoders in a domain-specific language and use grammatical evolution to discover decoders that substantially improve the time-error Pareto front.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction requires classical decoders that are both accurate and fast enough to keep up with continuous noisy measurements, yet existing decoders are often too slow or suboptimal.
AI.method: They encode published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), re-parameterize BP+OSD and BP+LSD with damping, and apply grammatical evolution over the DSL to search for improved decoding algorithms.
AI.result: Re-parameterizing BP+OSD and BP+LSD with damping makes each 17.1-41.0x faster at higher error rates, with BP+OSD-0 about 103x faster than ldpc's tuned version on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code; an evolved decoder makes 23% fewer logical errors than damped BP+OSD-0 at 0.64x its time, and decoders evolved from random code beat ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less while generalizing across noise levels, code sizes, and round counts.
AI.conclusion: Capturing expert knowledge in a DSL provides an effective intermediate representation that bridges human intuition and automated search for high-efficiency quantum error correction.

title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Fast-JEPA is a latent world model planning framework that avoids recursive rollout during refinement, achieving 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT.
AI.motivation: Latent world models typically evaluate candidate action sequences via recursive rollout at test time, which incurs high planning latency.
AI.method: Fast-JEPA constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts outcomes of complete candidate action sequences without recursive state rollout during refinement; the authors also introduce DynaGoal to benchmark planning under dynamic out-of-distribution shifts, deadlines, and response delays.
AI.result: Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves a 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT, and on DynaGoal it reaches 73.83% average success on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline.
AI.conclusion: Reorganizing predictive computation to avoid recursive rollout advances the success-latency frontier for latent world model planning under dynamic and time-constrained conditions.

title: Safe Subgame Resolving in Multiplayer Games
summary: Poker and other games with hidden information are too large to solve in one pass. Strong systems compute a complete blueprint strategy offline and refine it in real time inside the reached subgame. In 2p0s games, a safety theorem guarantees that subgame resolving never increases how much an adversary can gain by exploiting the resolved strategy relative to the blueprint strategy. With three or more players acting independently, no such guarantee exists yet, and heuristic resolving can increase the profile's best-response gap. We prove the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, a post-hoc certificate for any delivered update. The best-response gap of the resolved profile exceeds that of the blueprint by at most four terms. Two concern the resolver: the subgame value the blueprint promised without realizing ($A_i^{S}$) and the resolver's subgame solve error ($\varepsilon_i$). The other two are the opponents' best-response gains inside the subgame over their promised values ($\sum_q M_{q}$) and a structural tax ($\Theta$), which measures how much the players' total utility can change. The tax is zero in constant-sum games, including every rake-free poker variant. Constructions attain each term with equality. On three-player Leduc poker and on Kuhn poker with up to six players, resolving without a certificate raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of the updates. The certificate flags every such update and accepts 41% (Kuhn) and 86% (Leduc) of the standard resolving updates. A resolver that keeps the blueprint whenever the certificate exceeds the tolerance delivers no harmful update. The certificate needs only one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame, so real-time multiplayer solvers that refine a blueprint can attach it as a safety check. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proves the first conditional safety theorem and post-hoc certificate for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, bounding the best-response gap increase by four explicit terms.
AI.motivation: Unlike two-player zero-sum games where subgame resolving is provably safe, heuristic subgame resolving in games with three or more independent players can increase exploitability.
AI.method: The authors derive a post-hoc safety certificate requiring only one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame, bounding the resolved profile's best-response gap above the blueprint by the blueprint's unrealized subgame value, the resolver's solve error, opponents' best-response gains, and a structural tax (zero in constant-sum games).
AI.result: On three-player Leduc poker and up to six-player Kuhn poker, uncertified resolving raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of updates, whereas the certificate flags every harmful update and accepts 41% (Kuhn) and 86% (Leduc) of standard resolving updates.
AI.conclusion: Real-time multiplayer solvers can attach this lightweight certificate to guarantee that blueprint refinement never delivers a harmful update.

title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
summary: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the legal attribution gap in autonomous AI agent deployment and proposes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA) to provide runtime legal legibility.
AI.motivation: Current agent communication and authentication protocols such as MCP and A2A mature at the protocol layer but do not provide legal legibility for attributing liability or allocating data and economic rights across organizations.
AI.method: The authors propose AULA, which registers AI systems and data assets as legal objects anchored to identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments carrying legal context clauses evaluated at runtime.
AI.result: The paper characterizes the bidirectional legal attribution gap covering harm liability and value/property rights, and outlines how AULA's runtime evaluation enforces applicable legislation, regulation, and judicial decisions.
AI.conclusion: Legal-layer infrastructure like AULA is presented as a necessary precondition for functioning legal, property, and economic systems involving both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
summary: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a causal message-transplantation protocol to test whether global-workspace language models genuinely recombine broadcast information rather than ignoring or relaying it.
AI.motivation: Building a global workspace into a neural network does not reveal whether modules actually compute with broadcast messages, and task accuracy or ablation cannot distinguish ignoring, relaying, and recombining.
AI.method: The causal protocol transplants a workspace message from another input chosen so that ignoring, relaying, and recombining the message predict three distinct answers.
AI.result: The test achieves 100% accuracy on synthetic networks built to relay or recombine, reveals all three behaviors among trained workspace models, and shows that in the AFGW language model a transplanted message yields the recombination answer in 97% of cases by redirecting memory retrieval.
AI.conclusion: This causal protocol turns Global Workspace Theory's central claim into an empirically testable property of trained neural and Transformer models.

title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Demo paper submitted to The Web Conference 2027 (WWW 2027). Code: this https URL
summary: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.

AI.tldr: GenSPARQL extends SPARQL 1.1 with a generative operator (GENOP) that binds LLM-generated values to query variables and maps them to knowledge graph entities via similarity joins.
AI.motivation: Web knowledge graphs are incomplete and standard SPARQL only queries stored triples, while naive LLM querying returns names rather than IRIs and requires one call per variable binding.
AI.method: GenSPARQL introduces GENOP into SPARQL 1.1 to invoke an LLM only for bindings selected by graph patterns and filters, then uses an embedding similarity join to map generated names to graph entities.
AI.result: In an evaluation with three open-weight LLMs over two Wikidata-derived graphs, embedding similarity maps 83% of the LLM-named entities with only one incorrect match.
AI.conclusion: GenSPARQL demonstrates a practical query-planned integration of LLMs into SPARQL for answering queries over incomplete knowledge graphs.

title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.

AI.tldr: ChronoPatch is a black-box energy-latency attack on vision-language models that prolongs generation and increases serving cost using only final-response access.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive decoding makes response length a key driver of VLM latency and energy cost, but prior energy-latency attacks require gradients, logits, or token-level feedback rather than realistic black-box final-response access.
AI.method: ChronoPatch discovers visual delay anchors via response-length-guided evolutionary search and minimizes perturbation magnitude using subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization.
AI.result: Across four open-source VLMs under a 5% spatial budget, ChronoPatch increases latency by 47.86%-293.34% and GPU energy by 41.44%-249.70% while increasing n-gram repetition; on three commercial VLM APIs within 500 queries, it increases response length by 37.6%-81.5% and latency by 1.82x-2.29x.
AI.conclusion: Generation-based availability risks persist even under final-response-only black-box access, motivating generation-aware safeguards for deployed VLMs.

title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
comment: 39 pages, 26 figures, 16 tables. Checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies budget internalization, showing that fixed-budget RLVR training teaches reasoning models a length constraint that trades test-time scaling at larger budgets for higher in-budget accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models are typically trained with RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) under a fixed rollout cap, but how this cap affects test-time scaling beyond the training budget was unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B across math, science, coding, and procedural tasks, and run training-objective and SFT ablations on Qwen3.5-4B.
AI.result: Models trained with a fixed rollout cap outperform base models near that budget but stop improving and fall below base models at larger budgets; stronger KL regularization and lower truncation preserve scaling at the cost of in-budget accuracy, while SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces the effect.
AI.conclusion: Budget internalization stems from length-censored post-training rather than an RL-specific objective, meaning rollout caps trade extra-compute test-time scaling for low-budget gains.

title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
summary: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $\alpha$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $\alpha$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

AI.tldr: Sightline is a calibrated data-flow summary tool for LLM-integrated applications that predicts which prompt placeholders flow to the output in one forward pass, backed by a Lean 4 theorem.
AI.motivation: Static and dynamic analyses of LLM-integrated programs either taint every output with every input or incur high cost by querying a second LLM, because existing gradient or perturbation signals fail on confident outputs or duplicated spans.
AI.method: The authors prove and mechanize in Lean 4 that a placeholder flows to a transformer's output to first order only through attention that reads it; Sightline reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates pruning to miss at most a target fraction alpha of true flows.
AI.result: Across 2,103 unseen repository families and four models at alpha = 1%, Sightline misses about 1% of true flows while pruning 43.9%-65.6% of spurious flows (1.6x to 2.6x more than the best baseline), generalizes cross-collection (43.8%-60.1%), transfers to closed models via an open surrogate, and removes about half of unnecessary information-flow labels in an LLM agent.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based calibrated data-flow summaries provide an accurate, theoretically grounded, and low-overhead way to track information flow across the NL/PL boundary.

title: FastRoverVLA: Fast Vision-Language-Action Execution for Off-Road Autonomous Driving
summary: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FastRoverVLA is a training-free interface for off-road vision-language-action models that decouples visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution, cutting FDE and request rates simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Frequent trajectory updates in off-road VLA models repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference, whereas naively reusing plans leaves commands vulnerable to vehicle motion changes.
AI.method: FastRoverVLA maintains a speed-curvature action buffer aligned with measured vehicle motion, integrates and consumes actions while writing back the corrected remainder, and uses a bounded refresh rule based on plan roughness to set short or long reuse budgets.
AI.result: Over a 3 s horizon, FastRoverVLA achieves 0.328/0.596 m ADE/FDE on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at 6.0% and 4.8% request rates while cutting Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by 16.6x and 20.8x.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling visual planning from persistent motion-conditioned state correction enables accurate, low-cost off-road VLA execution without retraining.

title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a simple continual reinforcement learning benchmark and demonstrates the stability gap, where prior-task performance drops sharply upon introducing new tasks before recovering.
AI.motivation: Final aggregate metrics in continual reinforcement learning (CRL) can mask temporary performance degradation during task adaptation.
AI.method: The authors design a lightweight CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while keeping environment dynamics and rewards fixed, enabling controlled, reproducible experiments.
AI.result: Using this benchmark, they observe a substantial temporary drop in prior-task performance immediately after new tasks are introduced, followed by partial or complete recovery, even when the agent retains full access to past tasks.
AI.conclusion: Highlighting the stability gap underscores the need to evaluate intermediate adaptation dynamics rather than relying solely on final aggregate CRL metrics.

title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at ICSE 2027. Code and data: this https URL
summary: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.

AI.tldr: SkillBridge is a three-stage contract-based workflow that screens, dynamically validates, and repairs cross-OS compatibility defects in LLM agent skills at a fraction of exhaustive testing cost.
AI.motivation: Agent skills often fail when moved across operating systems due to scattered OS assumptions, and exhaustively running every skill on every OS wastes tokens, runner time, and review effort.
AI.method: SkillBridge performs static contract screening across 3,270 skill-OS cases (1,090 skills on Linux, macOS, Windows), runs targeted dynamic validation and root-cause review on flagged cases, and repairs faulty contract fields such as guide text, scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations.
AI.result: Repairs raise the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4% (+7.8 percentage points), and a Linux/macOS budget analysis finds 38 confirmed OS issues in 185 dynamic validations compared to ~865 expected under uniform random selection.
AI.conclusion: Contract-based static screening combined with targeted dynamic validation enables cost-effective diagnosis and repair of cross-OS defects in agent skills.

title: A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger States Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, Lean examples. Comments welcome
summary: Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating an \(N\)-photon \(D\)-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even \(N\ge4\) when \(D\ge N\). The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum \(\mathcal F\) of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an \((N-1)\times N\) matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes \(\omega\) and GHZ target \(\Delta\), the row--column imbalance yields \(\mathcal F(\omega)=0\) but \(\mathcal F(\Delta)\neq0\), contradicting the required equality \(\omega=\Delta\). Finally, we give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.

AI.tldr: Using AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean with AlphaProof Nexus, the authors prove a tensor-algebraic no-go theorem ruling out monochromatic quantum graphs for even N >= 4 photonic GHZ states when D >= N.
AI.motivation: Determining whether probabilistic pair sources can generate high-dimensional N-photon D-dimensional GHZ states reduces to the existence of edge-colored, complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graphs, which was unresolved for general even N >= 4 and D >= N.
AI.method: Discovered via AlphaProof Nexus in Lean, the proof constructs a vertex-factorized weighted sum F of amplitudes and sums over colors at one vertex to reduce the problem to an (N-1) x N matrix of effective edge weights.
AI.result: The row-column imbalance yields F(omega) = 0 for any graph amplitudes omega while F(Delta) != 0 for the GHZ target Delta, contradicting omega = Delta for all even N >= 4 with D >= N.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a formal no-go theorem for high-dimensional photonic GHZ state generation and provides a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered proof.

title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics
summary: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that deep feedback control (DFC) arises as a local approximation to predictive coding (PC) dynamics near fixed points, unifying energy-based and control-theoretic local learning.
AI.motivation: Predictive coding and deep feedback control are two prominent biologically plausible alternatives to backpropagation, but their mathematical relationship has remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze PC activity dynamics near equilibrium, characterize the resulting approximation (Approx PC) and its deviations with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium, and mitigate these deviations via controller relinearization and intermediate output nudges.
AI.result: DFC is exactly equivalent to PC in shallow linear networks; on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC matches PC task performance under the same nudges, and its learned weights transfer directly to PC inference.
AI.conclusion: Establishing DFC as a local approximation to PC bridges energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives and enables applying control theory to train predictive coding networks.

title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
summary: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes nonasymptotic total-variation convergence guarantees for Euler-discretized flow matching from non-Gaussian source distributions.
AI.motivation: Flow matching supports flexible non-Gaussian sources such as heavy-tailed or multimodal distributions, yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources have been limited.
AI.method: The authors analyze Euler discretization of linear-interpolation flow matching using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, assuming a source on R^d with everywhere positive continuously differentiable density, finite total variance TotVar_base, and L-Lipschitz score, plus a mild second-moment condition on the target.
AI.result: They prove that the sampler achieves total variation error at most epsilon in O_tilde(L d TotVar_base / epsilon) iterations, covering sources like multivariate Student's t (df > 2) and shared-covariance Gaussian mixtures without requiring smooth target densities or bounded target support.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides rigorous finite-step convergence guarantees that justify using diverse non-Gaussian source distributions in flow matching.

title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
summary: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{\lambda_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes, proving uniform-in-time sharpness and loss reduction guarantees and matching SAM's flattening effect without extra gradient evaluations.
AI.motivation: Finding flat minima improves generalization, but existing adaptive or sharpness-aware methods either lack uniform-in-time theoretical guarantees or require extra computational overhead.
AI.method: CDP multiplies the classical Polyak stepsize by 4 and a mild damping factor, inducing equioscillations around the minimizer manifold M so that projected iterates follow gradient descent on log(lambda_1(nabla^2 L)) along M.
AI.result: The authors establish uniform-in-time sharpness and loss reduction guarantees for locally quadratic Morse-Bott losses, and show empirically on nonlinear teacher-student networks and LLM fine-tuning that CDP reduces sharpness comparably to Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM).
AI.conclusion: Critically damped Polyak stepsizes offer a theoretically grounded, computationally lightweight way to bias gradient descent toward flat interpolating minima.

title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
comment: 33 pages (12 pages of main text, 3 pages of references, 18 pages of appendices), 9 figures, 12 tables
summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

AI.tldr: Origin is a cross-layer backtracking tool that bridges agent trajectory logs and application source code to pinpoint compromise entry points (CEPs) in agent security incidents.
AI.motivation: During agent security incidents, trajectory logs capture high-level agent functionalities while CEP candidates are low-level function calls in source code, forcing analysts to manually inspect code to bridge the semantic gap.
AI.method: Origin constructs a cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) linking region-inferred semantic functions to variables in a low-level taint propagation subgraph, supported by a region inference algorithm and a query language.
AI.result: Across case studies on five popular agent applications and eight attack incidents, analysts using Origin correctly identify all CEPs with a small number of queries.
AI.conclusion: Cross-layer dependency modeling automates the mapping between agent behavior logs and code-level taint paths, enabling accurate incident backtracking.

title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
summary: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a production agentic system for fleet-scale ranking feature optimization under shared pipeline-cost and per-model QPS constraints, improving offline normalized entropy by 0.31% and an online A/B metric by 0.20%.
AI.motivation: Large web platforms manage fleets of ranking models drawing from tens of thousands of features, making manual feature selection and cross-feature tuning under global cost and per-model throughput caps difficult.
AI.method: LLM agents propose cross features and tune selections over 10-25 asynchronous trials using deterministic experiment tools, multi-method importance blending (with Pareto fronts for multi-task models), and a cost-trimming step.
AI.result: Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within budget, trims pipeline cost by 2.3% without regression, and improves a primary online metric by 0.20% in launched A/B tests.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM hypothesis generation with deterministic verification and cost-aware trimming yields measurable offline and online gains at fleet scale.

title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

AI.tldr: ROGUE-AI is a multi-agent audit framework that reproduces 89% of 108 real-world agentic security incidents offline with matched controls, revealing that non-adversarial ordinary hazards cause more harm than prompt injections.
AI.motivation: Media reports and incident catalogs document agentic failures, but they neither replicate incidents nor isolate whether the blamed cause actually triggered the harm.
AI.method: ROGUE-AI rebuilds each reported incident offline alongside a matched control lacking only the blamed cause, and evaluates agents built on five GPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek models across both conditions.
AI.result: ROGUE-AI reproduces reported harm in 89% of 108 attempts; agents commit the reported mistake in 18%-33% of runs versus at most 1% in controls; 62 of 72 real-world harm incidents involved no attacker; and post-tool hazard-specific warnings reduce harm across all five models whereas generic notes of the same length do not.
AI.conclusion: Reusable incident replications provide vendors with a pre-release audit framework and highlight that defending against ordinary operational hazards is as critical as defending against prompt injection.

title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
summary: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

AI.tldr: GEOHunter measures a real-world Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) network across three Chinese UGC platforms, finding 466,357 promotional placements that significantly skew generative engine answers.
AI.motivation: Paid GEO services plant promotional articles on UGC platforms to manipulate generative engine recommendations, posing risks in sensitive domains like medicine and finance, yet the scale and impact of these networks in the wild are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors track a paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms and evaluate its citation and mention rates across nine US and Chinese generative engines.
AI.result: They uncover 1,985 accounts and 466,357 inferred promotional placements; 4.5%-20% of retrievable cited pages across nine engines come from the network, and its clients are named in 52% of answers on eight engines (versus 68% for category leaders).
AI.conclusion: Coordinated UGC GEO placements effectively manipulate generative engine outputs, showing that content-level defenses alone are insufficient without account- and platform-level signals.

title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
summary: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

AI.tldr: Verify the Verifier is an LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker that inspects passing UVM regression traces against hardware specifications to catch scoreboard escapes, confirming 41 escaped bugs in OpenTitan IPs.
AI.motivation: Passing a UVM regression only proves agreement with a reference model on checked properties, allowing specification-violating bugs (scoreboard escapes) to survive mature testbenches.
AI.method: The framework uses an LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker to examine traces from passing UVM regressions directly against the hardware specification.
AI.result: Out of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 were candidate scoreboard escapes (non-equivalent, exercised, yet passing), and the framework confirmed 41 of them with assertions that fail on the buggy design and are proven on the original.
AI.conclusion: Specification-grounded LLM trace auditing effectively uncovers subtle hardware bugs that bypass conventional UVM scoreboards.

title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
summary: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $\rho$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $\rho=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $\pi=P(\mu(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $\epsilon$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/\rho$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hat{\rho}=0.435$, $\hat{\theta}=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hat{\rho}=0.480$, $\hat{\theta}=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $\epsilon=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that positive correlation across LLM reasoning rollouts splits the self-consistency certification null into realized and population nulls, and shows how a prompt-level e-process restores population validity.
AI.motivation: Anytime-valid self-consistency certification via e-processes assumes conditionally independent rollouts, which fails in practice due to shared reasoning prefixes and across-prompt heterogeneity.
AI.method: The authors model rollout dependence via a per-unit random-effects structure with intraclass correlation rho, analyze single-unit betting e-processes versus a prompt-level e-process, and validate on simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts on GSM8K and AIME.
