AI.result: The single-unit e-process remains valid for the realized null but can exceed nominal Type I error on the population null (crossing on 24% of AIME prompts at nominal epsilon = 0.05 with rho_hat = 0.480), whereas the prompt-level e-process restores population validity (0.00 crossing on AIME) with optimal allocation of one rollout per prompt.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for rollout correlation is essential to ensure anytime-valid self-consistency certificates support the intended population-level reliability claim.

title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: PGX is a hierarchical framework for long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation that offloads temporal sequencing and spatial precision to training-free components, improving stage progression and task success on Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Monolithic vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle on long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation because temporal structure, skill execution, and spatial precision are tightly coupled.
AI.method: PGX combines a predicate-based state machine for phase transitions and recovery, VLA skills operating within active manipulation phases, and world-coordinate locking (WCL) for base station keeping and object-relative/world-anchored precision.
AI.result: Experiments on three simulated tasks and one real-world task with a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved stage progression and higher task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Offloading temporal and spatial control to classical training-free components allows VLA policies to focus on skill dynamics and succeed on long-horizon humanoid tasks.

title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
summary: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

AI.tldr: OracleImitator solves Active Feature Acquisition by distilling a closed-form training-time oracle teacher's feature ranking into a deployable policy, recovering 90% of attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the cost.
AI.motivation: Existing Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) methods train policies using self-constructed utility targets rather than distilling an explicit teacher, limiting sample efficiency and interpretability.
AI.method: Using training-time labels and unobserved features, the authors construct a closed-form oracle teacher that ranks candidate features by their effect on downstream predictor error, and distill this ranking into OracleImitator via soft-target imitation.
AI.result: Across multimodal medical diagnosis and AFABench, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA baselines across budgets, recovering 90% of attainable accuracy gain at under 25% of the acquisition cost.
AI.conclusion: Explicit oracle distillation provides a strong, transparent alternative to implicit utility optimization for budget-constrained active feature acquisition.

title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

AI.tldr: This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) rates LLM vulnerability-research capabilities on an autonomy scale, documents a doubling of disclosed vulnerabilities in 2026, and grades proposed mitigations.
AI.motivation: Claims about LLM agents discovering, validating, and patching real-world software vulnerabilities are scattered across papers and vendor reports without a comparable evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors introduce an autonomy scale modeled on driving automation, qualify claims by correctness, availability, and evidence strength, analyze a decade of public vulnerability and exploitation records, and grade literature mitigations with an explicit rubric.
AI.result: Agents autonomously discovered, validated, and patched real-world bugs before 2026 restricted frontier models, with open-weight models later matching discovery and validation; in 2026 disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled with more critical/high bugs and decade-old flaws, though report-to-fix and disclosure-to-attack times have not shifted noticeably.
AI.conclusion: The systematization provides stakeholders with an evidence-graded map of evolving LLM offensive/defensive security capabilities and the most strongly supported mitigations.

title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
comment: Accepted to the KDD 2027 AI for Sciences Track
summary: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

AI.tldr: PsyWorld is a profile-conditioned state world model that uses realized environment-behavior transitions as supervision, achieving 0.904 Top-1 accuracy on unseen participants in human behavior prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized agents condition actions directly on static psychometric profiles, leaving realized state transitions unused as explicit training supervision.
AI.method: A posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions during training while a prior predicts codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context; the prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator execution.
AI.result: On a participant-disjoint split (240 train, 25 val, 48 test) in VEET and AgentSociety, PsyWorld reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL on VEET, with ablations linking continuous next-state modeling to Top-1 gains and discrete codes/prior alignment to Top-3 and distributional alignment.
AI.conclusion: Transition-informed world-model supervision improves subject-generalized human behavior prediction without claiming causal psychological mechanisms.

title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
summary: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that first-order directional derivatives predict model-merging interference only when evaluated at the receiver model rather than the pretrained backbone, and introduces LR-Merge for label-free coefficient correction.
AI.motivation: Evaluating model-merging interference requires constructing and testing candidate merges, making coefficient search computationally expensive.
AI.method: The authors evaluate first-order directional derivatives at receiver models to build a receiver-local affine surrogate, and use it in LR-Merge to optimize merge coefficients via convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes without backpropagating through merged networks.
AI.result: Receiver-local derivatives halve accuracy error versus a no-change baseline and identify most prediction flips (whereas backbone derivatives are nearly orthogonal in vision); LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified mergers, matches exact teacher matching (which is ~3x slower to converge), and answers new coefficient/subset queries in seconds.
AI.conclusion: Linearizing at receiver models rather than the shared backbone enables fast, accurate, label-free prediction and correction of model-merging interference.

title: HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
comment: 41 pages, 22 figures, 8 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

AI.tldr: HapBO compiles natural-language expert or LLM priors once into a reusable non-Gaussian belief function for Bayesian optimization, achieving top HPOBench performance with zero in-loop LLM token cost.
AI.motivation: Prior-guided Bayesian optimization improves sample efficiency, but real-world domain knowledge is typically expressed in natural language rather than explicit probability distributions, and calling LLMs in the loop is costly.
AI.method: Building on alpha-piBO, HapBO elicits beliefs once from a human expert and/or LLM, deterministically compiles them into a bounded positive multiplier pi(x) in [0, 1] on any nonnegative acquisition function, and preserves standard Expected Improvement simple-regret rates even under adversarial beliefs.
AI.result: Across 40 HPOBench tasks, 6-15D synthetic functions, cortical neurostimulation, and constrained solar design, HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world results at 12-20 query budgets with zero in-loop token cost.
AI.conclusion: One-shot compilation of natural-language priors into bounded acquisition multipliers delivers sample-efficient, theoretically safe Bayesian optimization without ongoing LLM overhead.

title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. R package discoCVI available on CRAN
summary: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

AI.tldr: discoCVI v0.2.0 computes the DISCO density-based clustering validity index in linear memory by reading required quantities off the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree's single-linkage merge tree.
AI.motivation: Direct implementations of the DISCO index store multiple n-by-n pairwise distance matrices, creating prohibitive memory overhead for large datasets.
AI.method: The authors show that all quantities needed by DISCO can be extracted from the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, reducing memory complexity from quadratic to linear while keeping quadratic runtime.
AI.result: The R implementation matches the Python reference within 3e-13, fixes singleton cluster scoring, runs 23-138x faster than v0.1 (500-4,000 points) and 3-9x faster than Python (500-8,000 points), and scores 100,000 points in ~50 seconds under 200 MB of memory.
AI.conclusion: Tree-based computation makes the DISCO validity index practical for large-scale density-based clustering evaluation in R.

title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
summary: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, this paper shows that causal relevance in learned weather models does not require physical semantics and that steering convection features reduces tropical-cyclone intensity error by a median of 51%.
AI.motivation: Auditing whether AI weather forecasters rely on reliable mechanisms requires testing whether internal latent features with causal impact correspond to recognizable physical concepts.
AI.method: The authors extract sparse autoencoder features from DeepMind's GraphCast and perform activation ablations and feature-scaling interventions during autoregressive rollouts.
AI.result: Ablating a mesh-locked feature without conventional physical semantics increases global geopotential height error; suppressing convection and low-level-vorticity features weakens tropical-cyclone deepening, while amplifying convection features achieves a median 51% intensity error reduction across seven storms.
AI.conclusion: Sparse autoencoder features serve as effective experimental coordinates for auditing and steering learned weather dynamics, separating physical interpretability from causal utility.

title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
comment: 31 pages including appendix, 14 figures, D. Nayak and Y. Pu contributed equally to this work
summary: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

AI.tldr: A coupled TI-DeepONet and FNO predictor-corrector framework extrapolates elastic seismic velocity fields up to 2x beyond the training time interval with 0.61%-2.82% mean peak-normalized RMSE.
AI.motivation: Neural operator models struggle to extrapolate seismic wavefields temporally beyond the time horizon seen during training.
AI.method: A time-integrator-embedded DeepONet (TI-DeepONet) with an embedded RK4 scheme advances the velocity field, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a spatial residual correction in a jointly trained predictor-corrector setup conditioned on reference stress fields and prescribed excitation.
AI.result: Tested on SH waves in four-layer soil columns (50 m and 280 m depths, 0.5-6 Hz DOG3 wavelets) at up to 2x the training duration, the model achieves 0.53%-2.31% mean peak-normalized RMSE over full windows and 0.61%-2.82% over extrapolation intervals.
AI.conclusion: Stress-conditioned predictor-corrector neural operators accurately extrapolate elastic seismic velocity fields, though autonomous coupled velocity-stress continuation remains open.

title: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
summary: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes hierarchical content summarization as a rate-distortion problem, enabling quantitative benchmarking of LLMs on long-context QA and guiding more efficient RAG.
AI.motivation: Evaluating generative content manipulation and summarization remains largely subjective, limiting rigorous comparison of model efficiency and information retention.
AI.method: Inspired by Shannon rate-distortion theory, the authors extract the semantic hierarchy of source content to measure the trade-off between compression rate and information distortion, and use this hierarchy to guide retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
AI.result: Experiments on long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art LLMs characterize their rate-distortion efficiency, and hierarchy-guided RAG improves rate-distortion characteristics over current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Rate-distortion assessment provides a principled, quantitative framework for benchmarking generative summarization and improving hierarchical RAG.

title: Bayesian $κ$-Explorer for Minimax Model Estimation in MDPs
summary: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.

AI.tldr: Bayesian kappa-Explorer replaces confidence-set optimization in minimax MDP transition estimation with Dirichlet priors and posterior-mean planning, retaining the O_tilde(T^{-1/3}) rate with lower worst-case error.
AI.motivation: Frequentist kappa-Explorer achieves minimax transition estimation in unknown MDPs but requires computationally heavy confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over transition kernels and occupancy measures.
AI.method: Bayesian kappa-Explorer places Dirichlet priors on transition distributions, uses total posterior variance as a closed-form exploration signal for posterior expected squared l2 error, and plans directly under the posterior mean model.
AI.result: Under stated assumptions, it preserves the O_tilde(T^{-1/3}) surrogate convergence rate, bounds maximum posterior variance against the asymptotic minimax benchmark, and achieves lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than baselines on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi.
AI.conclusion: Posterior-mean planning with Dirichlet priors makes minimax active exploration in MDPs practical without sacrificing theoretical convergence guarantees.

title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

AI.tldr: DualSAE augments standard sparse autoencoders with a decorrelated Residual Branch to separate semantic interpretability from reconstruction fidelity, improving both by ~34% and ~29% respectively.
AI.motivation: Standard sparse autoencoders force a single sparse representation to handle both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, two objectives that often conflict.
AI.method: DualSAE pairs a standard SAE Sparse Branch (capturing dominant semantics) with a plug-in Residual Branch (capturing non-semantic details) trained with a decorrelation loss and a two-stage strategy.
AI.result: Across two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative gains of ~29% in reconstruction fidelity and ~34% in monosemanticity, and improves downstream topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic sparsity from residual reconstruction resolves the fidelity-interpretability trade-off in sparse autoencoders.

title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

AI.tldr: Conditioning a meta-learned PINN optimizer on an 11-dimensional PDE state via bounded FiLM improves all error metrics over Adam and unconditioned learned optimizers on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers equations.
AI.motivation: Learned optimizers for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) rely only on local parameter and history features, ignoring global PDE operator structure and domain-wide residual geometry.
AI.method: The authors design an 11-dimensional PDE state capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to modulate a structured meta-learned optimizer via bounded feature-wise modulation (bounded FiLM).
AI.result: Design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as strongest, outperforming Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer across relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating compact PDE-level residual-geometry state into learned optimizers consistently accelerates and improves PINN training.

title: ϕTD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. First two authors contributed equally
summary: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

AI.tldr: phiTD is a distributional reinforcement learning algorithm that computes the loss in the frequency domain using characteristic functions, unifying quantile and categorical RL while capturing continuous mixtures.
AI.motivation: Existing distributional RL methods are restricted to narrow distribution families such as discrete categoricals or fixed quantiles.
AI.method: phiTD represents return distributions via characteristic functions and optimizes the distributional Bellman loss directly in the frequency domain.
AI.result: The authors show theoretically that phiTD unifies quantile and categorical approaches and demonstrate empirically across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments that wider parametric flexibility improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain characteristic-function learning removes parametric bottlenecks in distributional RL and enables richer return-distribution modeling.

title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
summary: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

AI.tldr: On NextUnit-Bench, frontier LLM coding agents outperform AutoML and most published PHM methods by tailoring model designs to each machine's data, showing generality is shifting from the model to the modeler.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether generality in prognostics and health management (PHM) should reside in a single universal model or in an autonomous coding agent that builds a custom model per task.
AI.method: The authors introduce NextUnit-Bench (24 public datasets, 58 held-out unit/condition folds, 2-hour agent budget) and evaluate frontier coding agents, AutoML, published PHM methods, and plan-transfer ablations.
AI.result: Frontier agents beat AutoML (which scores under half the best agent) and 24 of 30 faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets; transferring a post-data plain-text plan accounts for most of the gap between strong and weak frontier agents, whereas pre-data plans or domain toolkits help little, and locally deployable open-weight models fail to execute strong plans half as often.
AI.conclusion: Generality in applied ML is moving from static models to data-adaptive agentic modelers, provided the executing agent is capable enough to implement the design.

title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables (under review for NAMRC55 - 2027)
summary: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

AI.tldr: A process-knowledge-guided latent diffusion model with ControlNet conditioning and regressor-gradient steering generates porous layouts tailored to aerosol jet printing flow settings, cutting utilization scores from 0.642 to 0.450.
AI.motivation: Unconditioned generative models sample the same porous layout distribution regardless of manufacturing process settings, even though optimal layouts depend strongly on process parameters.
AI.method: The framework combines a VQ-VAE, topology U-Net, ControlNet domain branch, and a noised-latent regressor predicting a process-dependent material utilization score, using regressor gradients to steer denoising for given atomizer and sheath gas flows.
AI.result: Across seven flow settings, the best candidate layout differed in 191 of 500 domains; in sampling on three validation and one test domain, the mean utilization score (lower is better) improved from 0.642 (domain conditioning alone) to 0.636 (weight 300) and 0.450 (weight 12,000).
AI.conclusion: Embedding process-physics models into latent diffusion via gradient steering enables process-specific generative design of porous architectures.

title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection
summary: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual-model adaptive adversarial detection framework that trains a separate verifier using activation signatures to guide challenging adversarial example generation, outperforming confidence-based and feature-based detectors under L-infinity adaptive attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly design adaptive attacks to bypass them.
AI.method: The authors keep the original classifier fixed and train a separate verifier using activation signatures (patterns of internal activations distinguishing genuine from adversarial examples of a target class) to guide the generation of hard adversarial examples, while preserving clean accuracy via knowledge distillation and requiring no signatures at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on public datasets against several adaptive attacks including unseen ones, the verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under L-infinity attacks, with ablations showing adaptive verifier training drives the robustness gain and signature guidance aids clean accuracy, though L2 evaluations show cross-perturbation limitations.
AI.conclusion: Signature-guided adaptive verifier training offers a stronger defense against adaptive L-infinity adversarial attacks without modifying the base classifier, while highlighting remaining challenges in L2 robustness.

title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
summary: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Scone, a color-equivariant graph neural network for sequential graph coloring that achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times and generalizes to unseen graph families.
AI.motivation: Graph coloring with a fixed palette is NP-hard, and learning-based methods need to exploit color-permutation symmetry to shrink the state space while still breaking node symmetries between adjacent nodes in the same automorphism orbit.
AI.method: Scone uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct node colorings sequentially, allowing information from prior assignments to propagate and break node symmetries.
AI.result: Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and generalizes to graph families not seen during training.
AI.conclusion: Combining color-equivariance with sequential symmetry breaking provides an effective and generalizable neural combinatorial optimization approach for graph coloring.

title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
summary: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes deep structured state space models (DS3M) with custom Triton GPU kernels to accelerate continuous-time nonlinear system identification.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time neural state-space identification methods like SUBNET require many sequential neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, leading to slow training speeds that hinder practical use.
AI.method: DS3M combines compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series, includes a port-Hamiltonian variant, and uses custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton to reduce launch and memory overhead during sequential evaluation.
AI.result: The authors present benchmark comparisons demonstrating the accuracy and training-time improvements of DS3M over existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Structuring state-space components and fusing their sequential evaluation via Triton kernels makes continuous-time nonlinear system identification practical on modern GPU hardware.

title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
summary: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CARE, a cross-question reinforcement learning reward that calibrates LLM verbalized confidence relative to other questions, boosting selective prediction coverage at 5% risk from 0.8% to 42.4% on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Pointwise correctness-matching rewards push LLM confidence scores toward 0 or 1, which is unattainable in practice and destroys the relative ordering needed for selective prediction at non-zero risk tolerances.
AI.method: CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation) computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs by deriving abstention thresholds from the set's confidence distribution at multiple risk tolerances and rewarding each confidence for falling on the correct side of the threshold.
AI.result: On math benchmarks (MATH-500, GSM8K, Big-Math-Digits), CARE increases coverage at 5% risk (C@5) from 0.8% to 42.4% over pointwise rewards, and when trained on HotpotQA, it improves out-of-distribution C@5 across CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA from 12.3% to 23.6%.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcing relative confidence across sets of questions rather than pointwise binary targets enables reliable abstention and selective prediction in LLMs.

title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
summary: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper compares federated optimizers for training car aerodynamics surrogates and shows that spectral optimizers (FedMuon, FedMARS-M) reach within 2% of centralized drag error while non-spectral methods lag by 17 to 37%.
AI.motivation: Training neural aerodynamics surrogates requires thousands of proprietary CFD simulations across car manufacturers, motivating federated learning, yet it is unclear which federated optimizer best matches centralized training.
AI.method: On DrivAerNet++, the authors train a Transolver surrogate across six single-body-type clients and compare three spectral optimizers that orthogonalize weight-matrix updates (FedMuon, FedMARS-M, FedOLion) against three non-spectral optimizers (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam, FedLion).
AI.result: FedMuon and FedMARS-M achieve drag errors within 2% of centralized Muon training using 2 to 4 local epochs per round, whereas the best non-spectral methods (at 16 local epochs) still have 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M, a gap explained by low stable rank of weight gradients.
AI.conclusion: Spectral optimizers that orthogonalize weight updates substantially close the gap to centralized training for federated physics surrogates.

title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
summary: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise split federated unlearning that achieves the lowest gap to retraining across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Split federated learning couples class-specific knowledge across client and server representations, making class-wise unlearning difficult under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints.
AI.method: SplitReAlign constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated by a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside active subspaces, with tailored update mechanisms for Client-only, Server-only, and Joint regimes.
AI.result: Across six heterogeneous settings on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to full retraining among compared methods, with Server-only updates yielding the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets.
AI.conclusion: Partition-aware representation realignment enables effective class-wise unlearning in split federated learning even under restricted server-only or client-only updates.

title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
summary: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the exact trade-off between cumulative expected excess loss and finite expected lifetime adjustment charges for Bayesian learners retaining issued actions.
AI.motivation: A Bayesian learner updating its posterior can retain previously issued actions to avoid adjustment charges, but the precise boundary of jointly attainable excess-loss profiles and lifetime adjustment costs under general nonconvex or unbounded losses was not characterized.
AI.method: Under population curvature, boundary control, an order-1/n posterior uncertainty lower bound, and an observable unbiased gradient witness, the authors derive a prefix-constrained allocation criterion (and its decreasing-weight dual) characterizing attainable excess O(G(J)) at horizons T=2^J with finite lifetime charge, and construct a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy.
AI.result: Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region, every policy requires Omega((log T)^{2-r}) expected revisions for excess O((log T)^r) with 0 < r < 1, a charge-independent schedule matches this bound pathwise, and the assumptions are verified for logistic decision models.
AI.conclusion: The results establish tight, deterministic checkpointing bounds for sequential Bayesian decision-making under lifetime adjustment costs.

title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
summary: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes completion gain for multi-phase residual reinforcement learning and shows that allocating training budget by completion gain outperforms failure-count and uniform allocation in docking and robotic assembly.
AI.motivation: In multi-phase tasks, residual reinforcement learning must allocate a limited interaction budget across phases, and the phase with the most base-policy failures is not necessarily where corrections most improve overall task completion.
AI.method: The authors define completion gain as the change in full-task completion probability when a state-feedback controller replaces selected base-policy action components in a single phase, decompose it into phase reachability and conditional improvement, estimate it from paired episodes, and use positive estimates to allocate training episodes and action components.
AI.result: In point-mass docking, completion gain peaked in the channel phase rather than the failure-heavy docking phase, outperforming failure-proportional allocation and matching uniform allocation at half the budget on longer approaches; in bimanual robotic assembly, gain-based allocation improved completion from held-out release-start states by 16.9%.
AI.conclusion: Allocating residual RL budgets using estimated completion gain rather than failure counts yields more sample-efficient improvements on multi-phase manipulation tasks.

title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
summary: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-part framework to quantify feature proxy capacity for disparate treatment and preprocess proxy features to reduce demographic leakage while preserving more predictive performance than feature removal.
AI.motivation: Existing disparate treatment workflows rely on ad-hoc review and simply remove suspected proxy features, which degrades predictive performance in favor of fairness through unawareness.
AI.method: The framework introduces a quantitative conditional-independence-based test for proxy capacity to detect whether a feature's values reveal demographic group membership, paired with a pre-processing adjustment that reduces proxy capacity while retaining task-relevant signal.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on synthetic and public datasets show the framework identifies demographic proxy features, reduces their proxy capacity, and improves predictive performance compared to removing the features entirely.
AI.conclusion: Quantifying and adjusting proxy capacity offers a practical alternative to naive feature removal for mitigating disparate treatment risk in regulated ML domains.

title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance
summary: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates conformal prediction as a triage layer for ICAO face-image compliance and finds that class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction restores minority-class coverage compared to marginal conformal prediction.
AI.motivation: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers output deterministic pass/fail verdicts without uncertainty quantification to guide accept, reject, or retake decisions under class imbalance.
AI.method: Without retraining the BioGaze analyser, the authors fit per-criterion logistic classifiers across 14 criteria on the TONO benchmark and compare marginal conformal prediction, label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction, and conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits.
AI.result: Marginal conformal prediction achieved ~0.90 overall coverage but under-covered violations (0.37 ten-partition mean on one criterion), whereas Mondrian conformal prediction achieved 0.89 to 0.92 means; however, the logistic layer drove most false-positive reduction (0.145 to 0.048), tuned abstention rules beat Mondrian on false positives at similar retake rates, and Bonferroni joint coverage required retaking nearly all images.
AI.conclusion: Class-conditional conformal prediction provides reliable minority-class statistical coverage for face-image compliance triage, though practical deployment must balance coverage guarantees against retake rates.

title: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space
summary: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-step training algorithm for drifting policy models that improves sample efficiency and control performance in high-dimensional reinforcement learning action spaces.
AI.motivation: Drifting models can represent complex action distributions in a single forward pass, but training them solely via Q-gradient backpropagation fails to capture necessary coordination across high-dimensional action spaces.
AI.method: The authors co-optimize the drifting model's source distribution as a diagonal policy so the drifting model learns residual coordination, apply adversarial training with a discriminator between pre- and post-drifting distributions, and use best-of-N sampling during rollouts for directional exploration.
AI.result: Across three high-dimensional locomotion tasks, the method consistently improves sample efficiency and final control performance over diagonal distribution modeling by reducing variance in specific action dimensions and coupling them.
AI.conclusion: Combining residual drifting, adversarial discrimination, and best-of-N rollouts enables lightweight single-pass policies to learn effective action coordination in high-dimensional RL.

title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
comment: 45 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TuringSpace, an interactive benchmark and training gym of 125 spatial CAPTCHAs, showing that leading MLLMs lag behind humans and that fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on the gym transfers to real-world spatial benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and non-spatial, while existing spatial benchmarks rarely require interactive screen actions and feedback-driven self-correction.
AI.method: The authors build TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 programmatic interactive CAPTCHAs spanning five spatial abilities solved via clicks and drags, and fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on generated gym trajectories.
AI.result: Humans solve 94.1% of tasks while GPT-6 Astra fails 25.9% and Kimi K3 fails 68.0% due to screenshot misreading and hallucinated justifications; fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B raises its success rate from 1.6% to 33.1% and improves all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including +9.9 points on VSI-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Grounding spatial intelligence in interactive screen actions exposes MLLM reasoning failures and provides a scalable training signal that transfers to real-world 3D scenes.

title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
summary: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SAVR, a homology-guided contrastive post-training method using Pfam co-membership that rectifies protein language model representations and achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Pretrained protein language models entangle functional signals with non-functional sequence regularities such as sequence identity and compositional bias, creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction.
AI.method: SAVR (Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification) applies contrastive post-training using Pfam family co-membership as a discrete semantic signal to reduce directional dominance, redistribute variance, and increase effective embedding dimensionality without task-specific labels.
