AI.result: Under frozen-backbone evaluation, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art performance on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive performance on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Homology-guided contrastive post-training effectively rectifies protein language model geometry for sequence-based function prediction without requiring downstream task labels.

title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
summary: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a 7B-parameter (1.7B active) payment foundation model integrating sequence, tabular, and graph representations that reduced online payment loss rates by 37.88% over XGB-Online.
AI.motivation: Payment risk detection requires modeling complex behavioral and relational patterns across heterogeneous data modalities, which traditional task-specific models struggle to transfer across business domains.
AI.method: The authors pretrain a 7B-parameter (1.7B activated per route) Transformer integrating sequence, tabular, and graph representations on Ant International's internal payment data.
AI.result: Pretraining improves cross-business transfer by 34.5% over training from scratch, outperforms full-label scratch baselines in AP and Recall@0.5% using only 25% of labels, and reduced overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online in a four-month billion-scale online experiment.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal foundation model pretraining provides substantial label efficiency and risk-reduction gains in large-scale industrial payment systems.

title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
summary: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework over biomedical knowledge graphs that converts genomic sequence predictions and calibrated uncertainty into traceable phenotype hypotheses without patient-level supervision.
AI.motivation: Connecting variant-level genomic foundation model predictions to phenotype hypotheses requires propagating predictive uncertainty through structured biological reasoning rather than ignoring evidence quality.
AI.method: A learned interpretable energy scores admissible gene-disease-phenotype paths with query uncertainty controlling the target temperature, aggregating path probabilities into phenotype distributions evaluated against exact normalization and a Hastings-corrected revision operator.
AI.result: On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype entropy tracks upstream uncertainty (Spearman 0.951 and 0.878), uncertainty-conditioned training outperforms constant temperature on held-out recall@10, and gene hold-out recall@10 beats DistMult on 24 of 30 masks (0.183 vs. 0.123, driven mainly by three multi-variant genes).
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-conditioned path-energy inference provides an interpretable, evidence-aware interface between genomic models and biomedical knowledge graphs.

title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
summary: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm, which uses clustering and exact orthonormal bases to reduce per-round update complexity to O(r_bar^2) while guaranteeing sublinear regret.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional linear bandits incur O(d^2) per-round update costs, and existing sketching methods like SOFUL risk vacuous linear regret when data has a heavy spectral tail and the approximation rank is mis-specified.
AI.method: CBL clusters arms and maintains an exact orthonormal basis of each cluster's column space alongside low-dimensional coordinates, using cluster sentinels for switching to reduce update cost to O(r_bar^2) where r_bar = min(r, l).
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes that CBL preserves full covariance information per cluster and guarantees sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Cluster-wise exact orthonormal bases offer a computationally efficient and regret-safe alternative to matrix sketching for high-dimensional linear bandits.

title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
comment: Submitted to a journal. The journal info will be confirmed once the paper is accepted
summary: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes model composability via an interference functional of cross-task curvature overlap and update alignment, showing that curvature-guided regularization bounds merging interference during fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Composing fine-tuned task vectors is a standard alternative to multi-task training, but the exact conditions and training dynamics governing cross-task interference during merging remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors prove that merged excess loss is controlled by an interference functional in the curvature metric, and analyze fine-tuning with a curvature-guided regularizer constructed from optimizer curvature statistics.
AI.result: Curvature-guided regularization caps base-curvature displacement at the O(1/sqrt(T)) rate and bounds the curvature interference term, though a first-order non-stationarity term persists; experiments confirm the budget and ceiling, and a three-seed transformer study finds the functional rank-correlates with merging degradation similarly to Euclidean displacement norm.
AI.conclusion: Curvature-aware analysis clarifies when task vectors compose cleanly and highlights the trade-off between curvature interference control and first-order regularization bias.

title: Inverse ECG Reconstruction via a Preconditioned Variational Quantum Linear Solver
summary: Inverse electrocardiography (ECG) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface measurements, enabling noninvasive mapping of cardiac electrical activity. However, the reconstruction requires solving dense and ill-conditioned linear systems, whose computational cost grows rapidly with the refined heart mesh. Quantum computing offers new opportunities for solving such systems. This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework for inverse ECG reconstruction, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to apply a quantum linear solver to this problem. We first propose a Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding procedure to reduce the dimension of the system while improving its conditioning. Second, the resulting reduced system is encoded and solved using a coherent variational quantum linear solver (VQLS). Finally, we provide a rigorous theoretical proof establishing that the proposed framework preserves the exact solution of the original reconstruction problem throughout all stages of the computational process. Experimental results on a realistic heart-torso geometry demonstrate that our approach holds significant ability for accurate inverse ECG reconstruction. These findings highlight the potential of quantum solvers for noninvasive cardiac imaging, providing a foundation for further research into quantum-enhanced cardiac assessment and other healthcare applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework for inverse ECG reconstruction using Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding and a coherent variational quantum linear solver (VQLS).
AI.motivation: Inverse electrocardiography requires solving dense, ill-conditioned linear systems whose computational cost scales rapidly with heart mesh refinement.
AI.method: The authors apply a Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding step to reduce system dimension and improve conditioning, then solve the reduced system using a coherent VQLS while proving exact solution preservation across all stages.
AI.result: Experiments on a realistic heart-torso geometry demonstrate that the hybrid framework achieves accurate inverse ECG reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Preconditioned variational quantum linear solvers provide a mathematically sound foundation for quantum-enhanced noninvasive cardiac imaging.

title: FamilySpace: From Emergent Chemical Semantics to Controllable Crystal Generation
summary: Latent crystal generative models typically combine a variational autoencoder (VAE) for learning atom-wise representations with a flow model that transports a simple source distribution to the learned latent distribution. However, previous studies have mainly focused on the quality of generated crystals, leaving the structure and generative utility of the atom-wise latent space largely unexplored. In this work, we show that even a vanilla crystal VAE implicitly organizes atom-wise latent representations according to elemental families, with different families occupying largely separated regions of the latent space. We term this phenomenon emergent chemical semantics. This structure suggests that sampling from a family-specific latent region can bias the decoder toward atoms from the corresponding elemental family. Building on this insight, we propose FamilySpace, a framework for controlling the elemental-family composition of generated crystals. FamilySpace assigns each elemental family a distinct source component, forming a family-indexed multi-source distribution, and trains a flow model using source-target pairs matched by family. In inference, a user-specified family template selects the source component for each atom-wise representation, enabling direct control over the family composition of generated crystals. Experiments on MP-20 and MPTS-52 show that FamilySpace achieves competitive crystal-generation performance while matching prescribed elemental-family compositions. Moreover, selected family templates increase the fraction of generated crystals predicted to be stable or metastable, demonstrating that latent-space composition control can support targeted exploration of promising chemical regions without additional optimization techniques such as reinforcement learning. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper discovers that crystal VAEs implicitly organize atom-wise latents by elemental family and introduces FamilySpace, a multi-source flow framework enabling controllable crystal composition generation.
AI.motivation: Latent crystal generative models focus on overall crystal quality, leaving the structure and controllability of atom-wise latent spaces largely unexplored.
AI.method: Exploiting emergent chemical semantics in vanilla crystal VAEs, FamilySpace assigns each elemental family a distinct source component in a multi-source flow model trained on family-matched pairs, allowing user-specified family templates at inference.
AI.result: On MP-20 and MPTS-52, FamilySpace achieves competitive generation quality while matching prescribed elemental-family compositions and increasing the fraction of predicted stable or metastable crystals without reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging emergent chemical semantics in latent space enables direct, RL-free composition control for targeted crystal discovery.

title: Dimension-Free Buffer Bounds for Compressed-Momentum Error Feedback
comment: Submitted to a journal and details will be confirmed once paper accepted
summary: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $\beta_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-\beta_1)\|G_t\|_F + \gamma\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $\Theta(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}\eta_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.

AI.tldr: This paper proves dimension-free and rank-free buffer bounds for compressed-momentum error feedback, replacing standard contraction constants with O(1) bounds.
AI.motivation: Existing error-feedback analyses bound the memory buffer using compressor contraction constants such as r/p, which degrade convergence rates in high-dimensional or low-rank regimes.
AI.method: By observing that previous compressed momentum is an admissible competitor in metric projection onto a closed cone (covering top-k and truncated SVD), the authors bound the buffer norm independently of dimensions m, n and rank r, and bound rate-transfer leakage by step-weighted gradient mass.
AI.result: The analysis replaces a Stage-2 constant of order p^2/r^2 (or Theta(p/r)) with O(1) at the cost of an additive O(log^2 T) floor, and on BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio 32/768, feedback decay costs under 0.008 validation F1.
AI.conclusion: Metric-projection geometry yields tight, dimension-free error-feedback guarantees that explain the practical robustness of low-rank compressed momentum.

title: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
summary: Smoothed online learning has recently been studied as a way to bypass hardness results for the fully adversarial setting, which can be overly pessimistic. In this framework, the adversary is constrained to generate contexts from distributions having a bounded density with respect to some fixed base measure $\mu$. Prior work makes the strong assumption that $\mu$ is known to the learner, with notable exceptions including Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). In this paper, we study sequential probability assignment (a.k.a., online learning with log loss) with smooth, well-specified data in the more general setting where $\mu$ is \emph{unknown}, without the Lipschitz condition imposed in the work of Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). We prove regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries: the adaptive bound is controlled by empirical $\ell_\infty$ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound improves this dependence to empirical $\ell_2$ Hellinger entropy, the notion that has been shown to characterize the complexity of learning with i.i.d. data (Bilodeau et al., 2023). Both bounds are obtained through algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. We complement these results with a general lower bound, showing that our upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, which implies a separation in the difficulty of smoothed online learning between regimes where $\mu$ is known and where it is unknown.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes tight regret bounds for sequential probability assignment against smoothed adversaries with an unknown base measure and no Lipschitz assumptions.
AI.motivation: Prior smoothed online learning analyses either assume the base measure mu is known to the learner or impose restrictive Lipschitz conditions.
AI.method: Using algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers, the authors derive regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries in the unknown-mu log-loss setting, alongside a general lower bound.
AI.result: Adaptive regret is governed by empirical l_infinity Hellinger entropy while oblivious regret improves to empirical l_2 Hellinger entropy, and the matching lower bound establishes a fundamental separation between known-mu and unknown-mu regimes.
AI.conclusion: Truncated empirical Hellinger covers characterize the exact statistical complexity of smoothed sequential probability assignment when the base measure is unknown.

title: Is a Description Worth a Thousand Demonstrations? Specificity and Reliability of Task Descriptions in In-Context Learning
summary: A prompt for in-context learning (ICL) can describe a task in addition to, or instead of, demonstrating it through examples. Yet how task descriptions work remains poorly understood theoretically. Through the Bayesian view of ICL, we model descriptions as informative priors characterized by their specificity and reliability. We adapt the effective sample size (ESS) from Bayesian statistics, quantifying a description's predictive value as an equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, we show that a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and with the task's dimension. A description that may be irrelevant, however, gains little from its specificity unless demonstrations are given. In practice, do in-context learners use descriptions as a Bayes-optimal predictor would? Our experiments show that meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS when tested on their training distribution. Pretrained language models, however, make too little use of highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning; most of them closely match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled. These results extend the Bayesian analysis of ICL from demonstrations to descriptions.

AI.tldr: This paper models task descriptions as Bayesian priors with specificity and reliability, showing that meta-trained Transformers match Bayes-optimal effective sample sizes while pretrained LLMs require reasoning to fully use specific descriptions.
AI.motivation: Prompts for in-context learning often combine or replace demonstrations with task descriptions, yet the theoretical predictive value of descriptions compared to examples is poorly understood.
AI.method: Adopting a Bayesian view of in-context learning, the authors model descriptions as informative priors parameterized by specificity and reliability, and measure their value via effective sample size (ESS) in linear regression and Transformer experiments.
AI.result: Theoretically, a reliable description's ESS grows with specificity and task dimension, whereas potentially irrelevant descriptions need demonstrations to gain value; empirically, meta-trained Transformers match Bayes-optimal ESS in-distribution, while pretrained LLMs underuse specific descriptions unless reasoning is enabled.
AI.conclusion: Effective sample size provides a principled Bayesian bridge between task descriptions and demonstrations, revealing that reasoning unlocks description-driven prior utilization in LLMs.

title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
comment: 28 pages, 11 figures, 15 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WeatherCraft, a discrete-token autoregressive weather forecasting model aligned with GRPO that outperforms deterministic baselines on ERA5 day-15 RMSE and runs 18x faster than GenCast.
AI.motivation: Global medium-range weather forecasting needs efficient ensemble generation alongside direct alignment for downstream applications like extreme-event warnings and coupled simulations.
AI.method: WeatherCraft uses a multiscale tokenizer to represent atmospheric states as coarse-to-fine discrete tokens, a Transformer predicting tokens causally across time/scale and in parallel within scales, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on exact token log-probabilities.
AI.result: On ERA5, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% over the strongest deterministic baseline, achieves ~18x inference speedup over GenCast with KV caching, and improves extreme-event forecasts via fair-CRPS and reward post-training.
AI.conclusion: Discrete autoregressive modeling with RL alignment establishes a fast, task-alignable paradigm for Earth system foundation models.

title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
summary: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Epira, a protocol-controlled LLM interviewer for case investigation and contact tracing that recovers 31.1 to 41.9 percentage points more required fields than open-ended LLM interviewers.
AI.motivation: Manual contact tracing is labor-intensive, web forms lack clarification support, and open-ended LLM chatbots risk deviating from public health protocols.
AI.method: Epira pairs an LLM dialogue interface (tested with local Qwen2.5 and cloud GPT-5.4) with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and structured records, evaluated across 864 simulated sessions and 72 human volunteers.
AI.result: In simulated cases, local Epira captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts (31.1 to 41.9 percentage points more fields than open-ended baselines); in volunteer trials, completion was 100% with mean SUS usability 82.95 and mean trust 3.85/5.
AI.conclusion: Combining protocol-enforcing rule controllers with local or cloud LLMs enables accurate, usable, and privacy-preserving automated public health interviews.

title: From Data Alignment to Parameter Generation: Few-Shot Cross-City Traffic Prediction with Conditional Diffusion
summary: Accurate mobile traffic forecasting is crucial for network service management, supporting proactive capacity provisioning, congestion mitigation, and energy-efficient operation. However, many cities and regions are data-scarce (e.g., newly deployed or poorly instrumented areas), thus making traffic prediction a few-shot learning problem and limiting the practicality of standard data-driven models. Existing cross-city solutions primarily rely on data-space alignment to match traffic distributions between data-rich and data-scarce cities, but such alignment is often brittle under real-world distribution shifts, measurement noise, and city-specific bias. To address these limitations, we propose a Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (CDPG) framework. Instead of aligning raw data, CDPG learns the conditional distribution of high-performing predictor parameters for source cities and directly generates node-specific model parameters for the target city. To support reliable adaptation for network traffic prediction, CDPG conditions parameter generation on multi-modal spatio-temporal context. Specifically, CDPG captures spatial environment cues by combining satellite imagery with large language model (LLM)-derived semantic descriptions, and summarizes complex temporal behaviors via unsupervised pattern clustering. These contextual components guide CDPG in producing parameters tailored to each base station's operational context, thereby improving robustness under cross-city and cross-region shifts. Extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets show that CDPG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72% on standard forecasting metrics and remains robust for few-shot multi-step prediction. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CDPG, a conditional diffusion framework that generates node-specific traffic predictor parameters from multimodal context, outperforming cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72%.
AI.motivation: Cross-city traffic prediction for data-scarce cities typically relies on data-space alignment, which is brittle under distribution shifts, measurement noise, and city-specific biases.
AI.method: Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (CDPG) learns the conditional distribution of high-performing source-city predictor parameters conditioned on satellite imagery, LLM-derived semantic descriptions, and unsupervised temporal pattern clusters, directly generating target-city parameters.
AI.result: Across three large-scale datasets, CDPG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72% on standard forecasting metrics and remains robust for multi-step prediction.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning parameter generation on multimodal spatio-temporal context provides a more robust alternative to data-space alignment for few-shot cross-city forecasting.

title: PSTO: A PDE-structured transport operator with shared implicit updates for multiscale CDR systems
summary: Multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems couple spatial transport with local stiff reaction kinetics, making their numerical simulation computationally demanding. Conventional neural surrogates require costly coupled CDR training data, and their parameter counts scale with the number of transported variables, limiting scalability to high-dimensional CDR systems. Here we propose a PDE-Structured Transport Operator (PSTO) that learns convection--diffusion dynamics solely from reaction-free data. By embedding the PDE structure into the neural architecture, PSTO generalizes to full CDR systems at inference without retraining. A single transport operator block is shared across all transported variables and refined through relaxed fixed-point iterations, performing an implicit-like correction in latent space. This improves stability during recursive multi-step prediction without adding trainable parameters. We evaluate PSTO on three benchmarks: a canonical 2D CDR system, a multiscale Robertson counterflow flame, and a multiscale hydrogen planar jet flame. In every case, PSTO reduces the mean relative $L_2$ error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% compared to the strongest neural baseline. Ablation studies on the fixed-point iterations and detailed error decomposition further confirm that PSTO achieves both high one-step accuracy and long-term stability in coupled rollouts. Time-step sensitivity analysis shows that PSTO maintains accuracy even with a tenfold larger time step, whereas baseline accuracies decay rapidly as the time step increases. This framework enables efficient, modular modeling of multiscale CDR dynamics by separating transport learning from the treatment of local kinetics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PSTO, a PDE-structured transport operator trained solely on reaction-free data that generalizes to coupled multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction systems and cuts 100-step error by at least 50%.
AI.motivation: Conventional neural surrogates for multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems require expensive coupled training data and scale poorly in parameter count with the number of transported variables.
AI.method: PSTO embeds PDE structure into a single transport operator block shared across all variables, trained only on reaction-free data and refined via relaxed fixed-point iterations in latent space for implicit-like stability.
AI.result: Across a 2D CDR system, a Robertson counterflow flame, and a hydrogen planar jet flame, PSTO reduces mean relative L2 error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% over the strongest neural baseline and maintains accuracy at 10x larger time steps.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling transport learning from local stiff kinetics via shared, fixed-point-refined PDE-structured operators enables scalable and stable multiscale CDR simulation.

title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
summary: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically investigates joint depth-width scaling in CNNs and finds that NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training are governed by the depth-to-width ratio L/C in distinct ways.
AI.motivation: While joint depth-width scaling of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) is studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its behavior in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors conduct numerical experiments on CNNs with L convolutional layers and C channels per layer, measuring NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training across ordered, critical, and chaotic initialization regimes.
AI.result: NTK dispersion increases with L/C in critical and chaotic regimes (collapsing approximately as a function of L/C at criticality) while remaining small in the ordered regime, whereas training-time kernel rotation generally increases with L/C across all regimes including ordered.
AI.conclusion: The ratio L/C governs finite-width NTK deviations in CNNs, with initialization concentration and training-time stability following different scaling behaviors.

title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design
summary: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates Cartesian MRI undersampling mask design as QUBO-based feature selection using mutual information, outperforming four conventional sampling methods on fastMRI knee reconstructions.
AI.motivation: Designing effective Cartesian MRI undersampling patterns requires selecting informative k-space lines, which is traditionally done with heuristic or univariate criteria.
AI.method: Binary line-inclusion indicators are scored using estimated mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI) with a sampling-count penalty to form a QUBO problem solved via simulated annealing and quantum annealing.
AI.result: Evaluated via zero-filled reconstruction on patient-disjoint fastMRI knee magnitude images across six sampling rates (15% to 40%), QUBO-selected masks achieve lower mean RMSE than four conventional methods and higher mean SSIM than univariate MI ranking at all rates.
AI.conclusion: Information-theoretic QUBO feature selection provides a principled and effective approach to MRI undersampling pattern design.

title: NIMIS: A Structure-Agnostic, Chemically Informed Slot-Attention Framework for Demixing 1D $^1$H-NMR Mixture Spectra
summary: The products of chemical reactions are usually complex mixtures that must be separated into their components before interpretable $^1$H-NMR spectra can be obtained. Direct analysis of the spectra of crude mixtures would accelerate reaction analysis and facilitate the exploration of new chemical space. We present NIMIS, a structure-agnostic, attention-based deep learning framework that groups the peaks of a 1D $^1$H-NMR mixture spectrum according to the component from which they originate. J-coupling information is introduced directly into the attention mechanism of a multi-head Transformer encoder, and the resulting contextualised peak embeddings are separated into components by slot attention. NIMIS was trained on 158,005 synthetic mixtures constructed from experimental spectra in the NMRexp database, covering molecules of up to 20 heavy atoms composed of C, H, N, O, S, F, Cl, Br and I. On held-out molecules it reaches a peak-to-component assignment accuracy of 82.28% for noise-free input and 77.34% with 10% integral noise, with a mean NIMIS score of 0.83 for correct assignments. NIMIS outperforms a conventional Transformer and simple baselines, and its performance carries over to a scaffold-disjoint evaluation. By grouping peaks into component-level sets, NIMIS provides a foundation for more robust mixture analysis methods, including methods capable of handling overlapping signals.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NIMIS, a structure-agnostic Transformer and slot-attention framework informed by J-coupling that demixes 1D 1H-NMR mixture spectra with up to 82.28% peak-to-component accuracy.
AI.motivation: Analyzing crude chemical reaction mixtures via 1D 1H-NMR currently requires physical separation before spectra can be interpreted.
AI.method: NIMIS injects J-coupling information directly into the attention mechanism of a multi-head Transformer encoder and uses slot attention to group contextualized peak embeddings into individual mixture components.
AI.result: Trained on 158,005 synthetic mixtures from NMRexp (molecules up to 20 heavy atoms), NIMIS achieves 82.28% peak-to-component assignment accuracy on noise-free inputs and 77.34% with 10% integral noise (mean NIMIS score 0.83), outperforming conventional Transformers and generalizing to scaffold-disjoint splits.
AI.conclusion: Chemically informed attention with slot-based grouping enables direct, structure-agnostic demixing of 1D 1H-NMR spectra.

title: Explainability of genotype embedding models through observed cohort paths
summary: Deep learning models that combine genotypes with neuroimaging predict neurological diseases more accurately than either modality alone. Their clinical use, however, requires identifying which genetic variants a prediction is based on. Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients address this by integrating the model's gradient from a baseline to the input. These methods assume the model accepts any point along that path as a valid input. Genotype models violate this assumption. They map the three discrete allele dosages \{0,1,2\} to vectors through a learned embedding defined only at those values, so a straight line passes through fractional genotypes at which no embedding, and therefore no gradient, exists. Attribution must therefore proceed in embedding space where the choice of path can affect the resulting attribution. We show that the commonly used per-variant estimator does not generally satisfy completeness. Additive separability guarantees completeness for this estimator, but interactions between variants generally break that property. Instead, we integrate along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths connecting genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. Each path satisfies completeness in the continuum although the interiors of its segments are not necessarily observed. Our method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations, and is competitive with a support-background Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations. It also shows higher seed stability and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an attribution method for genotype embedding models that integrates along piecewise-linear embedding paths connecting observed cohort genotypes, improving faithfulness and stability over Integrated Gradients.
AI.motivation: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients assume continuous valid inputs, which genotype models violate because discrete allele dosages {0,1,2} map to learned embeddings with no gradients at fractional values.
AI.method: The authors show per-variant estimators lack completeness under variant interactions and instead integrate gradients along piecewise-linear paths in embedding space connecting observed training-cohort genotype waypoints.
AI.result: The method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves top Parkinson's disease classification results under support-preserving perturbations, matches a Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations, and improves seed stability and non-additive effect recovery.
AI.conclusion: Integrating along observed-cohort embedding paths restores completeness and improves clinical interpretability for discrete genotype deep learning models.

title: Measurable Does Not Imply Transportable: A Prospective Audit of Model Explanations in Multi-Year Field Trials
summary: Model explanations are increasingly used as scientific evidence, yet it remains unclear what they license scientists to conclude beyond the data on which they were constructed. When a fine-grained explanation fails to replicate, the failure may be attributed to noisy measurement of its target, raising a fundamental question: does reliable measurement imply a reproducible explanation? We test this directly. We formalize prospective explanation transportability: the extent to which an explanation learned from past data is recovered in a genuinely future context. This property is distinct from feature importance and measurement reliability. Using multi-year Genomes-to-Fields maize trials, where each new year is a real future context rather than a random resample, we evaluate 16 agronomically interpretable environmental concepts across five forward splits and one prospectively locked test year. Coarse environment-level explanations transport reliably (median cosine 0.83); their locked 2024 value, 0.811, fell within a prespecified 80% bootstrap percentile interval. For grain yield, genotype-conditioned explanations have a historical median cosine of 0.30 and range from 0.006 to 0.822 across years. Reliability does not order these outcomes: the year with the highest split-half reliability had the lowest explanation transport. Within-context resampling showed that GxE explanations were reproducible within a fixed context (0.77-0.95) while exhibiting lower prospective alignment across the 2020-2023 transitions (0.01-0.36). A second phenotype transports strongly at both resolutions, and non-temporal validation inflates apparent interaction-level transport by +0.22. These results show that target reliability and within-context explanation reproducibility do not by themselves establish when a model explanation can support a reproducible scientific claim.

AI.tldr: This paper audits explanation transportability across multi-year maize field trials and shows that high measurement reliability and within-context reproducibility do not guarantee that model explanations transport to future years.
AI.motivation: Model explanations are often treated as scientific evidence, yet it is unclear whether reliable target measurement and within-context reproducibility license claims in genuinely new future contexts.
AI.method: The authors formalize prospective explanation transportability and evaluate 16 environmental concepts across five forward splits and a locked 2024 test year in multi-year Genomes-to-Fields maize trials.
AI.result: Coarse environment explanations transport reliably (median cosine 0.83; 0.811 in 2024), whereas genotype-conditioned grain-yield explanations drop to 0.30 median cosine (0.006-0.822 across years), with the highest split-half reliability year showing the lowest transport and non-temporal validation inflating interaction transport by +0.22.
AI.conclusion: Target reliability and within-context resampling reproducibility are insufficient to establish prospective scientific transportability of model explanations.

title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
summary: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the CCGP-2M dataset and a two-stage VLM-guided RL framework using KLTDPO offline alignment, enabling earlier diamond collection and higher achievement scores in Craftax-Classic.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning agents in Craftax-style environments struggle with sparse-reward, long-horizon exploration, while unadapted LLMs rely on brittle prompts and generate inconsistent goals.
AI.method: The authors construct CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset from Craftax-Classic trajectories, fine-tune a VLM offline using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO) with distributionally robust reweighting, and deploy it for online goal-guided RL.
AI.result: On Craftax-Classic, the framework collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines and achieves the highest overall score, reward, and success rates on most achievements.
AI.conclusion: Offline preference alignment of VLMs on trajectory-derived goal datasets produces reliable, environment-grounded exploration guidance for long-horizon RL.

title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
summary: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework for intraoperative EEG and hemodynamic monitoring across 5,439 surgeries, bounding subgroup shift risk within 5% in real time.
AI.motivation: Commercial intraoperative monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing lags, DC drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration.
AI.method: Across TIVA (N=3,214), volatile anesthesia (N=2,046), endoscopy (N=171), and DC-coupled surgery (N=8), streaming causal filters blank 10.13-min impedance checks and separate 63-s suppression lag, paired with tree ensembles, Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC), and online Conformal PID tracking.
AI.result: Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving ~99% of deep suppression; on unseen TIVA (N=525), cortical features achieved 0.3135 AUPRC (matching deep encoders, p >= 0.36), zero-retraining volatile transfer matched an end-tidal oracle (p = 0.472), and Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch.
AI.conclusion: Causal hardware-artifact disentangling combined with shift-aware conformal calibration enables reliable, real-time intraoperative risk bounds within physiological observability limits.

title: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats?
summary: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.

AI.tldr: This paper audits internal feature explanations of language-model insider-threat detectors on CERT logs and introduces the tipping radius, revealing that most explanation results are fragile to the choice of control metric.
AI.motivation: Insider-threat detectors flag unusual workplace activity using opaque neural networks, and evaluating their internal feature explanations by comparing feature removal against a "similar" control depends heavily on the chosen similarity metric.
AI.method: The authors formalize the tipping radius—a first-order prediction of how far a similarity metric must change before the difference between feature removal and control vanishes—and audit seven language models across 34 runs on CERT workplace logs.
AI.result: In 33 of 34 runs, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard metrics, and moving that far eliminates at least 58% of the difference or reverses it (replicated in 13 of 14 primary runs); moreover, flags partly reflect worker identity and named features depend on the comparison baseline.
AI.conclusion: Audits of neural insider-threat explanations should pre-register control metrics, report tipping radii, and disclose comparison baselines to avoid fragile interpretability claims.

title: A Sparse Low-Rank Biclique Decomposition for Graphs
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 29 pages, including references and appendices
summary: Low-rank plus sparse decompositions, such as robust PCA, typically model the low-rank component as dense and the sparse component as corruption. This viewpoint is poorly suited to graph adjacency matrices, where sparsity is structural and dense low-rank factors destroy the combinatorial and computational properties of the graph. We propose signed biclique decomposition (SBD), a sparse low-rank decomposition for integer-weighted graphs that represents the structured component as a sum of sparse signed binary rank-one factors, together with a sparse signed residual. The resulting representation remains discrete, interpretable, sparse, and compatible with standard linear algebra. We formulate fixed-rank and greedy SBD objectives and derive a gain-based greedy algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, SBD recovers block structure in noisy graphs, while its factorized representation enables efficient sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM). On real graphs with strong shared-neighborhood structure, SBD achieves compression factors above $10$ and SpMM speedups up to $6\times$ over cuSPARSE, suggesting a practical alternative to dense low-rank decompositions for graphs. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes signed biclique decomposition (SBD), a sparse low-rank decomposition for integer-weighted graphs that achieves over 10x compression and up to 6x SpMM speedup over cuSPARSE.
AI.motivation: Standard low-rank plus sparse decompositions like robust PCA produce dense low-rank factors that destroy the structural sparsity and combinatorial efficiency of graph adjacency matrices.
AI.method: SBD represents the structured graph component as a sum of sparse signed binary rank-one factors (bicliques) plus a sparse signed residual, solved via a gain-based greedy algorithm with theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: SBD recovers block structure in noisy graphs and, on real graphs with strong shared-neighborhood structure, achieves compression factors above 10 and SpMM speedups up to 6x over cuSPARSE.
AI.conclusion: Signed biclique decomposition offers a discrete, interpretable, and computationally fast alternative to dense low-rank decompositions for graph matrices.

title: Beyond Alignment: Whitening Geometry, Profile Synthesis, and Heterogeneous Ensembles for Cross-Environment WiFi Action Recognition
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of a manuscript submitted to IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing
summary: Cross-environment deployment is the central obstacle to practical WiFi sensing: a pipeline reaching 0.89+ top-1 in its training environments collapses to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with only K-shot labels. A ceiling analysis shows the collapse is not an alignment problem: the action signal is strong across seen environments (about 0.89 K10), environment identity is decodable from the encoder (0.965), and the failure concentrates in the encoder's extrapolation to the novel environment. A pre-registered falsification chain confirms that "align the domains" methods--training-time alignment, readout-level prototype alignment, adversarial confusion, and covariance/subspace alignment (CORAL -3.8pp, subspace -8.3pp)--degrade performance, and that source-domain statistics anti-correlate with cross-environment contribution. The effective levers lie elsewhere; we combine them into Dec-H: (i) closed-form source within-class whitening, provably re-geometrizing the readout's L2 regularization (+8.6pp, zero cost); (ii) profile-mixing augmentation (+1.0pp); (iii) few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit (+1.5pp; fixed preconditioners are 20/20 negative); (iv) heterogeneous decision ensembles (+1.7pp); homogeneous scaling and source-weighted stacking are saturated or harmful. Dec-H reaches 0.560 K10 (0.812 K40), +15.2pp over the baseline, consistent across all four environments and seeds; all thirteen configurations were pre-registered with frozen criteria.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that domain-alignment methods hurt cross-environment WiFi action recognition and introduces Dec-H, combining closed-form whitening and heterogeneous ensembles to gain +15.2pp under Leave-One-Domain-Out evaluation.
AI.motivation: WiFi action recognition pipelines drop from 0.89+ top-1 accuracy to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with K-shot labels, and standard domain-alignment methods fail to fix this collapse.
AI.method: After falsifying domain-alignment methods (e.g., CORAL -3.8pp, subspace -8.3pp), the authors propose Dec-H: closed-form source within-class whitening (+8.6pp), profile-mixing augmentation (+1.0pp), few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit (+1.5pp), and heterogeneous decision ensembles (+1.7pp).
AI.result: Across four environments and seeds, Dec-H reaches 0.560 at K10 (0.812 at K40), improving by +15.2 percentage points over the baseline under pre-registered frozen criteria.
AI.conclusion: Addressing encoder extrapolation via whitening geometry and heterogeneous ensembles rather than domain alignment is key to cross-environment WiFi sensing.

title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
summary: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes X Hedging, replacing neural networks in Deep Hedging with sequentially trained LightGBM tree ensembles to achieve comparable hedging performance with better explainability, speed, and low-data robustness.
AI.motivation: Deep Hedging relies on opaque neural networks that require large training datasets and hinder user-centered interpretability in financial risk management.
AI.method: X Hedging substitutes neural networks with LightGBM tree ensembles integrated into a reinforcement-learning-style sequential training loop with stochastic random training orders.
AI.result: In controlled numerical experiments, X Hedging matches Deep Hedging performance while delivering greater user-centered explainability, higher computational efficiency, and substantially stronger robustness under limited training data.
AI.conclusion: Sequentially trained tree ensembles offer an interpretable, data-efficient alternative to neural networks for dynamic option hedging.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
summary: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper pairs DINOv3 with all-layer PiSSA adaptation for radar micro-Doppler human activity recognition, outperforming full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and prior PEFT baselines under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Contactless radar micro-Doppler HAR suffers under deployment distribution shifts (cross-age, cross-orientation, cross-dataset), where full fine-tuning causes negative transfer and frozen features under-adapt.
AI.method: The authors apply DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA) to radar micro-Doppler HAR and evaluate against full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and other PEFT methods.
AI.result: DINOv3-PiSSA ranks first among PEFT methods in every setting; its Small variant matches the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art with 4.5x fewer total parameters (3% trainable) and beats a size-matched baseline by 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points across increasing shift severities.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-efficient adaptation of self-supervised vision backbones avoids both negative transfer and under-adaptation in shift-heavy radar HAR.

title: LIFT: Latent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Cell Fate Dynamics with Single Cell Snapshots
summary: Lineage tracing links cell states through clonal ancestry, but does not generally identify unique source-descendant pairings. Learning from such data therefore requires a model of conditional outcomes, rather than only the terminal population distribution. We introduce LIFT, a latent flow framework for probabilistic cell-state generation from lineage-informed couplings. Variational inference encodes alternative outcomes in a latent space, while a conditional prior enables sampling from the initial state alone. A Mean Flow decoder predicts future cell state directly, requiring one decoder evaluation per sampling, which makes it convenient to predict cell fate through large scale Monte-Carlo sampling. This construction combines a representation of one-to-many relationships with efficient sampling and an analysis of conditional prediction error. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate LIFT's ability to recover both population distribution and cell fate probabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LIFT, a latent flow matching framework with a Mean Flow decoder that learns probabilistic cell fate dynamics from lineage-traced single-cell snapshots in a single decoder evaluation.
AI.motivation: Lineage tracing links cell states via clonal ancestry without unique source-descendant pairings, requiring models of conditional one-to-many outcomes rather than just terminal population distributions.
AI.method: LIFT uses variational inference to encode alternative outcomes in a latent space, a conditional prior to sample from initial states alone, and a Mean Flow decoder that predicts future cell states in one evaluation for large-scale Monte-Carlo sampling.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real single-cell datasets demonstrate that LIFT accurately recovers both population distributions and conditional cell fate probabilities.
AI.conclusion: Latent flow matching with single-step Mean Flow decoding enables efficient, probabilistic modeling of one-to-many cell fate dynamics.

title: A Lightweight Hybrid Approach for Milling Force Reconstruction from Internal Machine Signals
summary: Data-driven monitoring based on milling force can enable advanced manufacturing services including process optimization and condition monitoring. However, industrial implementation is often hindered by costly and intrusive hardware and large training data requirements. This paper therefore presents a hybrid approach using machine-internal signals and machining metadata to enable force-based monitoring on brownfield machines without additional sensors. Commonly available machine signals have relatively low sampling rates and cannot directly represent high-frequency milling-force variations, especially at higher spindle speeds. Instead of learning the complete force signal, which would increase model complexity, data requirements, and overfitting risk, a supervised machine-learning model predicts only the average milling force from selected machine-signal features and machining parameters. This low-frequency estimation parameterizes a static milling force model that reconstructs the force behavior over one spindle revolution. Although the static model does not reproduce all dynamic effects, it captures the force distribution, load levels, and angular regions of highest tool engagement. The approach is evaluated on one milling machine across varying process parameters, engagement conditions, cutting tools, and two workpiece materials. Dynamometer measurements are required only for development and validation. Ridge regression achieves an $R^2$ of $0.984$ and $0.991$ for average-force prediction on the test data ($\bar{F}_x$ and $\bar{F}_y$). The reconstructed force behavior over one spindle revolution achieves an $R^2$ of $0.962$ and $0.982$ ($F_x$ and $F_y$) compared with the reconstruction based on measured force features. The method provides a cost and computationally efficient basis for process monitoring, tool condition assessment, and process optimization on existing machines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a lightweight hybrid approach that uses ridge regression on machine-internal signals to predict average milling force and parameterize a static force model over one spindle revolution.
AI.motivation: Data-driven milling force monitoring typically requires costly, intrusive dynamometer hardware and high-frequency data, hindering deployment on existing brownfield machines.
AI.method: A supervised ridge regression model predicts low-frequency average milling force from machine-internal signals and machining metadata, which then parameterizes a static milling force model to reconstruct force behavior over one spindle revolution.
AI.result: Evaluated across varying process parameters, engagement conditions, tools, and two materials, ridge regression achieves R^2 of 0.984 and 0.991 for average forces (Fx, Fy), and the reconstructed single-revolution force achieves R^2 of 0.962 and 0.982 against measured-force reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: Combining low-frequency machine-internal ML predictions with a static physical force model enables cost-effective, sensorless force monitoring on brownfield milling machines.

title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at DATE 2027. Emre Uğur and Jiawen Qi contributed equally
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for block sparse attention that achieves 3.3x prefill speedup at 512K tokens on 4 H100 GPUs while keeping accuracy within 0.10 percentage points of full attention.
AI.motivation: Long-context attention is a major prefill bottleneck for LLMs, and while block sparse attention skips unimportant blocks, accurately scoring those blocks can itself be computationally expensive.
AI.method: DTS selects query and key anchors based on local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones, and accelerates this via parallel delta packing over tile-aligned chunks before computing selected tiles with original Q, K, and V vectors.
AI.result: On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER (up to 128K tokens) and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, reduces scoring-pipeline latency by 38% over XAttention at 128K tokens, and achieves a 3.3x prefill speedup over PyTorch FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: DTS provides an efficient, training-free mechanism for block sparse attention that substantially accelerates long-context prefill without sacrificing task performance.

title: Gradient Boosting with Kolmogorov-Arnold Units for Interpretable Regression beyond Pairwise Interactions
summary: Interpretable models for tabular regression, such as the explainable boosting machine (EBM), restrict a prediction to main effects and pairwise interactions so that every part of it can be plotted. When the target depends on three or more inputs jointly, this restriction costs accuracy, and a black-box model with post hoc explanations becomes the usual fallback. Here we present MJBoost, a gradient boosting method whose weak learner is a single Kolmogorov-Arnold unit $g(\sum_p \phi_p(x_p))$ with penalized spline inner and outer functions. Each unit is fitted in closed form by alternating penalized least squares, starting from principal Hessian directions of the residual, and categorical and missing inputs enter the units directly. Because a unit depends on each input only through one inner function, the fitted model has an exact functional ANOVA decomposition into main effects, pair effects and a higher-order remainder, which one-dimensional convolutions compute. On synthetic targets of interaction order three to six, the test error of MJBoost is up to 13 times lower than that of EBM, and its decomposition recovers the true variance share of every order to within 0.04. On the 35 regression tasks of the OpenML-CTR23 benchmark, it has a lower test RMSE than EBM on 21 tasks and a higher one on 2 (geometric-mean RMSE -29.1%). On these tasks the main and pair effects of the fitted model explain a median 0.992 of its variance, so the model reads as plots where the data allow, and the decomposition measures the higher-order part where they do not. With Newton steps the same algorithm classifies: on 32 binary tasks of OpenML-CC18 its test log-loss is on par with that of EBM, and on 11 multiclass tasks its mean log-loss is lower than that of EBM on 8 and than that of tuned LightGBM on 7.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MJBoost, a gradient boosting method using single Kolmogorov-Arnold units as weak learners that outperforms explainable boosting machines (EBMs) on higher-order interactions while retaining an exact functional ANOVA decomposition.
AI.motivation: Interpretable tabular models like EBM restrict predictions to main effects and pairwise interactions, which sacrifices accuracy when targets depend on three or more inputs jointly.
AI.method: MJBoost fits a single Kolmogorov-Arnold unit g(sum_p phi_p(x_p)) with penalized spline inner and outer functions in closed form via alternating penalized least squares initialized from principal Hessian directions, enabling exact functional ANOVA decomposition into main, pair, and higher-order effects.
