AI.result: On synthetic targets of interaction order 3 to 6, MJBoost achieves up to 13x lower test error than EBM and recovers variance shares within 0.04; on 35 OpenML-CTR23 regression tasks it beats EBM on 21 tasks (-29.1% geometric-mean RMSE), and on 11 OpenML-CC18 multiclass tasks it beats EBM on 8 and tuned LightGBM on 7.
AI.conclusion: MJBoost bridges the gap between interpretable additive models and black-box predictors by capturing higher-order interactions while quantifying exactly how much variance is explained by plottable main and pairwise effects.

title: Power Setpoint Tracking for Large-Scale EV Charging: Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning with Self-Tuning Constraint Prices
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Transportation Electrification
summary: In power setpoint tracking (PST), an operator follows a purchased charging profile without overloading shared transformers or undercharging vehicles. PST is cast as a constrained Markov decision process that minimizes tracking error subject to overload and mean user-satisfaction constraints. Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning (TC-CPL) extends soft actor-critic with proportional-integral Lagrange-multiplier updates from measured violations, a residual on the incumbent dispatcher that is warm-started from its demonstrations, and a transformer-aware encoder shared by all ports. It observes no departure times or states of charge. Simulations (five seeds, 100 paired days) compare it with the incumbent, Round-Robin. On a 600-port, 122-substation district, raw overload falls from 3.59 to 0.0017 kWh/day (overloaded seed-days from 77% to 0.4%), and absolute tracking error falls by 27%. Delivered energy rises by 16%, and satisfaction rises from 0.959 to 0.989. On a 42-kW transformer with household load, overload falls from 1.86 to 0.0014 kWh/day and satisfaction rises from 0.974 to 0.985, but absolute tracking error is 22% higher. Against hand-set fixed multipliers, self-tuning is statistically indistinguishable on the district. On the single transformer, it raises satisfaction by 0.011 at similar overload, but a short sweep found a better-serving fixed pair. The overload multipliers stay below their cap.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates EV charging power setpoint tracking as a constrained Markov decision process and proposes TC-CPL, which reduces transformer overloads by orders of magnitude and improves user satisfaction over Round-Robin.
AI.motivation: Power setpoint tracking (PST) requires following a purchased charging profile without overloading shared transformers or undercharging vehicles, without observing departure times or states of charge.
AI.method: Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning (TC-CPL) extends soft actor-critic with proportional-integral Lagrange-multiplier updates from measured violations, a warm-started residual policy over the incumbent dispatcher, and a shared transformer-aware encoder across ports.
AI.result: In 100-day simulations across 5 seeds on a 600-port district, TC-CPL cuts raw overload from 3.59 to 0.0017 kWh/day, reduces tracking error by 27%, and raises satisfaction from 0.959 to 0.989 over Round-Robin; on a 42-kW transformer, overload drops from 1.86 to 0.0014 kWh/day and satisfaction rises to 0.985, though tracking error is 22% higher.
AI.conclusion: TC-CPL demonstrates that self-tuning constrained reinforcement learning can safely manage large-scale EV charging infrastructure without requiring private user departure or state-of-charge information.

title: Seeing Beyond the Obvious: Complementary Semantic Guidance for Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning
summary: Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SalSPML) assigns each image its most salient positive label, leaving other classes unlabeled. Existing methods construct class-level Salient Prototypes from observed positives to guide the recognition of unobserved classes. However, since salient annotations favor visually prominent instances, these prototypes may not fully capture the visual diversity of hidden positives, resulting in insufficient positive supervision. To address this limitation, we propose CoST, a Coverage-guided Complementary Soft-Target Refinement framework that supplements Salient Prototypes with complementary class-semantic information. Specifically, CoST identifies semantically relevant candidates from unknown classes by leveraging task-learned category information and image-text semantic correspondence. The selected candidates are then aggregated into class-wise Coverage Prototypes to complement the semantic representations provided by Salient Prototypes. Furthermore, we introduce a ranking-based selective refinement strategy that identifies classes receiving stronger semantic support from Coverage Prototypes and selectively enhances their soft targets while preserving the base soft targets for the rest. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of CoST, with strong performance gains over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CoST, a Coverage-guided Complementary Soft-Target Refinement framework for Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SalSPML) that supplements salient prototypes with semantically relevant coverage prototypes.
AI.motivation: Existing SalSPML methods rely on Salient Prototypes built from visually prominent observed positives, which fail to capture the visual diversity of hidden positives and provide insufficient positive supervision.
AI.method: CoST identifies semantically relevant candidates from unknown classes using task-learned category information and image-text semantic correspondence, aggregates them into class-wise Coverage Prototypes, and applies a ranking-based selective refinement strategy to enhance soft targets for classes with strong semantic support.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple SalSPML benchmarks demonstrate that CoST achieves strong performance gains over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining salient prototypes with image-text semantic coverage prototypes effectively addresses the supervision gap for non-salient, unlabeled positive classes in multi-label learning.

title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
comment: Code available at this https URL
summary: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), a reinforcement learning method for few-step diffusion models that renoises generated samples into shadow inputs to obtain accurate reward credit while anchoring to an undistilled teacher.
AI.motivation: Reinforcing few-step diffusion models with black-box rewards is challenging because a few-step generator's velocity does not match the generated distribution's forward velocity, and it must remain anchored to an undistilled teacher with which it shares no transitions.
AI.method: SPM renoises generated samples into shadow inputs, computes reward credit from their shadow posterior, and derives a regression loss from a KL-regularized reward objective that converts rewards into a direction while anchoring outputs to the teacher and aligning shadow inputs with deployed inputs.
AI.result: Applied to 4-step diffusion generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
AI.conclusion: Shadow Posterior Matching resolves the credit-assignment and teacher-anchoring mismatch in few-step diffusion RL, enabling more effective and stable reward optimization.

title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
comment: 15 pages (12 pages main text + references), 12 figures, 4 tables
summary: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FrontierReplay, a split-free exact prefix caching system for hybrid language models that materializes checkpoints at predictable structural boundaries without cutting the prefill forward pass.
AI.motivation: Hybrid language models with recurrent layers restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions, and existing fine-grained exact caches must split the prefill forward pass at mid-prompt checkpoints, incurring scheduler overhead that outweighs reuse gains under load.
AI.method: FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs during an uncut prefill and runs a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel at structural boundaries (such as turn ends and branch points) to materialize exact checkpoints 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation, paired with a frontier-aware retention policy.
AI.result: Across diverse hybrid architectures and workloads, FrontierReplay lowers median TTFT by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raises 80% SLO capacity by up to 1.73x, improves goodput by up to 4.26x over exact caches, and delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput than approximate replay without its up to 17% long-context accuracy drop.
AI.conclusion: FrontierReplay enables high-throughput, exact prefix reuse in hybrid language models without sacrificing prefill efficiency or long-context accuracy.

title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
summary: Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy -- the loss incurred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic groups of decision-subjects (DS) -- on static data, where reducing one often comes at the expense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder without increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never lowers any group's acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM's break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which may lower the advantaged group's acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group. Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs, allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when a fairer decision policy can outperform a statically Pareto-optimal policy once evaluated on the post-deployment population it induces, showing that population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Fair ML typically evaluates decision-maker (DM) loss and group fairness on static pre-deployment data, ignoring how decisions alter qualification scores over time and potentially reverse static trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors analyze a dynamic setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and outcomes under both Rawlsian fairness (never lowering any group's acceptance rate) and egalitarian fairness (allowing the advantaged group's rate to drop).
AI.result: Under Rawlsian fairness, placing high weight on fairness reduces delayed societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged subjects at the DM's break-even point leaves them less costly than rejecting them; under egalitarian fairness, the DM loss reduction on the disadvantaged group must also outweigh the increase on the advantaged group, though accuracy-based DM gains can still stem from declining subject qualification.
AI.conclusion: Policy-induced population dynamics can allow fairer policies to reduce delayed societal costs for both stakeholders, though accuracy-based metrics require care to ensure improvements do not mask declining subject qualifications.

title: When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
summary: Can ranking a batch of antipodal query pairs recover a gradient direction with fewer evaluations than using within-pair signs alone? We study fixed-center recovery in $d$ dimensions for a linear signal plus an unknown differentiable even nuisance, counting function evaluations and feedback rounds separately. Shared pair offsets create an information hierarchy: Mirror retains within-pair signs, Reverse couples reversed cross-pair orders to cancel offsets, and Full enforces all ranking inequalities. Relative shell variation is the nuisance range over the query sphere normalized by the linear-signal scale. When it is at most $c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$, Reverse localizes every consistent direction to angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations in one round at fixed confidence, without a variation bound supplied to the decoder. This matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, versus the $\Theta(d/\varepsilon)$ one-round sign-only minimax cost on the same class. Over well-conditioned positive-definite quadratics with no common relative-curvature bound, the $R$-round minimax cost is instead $\Theta(dR(\varepsilon^{-1/R}-1))$, even with cumulative rankings. We extend validity beyond exact evenness under supplied error bounds. Matched-endpoint experiments certify information beyond signs and short cycles. On two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, short-cycle recovery attains lower terminal mean gaps than the tested batch-capable controls. An additional optimization benefit from fitting the complete ranking remains unestablished.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes when ranking antipodal query pairs recovers a gradient direction with fewer evaluations than using within-pair signs alone under an unknown even nuisance.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when cross-pair rankings in a batch of antipodal queries provide an information-theoretic advantage over within-pair signs for fixed-center gradient recovery under even nuisance perturbations.
AI.method: The authors analyze three feedback tiers (Mirror, Reverse, and Full) in d dimensions for a linear signal plus differentiable even nuisance, establishing sample-complexity bounds for Reverse and minimax rates over quadratics, and evaluating short-cycle recovery on ridge tasks.
AI.result: When relative shell variation is at most c*epsilon/sqrt(d), Reverse recovers the direction to angular accuracy epsilon in one round using O_tilde(d + sqrt(d/epsilon)) evaluations, matching a lower bound and beating the Theta(d/epsilon) sign-only minimax cost; on ridge tasks, short-cycle recovery achieves lower terminal mean gaps than batch-capable controls.
AI.conclusion: Cross-pair rankings provably beat within-pair signs in one-round gradient direction recovery when relative shell variation is sufficiently small, though additional benefits from fitting full rankings remain unestablished.

title: Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration: Bootstrapping Generative Auto-bidding from Narrow Support
summary: Auto-bidding is a core algorithmic component in online advertising auctions. In practical cold-start settings, iterative training is commonly used to compensate for low-quality, narrowly supported historical data. Unfortunately, in iterative training, representative diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods fail to sustain extrapolation beyond the narrow data support and stagnate at a suboptimal level. In this paper, we theoretically attribute this stagnation to Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse: the weak radial return signal is overwhelmed by a curvature-induced penalty. To break this stagnation, we propose \textbf{Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE)}, which introduces a guidance handoff: as the return signal collapses, scarcity subsequently takes over as an exploratory signal to elevate the SNR above a critical threshold. Specifically, ISGE iteratively alternates between a \emph{Judger} that assigns scarcity scores to trajectories and an \emph{Explorer} that performs guided generation of high-scarcity and high-return trajectories, thereby bootstrapping from the narrow support with such self-generated trajectories. Extensive experiments on the industrial AuctionNet benchmark demonstrate that ISGE, starting from cold-start datasets, effectively surpasses the performance of the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE) to overcome Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse in cold-start generative auto-bidding, surpassing full-dataset baselines within three iterations.
AI.motivation: In cold-start iterative training for online advertising auto-bidding, diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods stagnate because the weak radial return signal is overwhelmed by a curvature-induced penalty (SNR collapse).
AI.method: ISGE introduces a guidance handoff where scarcity takes over as an exploratory signal when the return signal collapses, alternating between a Judger that scores trajectory scarcity and an Explorer that generates high-scarcity, high-return trajectories to bootstrap beyond narrow support.
AI.result: On the industrial AuctionNet benchmark, ISGE starting from cold-start datasets surpasses the performance of the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations.
AI.conclusion: Scarcity-guided exploration provides an effective mechanism to escape SNR collapse and bootstrap generative auto-bidding policies from narrow cold-start data.

title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
summary: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a graph metanetwork framework that predicts internal representation similarity across unseen trained neural networks directly from their parameterized computation graphs without running inference.
AI.motivation: Comparing internal representations across trained models typically requires evaluating candidate models on reference inputs and collecting activations, which is costly when selecting components for model reuse.
AI.method: The framework uses a graph metanetwork to map each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while respecting hidden-coordinate permutations and internal attention-basis transformations, with conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching selection.
AI.result: Empirically, the learned predictors support relation estimation, low-regret layer retrieval, and useful stitching connection selection on unseen models despite not being trained on stitching outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Representational relations learned across a collection of trained models generalize to new computations, enabling candidate selection for model reuse directly from weights before functional evaluation.

title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models
summary: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two approximate adjoint methods, Zero-order and Pullback Reuse, that preserve full-trajectory recurrence while reducing peak memory by up to an order of magnitude and runtime by up to 4x in online hybrid-model learning.
AI.motivation: Exact adjoint methods (BPTT) for calibrating hybrid numerical-neural models have memory and compute costs that scale with trajectory length, while truncated BPTT introduces gradient bias and drops long-range dependencies.
AI.method: The methods compute exact pullbacks via automatic differentiation only at sparse anchor states and propagate sensitivities between anchors using either the identity (Zero-order) or a frozen reused pullback (Pullback Reuse), factorizing the gradient sum to one evaluation per chunk.
AI.result: Evaluated on Lorenz-63, 2D quasi-geostrophic turbulence closure, and a multilayer ocean model, peak memory drops by up to 10x and runtime by up to 4x, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to exact gradients and both achieving comparable training accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Effective online learning of hybrid physical-neural models does not require exact per-step gradients, enabling longer training windows and higher-resolution geophysical simulations.

title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
summary: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Complete Path Contribution, a method that decomposes network outputs into mathematically complete contributions of individual input-to-output paths and finds the k strongest paths in empirically linear time in k.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability methods analyze only pairwise component interactions and miss higher-order interactions along full causal paths, leaving questions like how inhibitory and excitatory pathways combine unanswered.
AI.method: Complete Path Contribution decomposes network outputs into exact path-level contributions with guaranteed completeness at any circuit granularity, paired with an algorithm that identifies the k strongest paths without enumerating all paths.
AI.result: Applied to image classification networks and a mouse retina model, the method quantifies excitatory-inhibitory pathway interactions and reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from pathway motifs under time-varying natural stimuli.
AI.conclusion: Complete Path Contribution makes path-level mechanistic analysis tractable at scale, revealing how causal pathways interact from input to output.

title: How Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity Shape Decentralized Learning: A Spectral Analysis
summary: Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to consensus dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a spectral framework for decentralized federated learning under irregular topologies, showing how dominant and non-dominant eigenmodes interact with IID and non-IID data distributions.
AI.motivation: Existing spectral analyses of decentralized learning often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking how irregular communication networks create topology-dependent node influence.
AI.method: The framework separates the dominant eigenmode (governing consensus trajectory and stationary node influence, shown to be proportional to degree plus one under uniform neighborhood averaging) from non-dominant eigenmodes (governing disagreement attenuation), and derives a disagreement bound.
AI.result: Experiments across regular and heterogeneous topologies show nearly identical dynamics under IID data, whereas under non-IID data, network size and connectivity govern how unevenly distributed information shapes consensus dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for both dominant-mode node influence and non-dominant spectral mixing is essential for understanding and designing decentralized learning over irregular graphs with heterogeneous data.

title: Loss-Guided Tsetlin Machines: Making the Learning Objective Explicit
summary: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has no explicit notion of a loss function. Its learning signal is fixed to an implicit, margin-based update rule (MBUR), with no way to choose an objective function suited to a specific task. This paper introduces Loss-Guided TM, which replaces MBUR with an explicit and swappable loss function. In our proposed method, clause feedback and weight updates are driven by the loss, while keeping the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic unchanged. The approach incorporates cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross entropy (SCE), and asymmetric loss (ASL). We evaluate Loss-Guided TM across six datasets that span multiclass, multilabel, and binary classification tasks. With a suitable loss, Loss-Guided TM matches or improves accuracy and F1 over MBUR on five of the six datasets. The gains are greatest for the imbalanced multilabel datasets, where ASL improves macro F1 by up to 9 percentage points. With CE, Loss-Guided TM is also significantly better calibrated than MBUR on all six datasets, reducing calibration error by a factor of 3 to 11. A qualitative inspection shows that the clause-based global interpretability, examined at the per-class level on image and text data, is preserved when using the Loss-Guided mechanism. These results show that our explicit TM learning objective allows direct targeting of uncertainty calibration, data imbalance, and task structure, opening the TM to the broader literature on loss functions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Loss-Guided Tsetlin Machines (TM), replacing the implicit margin-based update rule with explicit, swappable loss functions to improve calibration and handle class imbalance while preserving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Standard Tsetlin Machines rely on a fixed, implicit margin-based update rule (MBUR) with no explicit loss function, preventing task-specific objective tailoring for issues like calibration or data imbalance.
AI.method: Loss-Guided TM drives clause feedback and weight updates using explicit loss functions—cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross entropy (SCE), and asymmetric loss (ASL)—while keeping the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic intact.
AI.result: Across six binary, multiclass, and multilabel datasets, Loss-Guided TM matches or improves accuracy and F1 over MBUR on five datasets (up to +9 percentage points macro F1 on imbalanced multilabel data with ASL) and reduces calibration error by 3x to 11x with CE, while preserving per-class clause interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Making the learning objective explicit opens Tsetlin Machines to standard loss function design for targeted calibration and imbalance handling without sacrificing global interpretability.

title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
summary: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (this https URL), with inference available through our this http URL fork at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method calibrated on agent-session tokens that enables 3.0- and 2.5-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B to match BF16 on long-horizon agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing sub-3-bit quantizations calibrated on short web text match BF16 on short tasks like AIME but degrade severely on 100K+ token agentic tasks, solving at most 72% as many DeepSWE tasks as BF16.
AI.method: NariQ applies trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated directly on tokens generated by the BF16 model during multi-step agent sessions.
AI.result: On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight matches BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA, while a 2.0-bit checkpoint trails behind.
AI.conclusion: NariQ demonstrates that calibrating on agentic trajectories enables sub-3-bit weight quantization to preserve full-precision performance on long-horizon tool-use tasks.

title: Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks for a Universal Fluid Gibbs Free Energy Equation of State
summary: Over the past three centuries, many thermodynamics researchers have worked to develop fluid equations of state with both high accuracy and broad applicability, proposing various theoretical frameworks and models. Building on these efforts, this study uses Gibbs free energy as the starting point and introduces thermodynamically consistent neural networks to construct a fluid equation of state based on Gibbs free energy (GEoS). This approach establishes a novel machine learning framework that provides a unified representation of fluid states. GEoS performs well on the vapor- and liquid-phase density test sets, with average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25% and 3.96%, respectively. It outperforms conventional volume-translated cubic equations of state and existing machine learning models, demonstrating its effectiveness. Further analysis using the UMAP dimensionality reduction method shows that most molecules in the test set belong to extrapolation systems, confirming the strong generalization ability of the model. Finally, the test results show that the PC-SAFT equation fitted using GEoS maintains high predictive accuracy, providing a reliable basis for its practical application in industry.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GEoS, a thermodynamically consistent neural network framework for a universal fluid Gibbs free energy equation of state that outperforms conventional cubic equations and existing ML models.
AI.motivation: Developing fluid equations of state that combine high accuracy with broad applicability across molecular systems remains a longstanding challenge in thermodynamics.
AI.method: Starting from Gibbs free energy, the authors construct thermodynamically consistent neural networks (GEoS) to provide a unified representation of fluid states, and also use GEoS to fit the PC-SAFT equation.
AI.result: GEoS achieves average absolute relative deviations of 5.25% on vapor-phase density and 3.96% on liquid-phase density test sets, outperforming volume-translated cubic equations of state and existing ML models, with UMAP confirming strong extrapolation to unseen molecules.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamically consistent neural networks grounded in Gibbs free energy offer an accurate, generalizable fluid equation of state suitable for industrial applications.

title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity
summary: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that attention head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, explaining stagewise head emergence in transformers from a statistical perspective.
AI.motivation: While attention head specialization during training is well documented as a function of training time, how it depends on training dataset size and whether it has a statistical origin remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors empirically track syntactic head emergence in BERT across dataset sizes and analyze a solvable high-dimensional multi-head attention model to characterize test-error non-analyticities and stagewise transitions.
AI.result: Head specialization emerges in BERT as dataset size grows, and in the solvable model it manifests as a phase transition in sample complexity—either following uninformative differentiation or occurring as a cascade of transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features.
AI.conclusion: Statistical phase transitions in sample complexity provide a principled explanation for simplicity bias and the stagewise emergence of specialized attention heads.

title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
summary: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD), a sound and complete constraint-based causal discovery algorithm for nonstationary multivariate time series that runs up to 40.9x faster than baselines on 2000-node graphs.
AI.motivation: Causal structure learning on time series suffers from autocorrelation, distribution shift, and high computational and sample complexity in high-dimensional settings.
AI.method: ITPD uses a local-to-global approach that sequentially discovers each variable's parent set, exploiting temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to replace higher-order conditional independence tests with lower-order ones.
AI.result: With an exact oracle, ITPD performs the fewest tests with the smallest conditioning sets; in simulations it sits on the F1-runtime Pareto frontier and runs 2.3x, 9.1x, and 40.9x faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI on 2000-node graphs.
AI.conclusion: ITPD makes sound and complete causal discovery scalable to large, nonstationary time-series graphs.

title: Predicting Surface Displacement Fields of Laser Powder Bed Fusion Parts Using STL-Derived Graphs and Part-Level Descriptors
summary: Predicting part distortion before fabrication remains challenging in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), while thermomechanical simulation is computationally expensive for repeated design evaluations. This study presents a two-branch graph attention network (GAT) to predict three-dimensional surface displacement directly from STL-derived graphs. The first branch learns geometric relationships among connected vertices of a densified STL surface mesh, while the second incorporates 12 part-level descriptors of mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape. Displacement labels from ANSYS Additive Print simulations are mapped onto STL vertices using Gaussian-kernel weighted averaging. Evaluated on 117 parts using five-fold cross-validation split by part, the model achieves an R^2 of 0.946 and a mean absolute error of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude. Relative to a node-wise multilayer perceptron, GAT improves R^2 from 0.913 to 0.946; for build-direction displacement, R^2 increases from 0.903 to 0.939. GAT also outperforms GraphSAGE (R^2 = 0.936) and a graph convolutional network (R^2 = 0.934) across all five folds. Ablation experiments show that removing mass-distribution descriptors reduces magnitude R^2 to 0.900, while removing build-plate contact and overhang descriptors reduces it to 0.920. These results demonstrate the value of combining local mesh connectivity with global geometric descriptors to predict LPBF distortion, enabling faster design iteration and earlier identification of distortion-prone geometries.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a two-branch graph attention network (GAT) that predicts 3D surface displacement fields of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) parts directly from STL-derived graphs and part-level descriptors with an R^2 of 0.946.
AI.motivation: Predicting LPBF part distortion before fabrication is critical, but thermomechanical simulations are too slow for repeated design iterations.
AI.method: The two-branch GAT combines local geometric learning on a densified STL surface mesh with 12 global part-level descriptors (mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape), supervised by ANSYS Additive Print labels mapped via Gaussian-kernel averaging.
AI.result: Evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation on 117 parts, the GAT achieves an R^2 of 0.946 and MAE of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude, outperforming a node-wise MLP (0.913), GraphSAGE (0.936), and GCN (0.934), with ablations confirming the importance of mass-distribution and contact/overhang descriptors.
AI.conclusion: Combining local mesh connectivity with global geometric descriptors enables fast, accurate LPBF distortion prediction for earlier design-stage screening.

title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
summary: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B model trained with SFT and verification-guided GRPO that raises Pass@1 from 0% to 51.43% on a new automated ocean engineering simulation benchmark.
AI.motivation: Automated numerical simulation modelling in ocean engineering requires domain-specific correctness beyond syntax and execution, and suffers from scarce training data and specialised programming requirements.
AI.method: The authors build a pipeline generating 12,000 verified SFT examples across 12 task categories and design a three-layer verification framework (checking input parameters, analysis completion, and output plausibility) to provide graded rewards for GRPO, alongside a new ocean engineering benchmark.
AI.result: OceanCoder outperforms both base models and closed-source comparisons, increasing Pass@1 from 0% (base) to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer engineering verification provides an effective training signal for aligning LLMs with domain-specific numerical simulation requirements.

title: TRCF: Temporal-Reference Complementary Forecasting for Irregular Multivariate Time Series
summary: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting supports healthcare monitoring, environmental analysis, and activity recognition. Channel-independent (CI) approaches capture each variable's temporal patterns but do not explicitly use observations from other variables. Channel-dependent (CD) modeling exploits relationships among variables, yet asynchronous measurements make these relationships difficult to learn. Incorporating cross-variable information while preserving each variable's irregular history therefore remains a key challenge. We propose Temporal-Reference Complementary Forecasting (TRCF), a framework that augments a compact CI forecaster with a complementary CD branch. ANCHOR aggregates observed values and timestamps at shared temporal locations, retaining observation support to form compact CI features. BRIDGE constructs complementary features through history completion. It first estimates each variable's historical values from its own observations, then uses differences between other variables' observed and estimated values at nearby times to correct missing entries. The completed history preserves observed values and is encoded to supply context alongside the direct CI representation. Finally, the two representations are fused, combined with the query-time embedding, and passed to a shallow multilayer perceptron for forecasting. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that TRCF achieves the lowest mean squared error and mean absolute error in the main benchmark comparison, while reducing measured peak inference memory by 17.28% to 87.98% relative to APN.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TRCF, a framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that combines a compact channel-independent branch with a history-completion channel-dependent branch, achieving the lowest MSE/MAE and up to 87.98% lower peak memory than APN.
AI.motivation: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting struggles to incorporate cross-variable relationships from asynchronous observations without losing each variable's irregular temporal history.
AI.method: TRCF pairs ANCHOR, which aggregates observations at shared temporal locations for compact channel-independent features, with BRIDGE, which completes missing history using cross-variable differences at nearby times, fusing both with query-time embeddings in a shallow MLP.
AI.result: On four real-world datasets, TRCF achieves the lowest MSE and MAE in main benchmark comparisons while reducing measured peak inference memory by 17.28% to 87.98% relative to APN.
AI.conclusion: Combining compact channel-independent representations with difference-based cross-variable history completion improves both accuracy and memory efficiency in irregular time series forecasting.

title: Mamba Flow Matching Neural Processes: Linear-Time Inference for Irregularly Observed Spatial Fields
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. XX pages, X figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Interpolating a spatial field, such as daily maximum temperature, from sparse, irregularly located observations recurs across the environmental and health sciences. Standard Gaussian-process kriging refits hyperparameters and solves an $O(N^3)$ system for every new field. When many related fields are observed, such as daily maps from one sensor network, neural processes (NPs) instead learn the interpolation map from past fields and predict a new field in one forward pass. Joint-predictive variants, which sample whole fields rather than independent per-location values, typically use self-attention over context and query points, costing $O(K^2)$ in the combined point count $K$ and limiting practical use to a few thousand points. State-space models offer a linear-time alternative, but a direct state-space adaptation compresses the context into one hidden state before reading queries, reducing what the decoder sees. We propose MambaFlowNP, a linear-compute joint-predictive NP trained with conditional flow matching. A multi-directional Mamba-2 scan reads context and query tokens in one shared sequence, so each query's velocity is read from its own scan position rather than a compressed context summary, and because queries only read the scan state, predictions are consistent across query sets. MambaFlowNP is competitive with the strongest attention-based joint-predictive baselines on synthetic Matérn Gaussian-process benchmarks, and on regional to continental-scale NOAA temperature interpolation it attains the lowest RMSE and CRPS and near-nominal coverage on every tier, while running 114--784$\times$ faster than the strongest joint-predictive baseline. A single forward pass scales to $10^6$ points on one NVIDIA L40S GPU in under a second. This makes joint prediction feasible for continental-scale, irregularly sampled sensor networks; predictive quality is evaluated up to $K=5{,}580$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MambaFlowNP, a linear-time joint-predictive neural process trained with conditional flow matching that matches attention baselines on spatial field benchmarks while running 114-784x faster.
AI.motivation: Joint-predictive neural processes for interpolating spatial fields rely on self-attention with O(K^2) complexity, limiting them to a few thousand points, while naive state-space adaptations compress context into a single hidden state.
AI.method: MambaFlowNP uses a multi-directional Mamba-2 scan over context and query tokens in a shared sequence so each query's velocity is read from its own scan position, trained with conditional flow matching for consistent joint predictions.
AI.result: MambaFlowNP is competitive with top attention-based joint-predictive baselines on synthetic Matérn GP benchmarks, achieves the lowest RMSE and CRPS on NOAA temperature interpolation while running 114-784x faster, and scales to 10^6 points in under a second on one L40S GPU.
AI.conclusion: MambaFlowNP makes joint-predictive spatial field interpolation feasible at continental scale with linear-time inference.

title: Learning from Context: Leave-One-Out Prediction in Jump Diffusions
summary: Continuous diffusion models generate discrete data through stochastic dynamics in an embedding space. We consider jump diffusions that additionally reset coordinates to embeddings of categorical values. A coordinate's own corrupted state can make prediction easy, potentially reducing the pressure to learn dependencies between coordinates. We study leave-one-out (LOO) prediction, in which each coordinate is predicted from the corrupted states of the other coordinates. We show that, under stated assumptions, jump diffusions with complete coordinate resets and state-independent clocks preserve the prescribed marginals when reset destinations use exact LOO probabilities and the drift uses the full endpoint posterior. We further show that this drift can be constructed from LOO probabilities by analytic likelihood completion without additional network evaluations. We evaluate unrestricted, LOO, and completed predictions on Text8 and LM1B text generation and ZINC250k molecular graph generation. LOO-based variants improve key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls on all three datasets. Controlled interventions assess reliance on local inputs and context, and we analyze the effect of analytic likelihood completion.

AI.tldr: This paper studies leave-one-out (LOO) prediction in jump diffusions for discrete data, proving marginal preservation under complete coordinate resets and showing consistent generation improvements on text and molecular graphs.
AI.motivation: In continuous-time jump diffusions for discrete data, a coordinate's own corrupted state can make prediction trivial, reducing the model's incentive to learn inter-coordinate dependencies.
AI.method: The authors formulate LOO prediction (predicting each coordinate from other corrupted coordinates), prove that jump diffusions with complete resets preserve marginals using LOO probabilities and full endpoint posteriors, and construct the drift via analytic likelihood completion without extra network calls.
AI.result: Evaluated on Text8, LM1B, and ZINC250k, LOO-based variants improve key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls across all three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing leave-one-out prediction with analytic likelihood completion strengthens contextual dependency learning in discrete jump diffusions without sacrificing marginal exactness.

title: From Benchmarks to the Bench: Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional Drug-Target Screening
summary: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Drug-target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug-target pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates. Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 13 drug-target interaction (DTI) systems in bidirectional screening, revealing that models produce largely disjoint Top-10 recommendations and that high benchmark enrichment often masks a lack of target or drug selectivity.
AI.motivation: DTI models are typically evaluated on aggregate benchmarks, leaving unclear whether their Top-K recommendations are consistent or selective enough to guide real experimental screening.
AI.method: The authors compare bidirectional Top-10 recommendations of 13 DTI systems across 711 FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins, evaluate hit yields against published inhibition data for 79 molecules and 65 kinases, and test seed sensitivity via retraining.
AI.result: Pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively; some systems maintained hit yields even when recommendations were mismatched to different drugs or targets, and retraining with different random seeds yielded a mean pairwise Top-10 overlap of only about two candidates.
AI.conclusion: Strong benchmark scores do not guarantee target selectivity or recommendation stability, highlighting the need for selectivity-aware evaluation before deploying DTI models for experimental discovery.

title: Evidence from a Multi-Regime Causal Discovery Benchmark: UCMT Algorithms, Comparative Performance, and Controlled Ablation Studies
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Internal benchmark and controlled ablation study; not peer-reviewed
summary: We present an internal, pre-registered evaluation of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family alongside established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, complemented by a separately pre-registered, controlled study of UCMT v2 Global components. The contribution is both empirical and methodological: a family-stratified comparison of three actively developed algorithm configurations and targeted evidence about which internal stages affect their outcomes. In the main benchmark, UCMT v2 Global has higher directed F1 than NOTEARS and DAGMA in selected real, semi-synthetic and Gaussian-network comparisons at the paired-run level, while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings. The BOSS-based UCMT v4 produces a CSuite-specific directed-F1 improvement over BOSS (mean paired difference +0.279; pair-level Holm p < 0.001), but the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188). In a separate fixed-skeleton ablation, UCMT v2 Global exceeds an adapted R^2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on standardized iSCM data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, dataset-level Holm p = 0.031); absolute orientation accuracy is 0.563 and there is no established broad advantage over RESIT, ANM or DirectLiNGAM. Controlled ablations show that sparsity and BIC-based refinement materially affect some outcomes, whereas the examined arbitration and automatic regime-selection mechanisms do not yield confirmed general improvements. We report performance shortcomings, multiple-testing correction, runtime costs, evaluation limitations and reproducibility checks. The results support UCMT as an implemented and empirically investigated algorithm family, not a claim of overall superiority, independent validation or demonstrated commercial impact.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pre-registered, multi-regime evaluation and controlled ablation study of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family, finding mixed comparative performance and identifying key internal drivers.
AI.motivation: Rigorous, pre-registered empirical evidence is needed to evaluate where the UCMT causal discovery family outperforms established baselines and which internal stages drive its behavior.
AI.method: The authors conduct a family-stratified benchmark of three UCMT configurations against NOTEARS, DAGMA, BOSS, RESIT, ANM, and DirectLiNGAM, alongside a pre-registered ablation of UCMT v2 Global components.
AI.result: UCMT v2 Global beats NOTEARS and DAGMA on selected paired runs and beats an R^2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on iSCM data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, p=0.031), while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings; UCMT v4 improves over BOSS on CSuite at the pair level (+0.279 F1) but not at the dataset level (p=0.188), and ablations show sparsity and BIC refinement matter while arbitration/regime-selection do not.
AI.conclusion: The pre-registered evaluation clarifies the specific regimes where UCMT algorithms offer gains and where they fall short, establishing a transparent empirical baseline rather than broad superiority.

title: A Complete Geometric Message-Passing Architecture for Point Clouds
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Ancillary files: exact-arithmetic verifier, certificate and companion notebook for the Platonic color-atom computation
summary: Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality, and a large family of machine learning architectures has been developed to respect their natural symmetries to rigid motions and permutations. A principled way to compare these architectures, which vary widely in complexity and cost, is through their expressive power. That is, an architecture is complete if it can distinguish any two inputs not related by the symmetries it respects. Simple distance-based message-passing networks are known to be incomplete, and while there exist complete alternatives, they typically rely on computationally intensive mechanisms like high-order representations of the rotation group or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman-type tests. In this work, we devise a novel, simple, equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, and prove that it is complete. We complement our theoretical result with experiments showing that our architecture separates challenging point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish. Our results suggest that high-order equivariant features may not be necessary to enhance the expressivity of point cloud architectures, and can help settle completeness for other equivariant architectures for which such results are currently unknown. We give initial evidence for this by proving completeness of a slightly modified version of SEGNN.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a simple, equivariant message-passing architecture for 3D point clouds and proves that it is complete without relying on high-order rotation representations or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman tests.
AI.motivation: Simple distance-based message-passing networks for point clouds are provably incomplete, while existing complete alternatives require computationally expensive high-order equivariant representations or higher-order WL tests.
AI.method: The authors design a simple equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, prove its completeness theoretically, and extend the proof technique to a slightly modified version of SEGNN.
AI.result: Experiments confirm that the proposed architecture separates challenging point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish.
AI.conclusion: High-order equivariant features are not strictly necessary for completeness in point cloud networks, opening simpler paths to maximally expressive geometric architectures.

title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
summary: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $\alpha$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($\theta_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $\alpha$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/\alpha)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes e-RWSC, an anytime-valid sequential stopping rule for inference-time alignment using betting supermartingales that certifies majority answers with error probability bounded by alpha at lower token cost.
AI.motivation: Fixed-budget Best-of-N wastes compute on easy prompts, while existing adaptive stopping heuristics lack statistical control over early-stopping errors under continuous monitoring.
AI.method: e-RWSC aggregates candidates by final answer using reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) scores and runs a betting supermartingale (e-process) for each answer, halting only when an answer is certified to hold a majority (>1/2) with uniform error bound alpha.
AI.result: Certification requires O(log(1/alpha)/d_KL(theta_a* || 1/2)) samples; experiments across multiple LLMs, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted 1/d_KL scaling and show improved accuracy over baselines at substantially lower token cost.
AI.conclusion: e-RWSC provides rigorous statistical error control for adaptive inference-time alignment, cutting token waste without sacrificing reliability.

title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
summary: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates a Composites World Model—combining a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) memory block, and transformer blocks—into a non-linear FEA solver, predicting composite defect responses with 0.4% to 4.8% error.
AI.motivation: Concurrent multi-scale simulations of fibre-reinforced composites with manufacturing defects are computationally prohibitive at structural scale, requiring memory-efficient, recursively stable surrogates.
AI.method: The Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer uses an SNN memory block to track long-term irreversible material state and transformer blocks for short-term strain, trained in three stages including recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling before coupling to a non-linear FE solver.
AI.result: Benchmarked against experimental results for pristine and wrinkled IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression, and transverse shear, the model tracks internal state with prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.
AI.conclusion: Coupling an SNN-based world model with non-linear FEA enables accurate, computationally efficient structural-scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects.

title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
summary: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EDA-L2D, an expert-drift-adapted learning-to-defer framework that conditions deferral decisions on recent histories of expert outcomes to handle temporal fluctuations in human reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-to-defer (L2D) methods assume fixed expert reliability, ignoring temporal performance shifts caused by human fatigue, cognitive biases, or changing task difficulty.
AI.method: EDA-L2D models temporal expert shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model, enabling adaptive allocation between human and machine over time.
AI.result: Experiments across image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection under irregular reliability shifts show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods, improving overall system performance and deferral decisions.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling temporal expert drift via outcome histories makes human-AI deferral systems more robust in realistic, non-stationary deployment settings.

title: Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics
summary: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven framework that learns nonlinear dynamics in a conditional Gaussian latent space to enable closed-form data assimilation with sequential uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Conventional nonlinear filtering for data assimilation is computationally expensive and requires explicit governing equations, whereas standard data-driven surrogates often lack integrated sequential uncertainty propagation.
AI.method: Neural CGM maps physical states to a latent space with conditional Gaussian dynamics for closed-form assimilation updates, and maps latent posterior means and covariances back to physical space via a Gaussian decoder trained end-to-end with Gaussian negative log-likelihood.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost compared to conventional nonlinear data assimilation methods.
AI.conclusion: Neural CGM unifies equation-free dynamical modeling with closed-form sequential uncertainty quantification for efficient data assimilation.

title: Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features: A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the NeurReps and WiML workshops at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features.
