Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates boosting noisy parameterized quantum circuits for supervised binary classification as an alternative to quantum error mitigation (QEM). Theoretical bounds and teacher-student simulations show that boosting requires fewer circuit executions than probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) as depth and noise increase while achieving higher test accuracy.
AI.motivation: Recovering noiseless observables via QEM can require superpolynomial or exponential sampling overhead, whereas supervised binary classification depends only on classifier sign and margin rather than exact expectation-value reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors derive a common hypothesis-class complexity bound under Pauli noise linking empirical margin loss to expected classification risk, formulate resource criteria, and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost against PEC in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and noise strength.
AI.result: Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions than PEC as circuit depth and physical noise increase and achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting task-specific label information via boosting provides a resource advantage over ideal-output QEM for noisy supervised quantum classification.

title: Full Rank and Stable Sampling of $\tanh$ Networks
summary: We study the recovery of feedforward $\tanh$ networks of fixed architecture with $P$ parameters from finitely many point evaluations. First, we characterize the set of parameters where the differential of the realization map has full rank and show that it coincides with the regular parameters in the sense of Vla{č}i{ć} and B{ö}lcskei (2021). Second, we make use of this characterization to prove that almost every tuple of $2P+1$ sampling points yields uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of this parameter set. Third, we prove that for exact observations, projected gradient descent and projected Gauss--Newton converge locally from sufficiently close feasible initial guesses. The same evaluations also determine the realized function for arbitrary parameters and identify parameters in the characterized set up to permutations and sign changes of hidden neurons. Finally, we develop a general framework for real-analytic networks that highlights the role of full rank in stability and local reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the recovery of fixed-architecture feedforward tanh networks with P parameters from finitely many point evaluations. It characterizes full-rank parameter sets, proves uniform-norm Lipschitz stability from almost every tuple of 2P+1 points, and establishes local convergence of projected gradient descent and projected Gauss-Newton.
AI.motivation: Understanding when finite point evaluations uniquely and stably determine neural network functions and parameters is fundamental to network identifiability and reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors characterize parameters where the realization map's differential has full rank (showing equivalence to regular parameters of Vlacic and Bolcskei, 2021), analyze sampling stability on compact subsets, prove local convergence of projected gradient descent and Gauss-Newton for exact observations, and generalize the framework to real-analytic networks.
AI.result: Almost every tuple of 2P+1 sampling points yields uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of full-rank parameters, determines the realized function for arbitrary parameters, and identifies full-rank parameters up to hidden-neuron permutations and sign changes, with local convergence guaranteed from sufficiently close feasible initializations.
AI.conclusion: Full-rankness of the realization differential governs both stable finite-sample identifiability and local optimization convergence in tanh and general real-analytic networks.

title: Hellinger Decision Trees for Density Ratio Estimation: Finite-Sample Guarantees
summary: Density ratios play a central role in two-sample comparison, distribution-shift adaptation, and generative-model evaluation. However, estimating a density ratio through separate estimation of the underlying densities can be unnecessarily challenging. In this paper, we develop a direct approach to the log density ratio estimation by minimizing a balanced Hellinger risk over additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees, trained using Newton boosting. We establish finite-sample guarantees for the estimator produced by the algorithm and derive an explicit convergence rate. Under suitable tail and Hölder smoothness conditions, together with an additional assumption on the progress made at each boosting iteration, our rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical minimax-optimal $ \mathscr{L}^{2} $ rate for function estimation. A key technical contribution is an optimization analysis that exploits the special exponential structure of the Hellinger risk. In particular, we show that the decrease in the second-order Taylor approximation (which is computable) of the empirical risk controls the actual decrease in that risk, yielding a direct optimization guarantee for the boosting algorithm. This allows us to establish statistical convergence guarantees for the algorithm's output without relying on an idealized empirical-risk minimizer. Experiments on synthetic data corroborate the predicted convergence behavior, while experiments on public datasets demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed estimator.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a direct log density ratio estimator using additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees trained with Newton boosting to minimize a balanced Hellinger risk. It establishes finite-sample guarantees matching classical minimax-optimal L^2 rates up to logarithmic factors without assuming an idealized empirical-risk minimizer.
AI.motivation: Estimating density ratios by separately estimating underlying densities is unnecessarily difficult, and existing boosting-based estimators often lack finite-sample statistical guarantees tied directly to the actual optimization algorithm.
AI.method: The authors minimize a balanced Hellinger risk over additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees via Newton boosting, exploiting the exponential structure of Hellinger risk to show that decreases in the computable second-order Taylor approximation control actual empirical risk decreases.
AI.result: Under tail, Holder smoothness, and boosting-progress conditions, the estimator achieves finite-sample convergence rates matching the classical minimax-optimal L^2 rate up to logarithmic factors; synthetic and public-dataset experiments corroborate the predicted convergence and practical effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Hellinger decision trees with Newton boosting provide both minimax-optimal finite-sample guarantees and strong empirical performance for direct density ratio estimation.

title: Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 15 figures, Accepted at the 2026 IEEE-RAS 25th International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026)
summary: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reference-free, model-free deep reinforcement learning framework for humanoid skateboarding using termination-shaped rewards. Tested on the K1 humanoid, exploit-blocking terminations induce an implicit curriculum from stance control to sustained robot-board locomotion without human demonstrations or analytic steering models.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid skateboarding methods rely on human demonstrations or analytic steering models requiring system identification, making reference-free object-mediated locomotion difficult.
AI.method: The authors combine task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations that penalize or terminate losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion.
AI.result: As training progresses on the K1 humanoid, the changing prevalence of these termination constraints produces an implicit progression from stance control to sustained robot-board skateboarding locomotion without prior demonstration data.
AI.conclusion: Termination-shaped model-free RL enables humanoids to learn complex object-mediated locomotion such as skateboarding from scratch.

title: SlotFlow-GB: A Neural Framework for Trans-Dimensional Inference of Overlapping Galactic Binaries
summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe the millihertz gravitational-wave sky, including millions of long-lived Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands of which are expected to be individually resolvable throughout the mission's lifetime. Extracting these sources requires jointly determining their number and physical parameters from strongly overlapping signals, posing a computationally demanding trans-dimensional inference problem. We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework that constructs a learned approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior, producing a probability distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual binaries in a single evaluation, without requiring their number to be specified in advance. We demonstrate this framework using year-long LISA simulations containing up to ten binaries within a 2 $\mu$Hz frequency interval, focusing on a high-SNR regime in which source overlap, rather than individual-source detectability, is the primary challenge. The inferred source count differs from the true count by at most one in 94% of cases, while the model identifies individual binaries even when their signals overlap strongly in frequency. A complete evaluation, including parameter sampling, takes just 41 ms per band on one NVIDIA GH200 GPU, or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. We further demonstrate that these distributions can be used to initialize subsequent likelihood-based inference, connecting fast amortized predictions with joint parameter estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework for amortized trans-dimensional inference of overlapping Galactic binaries in LISA data. In a single forward pass, it infers source multiplicity within +/-1 in 94% of cases and recovers individual binary parameters in 41 ms per 2-uHz band on a GH200 GPU.
AI.motivation: Extracting tens of thousands of resolvable Galactic binaries from LISA millihertz gravitational-wave data requires jointly inferring unknown source counts and parameters from strongly overlapping signals, which is computationally demanding.
AI.method: SlotFlow-GB learns an amortized approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior, outputting a distribution over source multiplicity and individual binary parameter densities in one evaluation without pre-specifying source count, and can initialize downstream likelihood-based inference.
AI.result: On year-long high-SNR LISA simulations with up to ten binaries in a 2-uHz band, SlotFlow-GB infers source count within at most one of the true count in 94% of cases, resolves strongly overlapping binaries, and runs in 41 ms per band on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU (530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads).
AI.conclusion: SlotFlow-GB bridges fast amortized trans-dimensional predictions with joint likelihood-based parameter estimation for LISA Galactic binary analysis.

title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PhantoMasq, a graph neural network framework for detecting masquerade attacks in Controller Area Networks (CANs) by modeling traffic as signal-enriched message sequence graphs. Evaluated on the ROAD dataset, it outperforms a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline by 0.13 to 0.36 AUC-ROC across five attack types.
AI.motivation: CANs lack built-in security against masquerade attacks that mimic legitimate traffic, and prior graph-based intrusion detection systems rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification.
AI.method: PhantoMasq represents CAN traffic as message sequence graphs augmented with lightweight signal-behavior statistics and formulates detection as graph-level classification using graph convolutional networks (GCNs).
AI.result: Under a leak-free evaluation protocol on the ROAD dataset across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves 0.831 to 0.999 mean AUC-ROC—surpassing a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline by 0.13 to 0.36 AUC-ROC with lower sensitivity to window configuration—at 2.33 to 5.94 ms CPU latency per window (168 to 429 windows/s).
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning structural and temporal signal features via GCNs improves accuracy and robustness for real-time CAN masquerade attack detection.

title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
summary: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for this http URL that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system that integrates session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained LLM into the retrieval-stage user tower alongside sequential encoders. Ablation studies and nearline serving deployment confirm both technical feasibility and improved recommendation performance.
AI.motivation: Large marketplace websites with heterogeneous content and sparse, fast-changing user behavior require strong user-interest representations at the retrieval stage, not only during downstream ranking.
AI.method: LSER derives session- and history-level user embeddings from a pretrained LLM, incorporates them as auxiliary features in the retrieval user tower alongside learned sequence encoders, and asynchronously refreshes both sequential and LLM-derived user vectors via a nearline serving path.
AI.result: An ablation study across the full multi-content-type catalog demonstrates incremental value from the LLM features, and the nearline serving architecture successfully supports real-time recommendation freshness.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM-derived session embeddings with asynchronous nearline serving is practical and effective for production multi-content retrieval.

title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
comment: 13 pages (incl. cover page), 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. Please cite the published version (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.2026.3666306). Code: this https URL
summary: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an end-to-end physics-informed deep learning framework that jointly performs MR Elastography (MRE) image reconstruction and phase-gradient wave inversion from undersampled k-space data. It reduces shear wave speed (SWS) NRMSE by 30% compared to total variation minimization and enables accurate quantification at acceleration factors up to 19.
AI.motivation: MRE suffers from slow data acquisition and ill-posed wave inversion, and conventional approaches rely on handcrafted image priors and separate reconstruction and inversion steps.
AI.method: The framework concatenates a model-based neural-network-regularized reconstruction module with a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) block to estimate SWS directly from k-space data, trained end-to-end on retrospectively undersampled brain MRE data and evaluated on in vivo data.
AI.result: Compared to total variation (TV) minimization, the proposed method significantly reduces NRMSE by 30%, remains accurate up to acceleration factor 19, outperforms separate image-reconstruction pre-training, and generalizes to in vivo data.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end physics-informed MRE reconstruction enables rapid, accurate tissue stiffness mapping from highly undersampled k-space data for clinical and dynamic imaging.

title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
comment: 33 pages (15 pages main text and 18 pages Supplementary Information), 4 figures
summary: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that systematic misalignment between predefined numerical rewards and expert judgment in generative materials discovery can uncover valuable compounds that fixed rewards overlook. Applied to electronic flat bands, expert preferences learned from pairwise comparisons guide a crystal diffusion model to favor known flat-band compounds like KCo2As2 and CoGa that a numerical bandwidth score would discard.
AI.motivation: Reward misalignment is typically treated as a failure mode, but in materials discovery fixed heuristic scores may miss scientifically interesting candidates that domain experts value.
AI.method: The authors collect pairwise expert comparisons on electronic flat bands (finding systematic disagreements with a numerical bandwidth score beyond an estimated 5% label-noise rate), learn expert preferences, and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model, extending the framework to synthesizability and phonon properties.
AI.result: While learned preferences and the numerical score agree on the flattest bands, they diverge elsewhere; notably, learned preferences favor reported compounds with partially flat bands such as KCo2As2 and CoGa that the numerical score discards.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging reward misalignment via learned expert preferences can reveal overlooked opportunities in generative materials discovery.

title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
summary: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified statistical framework for LLM training-data auditing that performs document-level membership inference, collection-level global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate effective auditing of both pre-training and fine-tuning data.
AI.motivation: Training membership signals in long documents are often localized to a few passages and can be diluted by naive aggregation, while collection-level auditing requires rigorous error-rate guarantees.
AI.method: The authors combine complementary chunk-level membership evidence using Cauchy combination to form document scores and calibrated p-values, then apply multiple testing for global auditing and suspicious-document subset identification.
AI.result: Under stated exchangeability conditions, the framework proves finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification, with effectiveness demonstrated across BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic.
AI.conclusion: The proposed statistical framework provides principled, error-controlled auditing for LLM pre-training and fine-tuning corpora.

title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
comment: 10 pages (+4 pages of references, +14 pages of supplementary material, 29 total pages), 7 figures in the main text (+14 figures in the supplementary material, total of 21 pages)
summary: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/\psi$, and $\Upsilon$. The network was never told which muons come from a resonance, it was only trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state particles. We use these features to alter aspects of the $Z$ boson: we change its mass between $\sim80$ and $105$ GeV, and removing such a feature from the neural network produces a broader $Z$ peak. In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spectrum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was built from the gradients of the neural network, and its selectivity was built using pattern recognition methods. A generative particle physics model trained on unlabeled data can be modified internally to change a physical quantity.

AI.tldr: This paper applies mechanistic interpretability to ShellFlow, a generative collider physics model trained on unlabeled LHC data, and discovers internal features representing particle resonances such as Z, J/psi, and Upsilon bosons. Manipulating the Z-boson feature shifts the generated Z mass between ~80 and 105 GeV or broadens the Z peak while leaving the rest of the invariant mass spectrum largely unchanged.
AI.motivation: While mechanistic interpretability has uncovered human-aligned concepts in language and vision models, it remains unexplored whether generative physics models trained solely on unlabeled final-state kinematics learn interpretable physical resonance concepts.
AI.method: The authors construct selective resonance features inside ShellFlow using neural network gradients and pattern recognition methods, then intervene on the Z-boson feature during generation.
AI.result: ShellFlow internally represents Z, J/psi, and Upsilon resonances without ever being given muon-origin labels; steering the Z feature shifts its mass between ~80 and 105 GeV, and ablating it broadens the Z peak, with minimal effect on the remaining invariant mass spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Generative particle physics models trained on unlabeled data develop manipulable internal representations of physical quantities.

title: Scalable fault vulnerability analysis for ReRAM-based process-in-memory CNN accelerators
summary: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector multiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (\textit{SaH}) and stuck-at-low (\textit{SaL}) resistance states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accuracy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and measuring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate, it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerability at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our proposed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks, whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about $10^4\times-10^5\times$, enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only a few minutes or hours.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fast, analytical fault vulnerability analysis framework for CNNs deployed on ReRAM-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators, quantifying vulnerability to stuck-at-high and stuck-at-low faults across weights, kernels, and layers. It matches exhaustive fault-injection trends while achieving a 10^4x to 10^5x speedup.
AI.motivation: Permanent stuck-at-high and stuck-at-low resistance faults in ReRAM cells corrupt mapped CNN weights and degrade accuracy, while exhaustive fault-injection simulation takes days or weeks for large-scale CNNs.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical vulnerability score (VS) metrics at weight, kernel, and layer granularities without running exhaustive fault-injection simulations.
AI.result: The proposed VS metrics align closely with CNN accuracy degradation observed in fault-injection simulations while delivering a 10^4x to 10^5x speedup, completing large-scale CNN vulnerability analysis in minutes or hours instead of days or weeks.
AI.conclusion: Analytical vulnerability scoring enables rapid, scalable design of fault-tolerant ReRAM-based PIM accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications.

title: Conformal Selection for Hierarchical Streaming Data
summary: Many real-world tasks involve making sequential decisions about whether to select candidates before their responses of interest are revealed. In this work, we address the online selection problem in the context of hierarchical data, where candidates arrive sequentially from different populations. This extends existing online conformal selection frameworks beyond the standard i.i.d./exchangeable data assumption. The primary challenge lies in constructing valid statistics for each candidate sequentially under the hierarchical data structure. To this end, we first develop Online Hierarchical Selection (OHS), a distribution-free method that enables principled candidate selection for hierarchical data streams. Specifically, we introduce methods to construct rank-based e-values for both between-group and within-group samples, and apply averaged e-values to the online e-BH procedure. We then develop OHS with feedback (OHSF), which boosts the power of OHS by leveraging potential response feedback. Theoretically, the proposed methods achieve false discovery rate control under mild hierarchical exchangeability and data arrival assumptions at any time. We also generalize methods to broader settings, such as data with covariate shift and selection under effect-related responses. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Online Hierarchical Selection (OHS) and OHS with feedback (OHSF) for distribution-free conformal selection on hierarchical streaming data. Both methods provably control the false discovery rate at any time under hierarchical exchangeability and demonstrate strong empirical performance.
AI.motivation: Existing online conformal selection methods assume i.i.d. or exchangeable data, which fails when candidates arrive sequentially from hierarchical populations.
AI.method: The authors construct rank-based e-values for both between-group and within-group samples, apply averaged e-values within an online e-BH procedure (OHS), incorporate potential response feedback to boost power (OHSF), and extend the approach to covariate shift and effect-related responses.
AI.result: Theoretically, OHS and OHSF achieve anytime false discovery rate control under mild hierarchical exchangeability and arrival assumptions; extensive simulated and real-world experiments confirm their effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Rank-based hierarchical e-values extend distribution-free online conformal selection with rigorous FDR control to structured streaming data.

title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation
summary: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Perfumer, an LLM-based agentic framework coupling Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models (Perfumer-relax and Perfumer-band) to automate and accelerate first-principles structural relaxation and electronic band prediction. Pre-relaxation yields a 2.75x speedup over QE alone, and Perfumer-band achieves 0.157 eV median MAE on 2,607 test materials in ~97 ms per material on two CPU cores.
AI.motivation: First-principles structural relaxation and electronic band structure calculations require heavy computation and specialized domain expertise.
AI.method: Perfumer orchestrates Quantum ESPRESSO with Perfumer-relax for pre-relaxation and Perfumer-band—a periodic GNN with a latent Hermitian spectral head predicting 12 band energies at arbitrary wavevectors while preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing a Hamiltonian—driven by natural-language agent workflows.
AI.result: Pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax followed by QE refinement achieves a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone; trained on 125,153 band structures, Perfumer-band reaches 0.157 eV median per-material MAE across 2,607 held-out test materials (including lanthanide, actinide, and magnetic compounds spanning 85 elements) in ~97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores.
AI.conclusion: Coupling symmetry-preserving neural predictors with DFT engines inside an LLM agentic workflow substantially accelerates first-principles materials workflows.

title: Simulation-pretrained autoencoders versus PCA for compressing multimode fibre transmission matrices
comment: 31 pages, 14 figures, including supplementary material. Code, trained weights and data are linked in the Data and code availability section
summary: Multimode optical fibres can image through a thin, flexible probe once their transmission matrix (TM) has been measured, but a TM is large and must be re-measured whenever the fibre moves. A compact model of feasible TMs would make storing and re-estimating them cheaper, so we ask how compactly TMs can be represented, and from how few measured TMs. Here we benchmark a permutation-equivariant autoencoder, pretrained on simulated fibres and adapted to measured TMs, against principal component analysis (PCA). At 62x compression, adapting the pretrained autoencoder with just two measured TMs reconstructs the TM of a 50um fibre well enough to focus light at 98% of the ideal enhancement, and it stays accurate when the TMs are shifted by 25 pixels or zoomed by 10%, which quickly degrades a linear basis. It is not, however, a better compressor: PCA is about ten times more accurate when fitted on all 163 real TMs (1.1% against 11.9% error on held-out TMs) and is already more accurate from ten. The autoencoder's value is as a prior when few or no real TMs exist: with none it reaches 29% error, against 91% for PCA fitted on the same simulation. Transfer to a different fibre is only partial. The most important extension, not yet tested, is to recover pixel-basis TMs from fewer measurements than a full TM, which would turn the pretrained prior from a compressor into a measurement-saving tool.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks a simulation-pretrained permutation-equivariant autoencoder against PCA for compressing multimode optical fibre transmission matrices (TMs). At 62x compression, the autoencoder acts as a strong few-shot prior (reaching 98% ideal focusing enhancement from two real TMs and 29% error with zero real TMs vs. 91% for PCA), whereas PCA is ~10x more accurate when many real TMs are available.
AI.motivation: Measuring and storing large multimode fibre transmission matrices is costly whenever the fibre moves, raising the question of how compactly TMs can be represented and from how few measurements.
AI.method: The authors pretrain a permutation-equivariant autoencoder on simulated fibres, adapt it to measured TMs of a 50-um fibre, and benchmark it against PCA across sample counts, shifts, and zooms.
AI.result: At 62x compression with two measured TMs, the autoencoder achieves 98% of ideal focusing enhancement and tolerates 25-pixel shifts or 10% zooms that degrade linear bases; with zero real TMs it reaches 29% error (vs. 91% for simulation-fitted PCA), whereas fitted on all 163 real TMs, PCA is ~10x more accurate (1.1% vs. 11.9% error) and already outperforms from ten TMs onward.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-pretrained autoencoders are valuable as few-shot or zero-shot priors for fibre TMs, while PCA remains superior once sufficient measured TMs are available.

title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
summary: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-Hölder source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that random weight neural network (RWNN) sieves inevitably become ill-conditioned as their dimension grows, and develops approximation, ridge-regularized estimation, and studentized inference theory that explicitly accommodates a vanishing smallest population eigenvalue.
AI.motivation: Conditional on sampled hidden weights, RWNN regression forms a linear sieve, yet standard sieve theory assumes well-conditioned covariance matrices that fail to hold as RWNN dimension increases.
AI.method: The authors prove polynomial upper bounds on population covariance eigenvalues under covering and Lipschitz conditions, establish faster-than-Monte-Carlo L^2 and L^infinity approximation bounds via stratified sampling under a beta-Holder source condition, and derive ridge-regularized consistency and directional asymptotic normality using ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotients and Riesz representation.
AI.result: The theory establishes feasible studentized inference and consistent ridge-adjusted variance estimators even as the smallest covariance eigenvalue vanishes, with numerical experiments confirming both the conditioning deterioration and finite-sample inference behavior.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for ill-conditioning via ridge regularization and directional nondegeneracy enables valid statistical estimation and inference with RWNN sieves.

title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
comment: PhD thesis, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, defended 25 February 2026. 178 pages. Promotors: Maarten Messagie and Thierry Coosemans. Chapters 4-5 are based on Knowledge-Based Systems 309 (2025) 112756, doi:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112756%3B chapter 6 on Energy and AI 18 (2024) 100448, doi:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.egyai.2024.100448%3B chapter 7 on BuildSys '26, pp. 405-416, doi:https://doi.org/10.1145/3744256.3812575
summary: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases. The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.

AI.tldr: This thesis compares rule-based, optimization, and machine learning methods for residential energy management across three simulations and one real-world experiment, and introduces TreeC, an interpretable tree-based strategy. While energy management lowers costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, savings do not yet outweigh implementation costs on average.
AI.motivation: Electrifying residential heating and transport requires synchronizing consumption and storage with low-emission generation, yet existing ML controllers lack interpretability and simulation gains often fail to transfer to hardware.
AI.method: The author develops TreeC to learn understandable energy management strategies and compares it against simple rules, model predictive control (MPC), and reinforcement learning across three simulation studies and a hardware experiment.
AI.result: TreeC performs competitively with MPC and RL while offering transparent strategies; in hardware testing, both TreeC and MPC degrade relative to simulation due to unrepresentative training data and unreliable real-time inputs; in Belgian dwellings, cost savings are largest for poorly insulated homes, EV chargers, and PV, but on average do not yet offset implementation costs.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable ML like TreeC is competitive for residential energy management, but hardware validation and cost-effectiveness remain key barriers to deployment.

title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
summary: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CF-Prop, a sampling-free uncertainty propagation method using characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, enabling a closed-form variational inference algorithm (CF-VI). CF-VI reduces calibration error by ~35% on CIFAR-100 and accurately captures heavy-tailed uncertainty where Monte Carlo and Gaussian-assumed methods fail.
AI.motivation: Sampling-free variational inference for Bayesian neural networks typically assumes Gaussian output distributions, which is inaccurate in non-Gaussian or heavy-tailed applied settings, while Monte Carlo sampling is computationally expensive.
AI.method: CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions through Bayesian ReLU layers without sampling to obtain exact output distributions, allowing closed-form ELBO computation for Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma, and other likelihoods in CF-VI.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error among tested methods, improving over the next best by about 35%; on a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, it accurately captures tail uncertainty severely underestimated by both Monte Carlo and other sampling-free methods.
AI.conclusion: Characteristic-function propagation enables exact, sampling-free Bayesian inference beyond Gaussian assumptions, improving calibration and tail-risk modeling.

title: Should Belgians Install an Advanced Energy Management System in Their Electrified Dwelling ?
comment: Full version including appendices A-C, which are not part of the 11-page proceedings version. Published at ACM BuildSys '26 under CC BY 4.0. 17 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables. Data: this https URL
summary: As dwellings electrify and more complex electricity pricing spreads in Belgium, the question arises: What are the potential benefits of installing an advanced energy management systems in an electrified Belgian dwelling ? To answer this question, we simulate 500 representative Belgian dwellings in which fossil systems are replaced by controllable electric technologies: space heating via air-to-air heat pumps, domestic hot water via electric boilers, and private transport via electric vehicles with home chargers. Photovoltaic systems are assigned according to current adoption rates. We evaluate two advanced energy management systems (EMS): model predictive control (MPC) and TreeC, a machine learning method using decision trees to model the EMS strategy. These are compared to a rule-based controller (RBC) that mimics default operation and an MPC with perfect forecasts (MPC P) as an upper bound. Performance for these EMSs is assessed for 2023 under a real contract with hourly prices and a monthly peak tariff. Average annual savings versus RBC are 82.5 EUR, 116.6 EUR, and 177.4 EUR for TreeC, MPC, and MPC P, respectively. All EMSs deliver similar thermal comfort (26-31 Kh). MPC saves more, while TreeC achieves higher EV charge completion (93.3% vs 88.8% for MPC, with a max charge of 95%) and a smoother aggregate load across the 500 dwellings. Savings remain modest relative to EMS purchase (280-680 EUR) and subscription (0-360 EUR/year) costs which is not favourable towards widespread adoption. The data and code to reproduce this study are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether electrified Belgian dwellings benefit economically from advanced energy management systems (MPC and TreeC) compared to a rule-based controller (RBC) across 500 simulated homes in 2023. MPC and TreeC save 116.6 EUR and 82.5 EUR annually on average, which remains modest relative to purchase and subscription costs.
AI.motivation: As Belgian dwellings electrify with heat pumps, electric boilers, EVs, and complex hourly/peak electricity tariffs, homeowners need to know whether advanced EMSs justify their financial cost.
AI.method: The authors simulate 500 representative electrified Belgian dwellings under 2023 hourly prices and monthly peak tariffs, comparing a rule-based controller (RBC), TreeC (decision-tree ML), MPC, and perfect-forecast MPC (MPC P).
AI.result: Average annual savings over RBC are 82.5 EUR (TreeC), 116.6 EUR (MPC), and 177.4 EUR (MPC P) with similar thermal comfort (26-31 Kh); TreeC achieves higher EV charge completion (93.3% vs. 88.8% for MPC) and smoother aggregate load, while EMS purchase (280-680 EUR) and subscription (0-360 EUR/year) costs make widespread adoption financially unfavorable.
AI.conclusion: Although advanced EMSs reduce electricity bills and improve grid-friendliness, current hardware and subscription costs outweigh the modest annual savings for typical Belgian households.

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 Extended Data figures, 1 Extended Data table
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Rapids, an FPGA-co-designed streaming neural decoder for real-time quantum error correction that decodes distance-19 surface codes in under a microsecond per round. It achieves a 240x lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders and 16x higher accuracy than the Relay decoder on bivariate-bicycle codes.
AI.motivation: Superconducting quantum processors have fast syndrome cycles that force existing real-time decoders to sacrifice accuracy, requiring larger codes and extra physical qubits to compensate.
AI.method: Rapids co-designs a streaming neural network built from FPGA-friendly operations trained in integer arithmetic, and demonstrates scaling across multiple FPGAs or custom silicon.
AI.result: On a single FPGA, Rapids decodes distance-19 surface code rounds in under 1 us with a 240x lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders, and extends to color codes and [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle codes where it is 16x more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing integer-arithmetic neural decoders with classical hardware makes classical compute a scalable resource alongside qubits for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Bayesian optimization on amortized search space
summary: In real-world black-box optimization problems, a mechanistic simulator is often available that approximately predicts the behavior of the system as a function of the parameters being optimized. Here, we show how an amortized inverse map of such a simulator can be used in Bayesian optimization to restrict the search space while using a Gaussian process kernel that is aware of the original problem geometry. This allows for efficiently leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of the optimization problem. We characterize its approximation bias and information gain, and derive an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate under additional geometric and Gaussian Process assumptions. We illustrate the method with an application to drug dosing personalization in Parkinson's disease. We use, as a simulator, a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) model of a drug, a mechanistic model calibrated on population data with quantified parameter uncertainty. A dosing neural network is trained offline against the model, amortizing the map from patient PK/PD parameters to the regimen predicted to be optimal, and online Bayesian optimization then searches over this learned, low-dimensional representation rather than over raw dosages. Numerical simulations demonstrate the improved performance of our method in this application, as well as under simulator misspecification.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes performing Bayesian optimization over a low-dimensional amortized inverse map of a mechanistic simulator using a geometry-aware Gaussian process kernel. It derives intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret bounds and demonstrates improved performance in Parkinson's disease drug dosing personalization, even under simulator misspecification.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional black-box optimization problems often possess low intrinsic dimensionality governed by an approximate mechanistic simulator that standard Bayesian optimization does not exploit.
AI.method: The authors train an offline neural network to amortize the inverse map from simulator parameters to optimal decisions, then run online Bayesian optimization over this learned low-dimensional representation using a kernel aware of the original problem geometry, and apply it to a Parkinson's PK/PD simulator.
AI.result: The paper characterizes approximation bias and information gain, derives an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate, and shows improved dosing personalization performance in numerical simulations, including under simulator misspecification.
AI.conclusion: Amortized simulator-informed search spaces enable sample-efficient Bayesian optimization with theoretical regret guarantees.

title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
summary: Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes. In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code. We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance. In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes BuildPredictor, a random forest model that predicts Continuous Integration (CI) build outcomes from code, build-file, and complexity changes alongside historical build results. It achieves median MCCs of 0.82 (intra-project) and 0.86 (holistic), helping avoid unnecessary CI build runs.
AI.motivation: Frequent CI builds after every commit waste substantial time and compute resources on minimal changes that could be anticipated.
AI.method: The authors train a random forest classifier using features capturing source and build-code changes, code complexity changes, and historical build outcomes, evaluating both intra-project and holistic settings as well as a variant without historical features.
AI.result: BuildPredictor achieves median MCCs of 0.82 (intra-project) and 0.86 (holistic), reaches peak performance quickly over time, identifies historical build results as the most important features, and retains decent, more interpretable performance when historical features are removed.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning-based build outcome prediction can reliably anticipate CI results and save development resources.

title: Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity
summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in expectation and with high probability.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that single-pass differentially private Noisy SGD with fixed stepsize and constant batch size is minimax-optimal for smooth, strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, it yields the first minimax-optimal rate for private logistic regression without extra poly-logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: While standard SGD is minimax-optimal for many regression tasks, it was unknown whether simple Noisy SGD achieves minimax-optimal parameter estimation error under differential privacy on strongly convex losses.
AI.method: Using standard convex analysis, the authors upper bound parameter estimation error for single-pass Noisy SGD under Renyi DP and match it against minimax lower bounds derived via the Score Attack framework for strongly convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs).
AI.result: The derived upper bounds match the GLM minimax lower bounds in both expectation and high probability, establishing the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression without poly-logarithmic terms.
AI.conclusion: Simple single-pass Noisy SGD suffices for statistically minimax-optimal differentially private estimation under population strong convexity.

title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

AI.tldr: TideCache is a serving system for hybrid LLMs on CPU-GPU superchips that dynamically manages heterogeneous caches and overlaps layer-wise prefix streaming with bounded-state computation, completing up to 2.04x more agent turns and reducing P50 per-token latency by 20-59%.
AI.motivation: Hybrid LLMs combine global-attention and bounded-state layers with heterogeneous caches whose memory demands vary with context length and concurrency, creating memory allocation and residency bottlenecks in existing serving systems.
AI.method: TideCache integrates a Transparent Cache Pool that redistributes physical pages behind fixed virtual addresses, a Cache Streamer that prefetches global-attention prefixes into shared GPU slots during bounded-state layer computation while keeping generated KV resident, and a Request Scheduler that selects resident or streamed execution and adjusts capacities based on request size and queue state.
AI.result: Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20-59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40-3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.
AI.conclusion: TideCache enables higher concurrency and lower latency for hybrid LLM serving on CPU-GPU superchips by transparently pooling memory and overlapping layer-wise cache transfers with computation.

title: The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions
summary: We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic Gaussian distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, when the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, distance-based and spectral procedures require a squared separation $\Delta^2$ of order $\sqrt d$. In contrast, tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation but need a sample size that is a large polynomial of $dK$, and the low-degree lower bounds known for random centers only show that $n$ must exceed $dK^2$. Focusing on normally distributed centers, we characterize the minimal separation for clustering with low-degree polynomials in the regime $K>d$, through a low-degree lower bound and a matching upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. In particular, for $K=d^{p/2}$ with $p> 2$ a real number, we show that a sample size of the order of $K^3 d^{(\lceil p\rceil-p)/2}$ is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and that it suffices when $p$ is not an integer.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the low-degree sample complexity and minimal separation required for clustering mixtures of K isotropic Gaussians in R^d when K exceeds d and centers are normally distributed.
AI.motivation: In the regime where the number of groups K is much larger than the dimension d, distance-based and spectral methods require squared separation of order sqrt(d), while tensor-based methods achieve polylogarithmic separation at the cost of large polynomial sample sizes, and existing low-degree lower bounds only show n must exceed dK^2.
AI.method: The authors focus on normally distributed centers and establish a low-degree lower bound together with a matching upper bound up to subpolynomial factors for clustering with low-degree polynomials when K > d.
AI.result: For K = d^(p/2) with real p > 2, a sample size of order K^3 d^((ceil(p) - p)/2) is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and this sample complexity is shown to be sufficient whenever p is not an integer.
AI.conclusion: The results pin down the computational sample complexity of low-degree polynomial clustering for high-group-count Gaussian mixtures, bridging the gap between spectral and tensor-based regimes.

title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
summary: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

AI.tldr: The authors propose TSGSurv, a two-stage generative framework for censored time-to-event data, and establish theoretical guarantees for distributional convergence, Cox model consistency, and valid statistical inference.
AI.motivation: Synthetic time-to-event data for clinical trials and survival analysis lacks theoretical guarantees for distributional fidelity, and it remains unclear whether downstream statistical analyses on synthetic survival data produce reliable inference.
AI.method: TSGSurv jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status in two stages, and pairs this with variance correction and distribution calibration procedures to recover valid inference for the Cox proportional hazards model.
AI.result: The authors establish the distributional convergence rate of TSGSurv, prove conditions for consistency of Cox model coefficient estimates, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the generative and inferential framework on extensive simulations and two real data applications.
AI.conclusion: TSGSurv provides a theoretically grounded approach to generating faithful synthetic survival data that supports valid downstream statistical inference.

title: Supervised Contrastive Learning of Environment-Invariant Representations

AI.tldr: The authors propose Supervised Contrastive Invariance Learning (SCIL) to learn task-supervised representations that are regularized against environment-associated correlations, evaluating it on Colored MNIST, Camelyon17-WILDS, and 26 million Optical Pooled Screening images.
AI.motivation: Combining data collected under different experimental conditions increases dataset size but introduces environment-associated correlations that hinder modeling the underlying phenomena of interest.
AI.method: SCIL uses Supervised Contrastive Learning with a single hyperparameter alpha to regularize environment-related structure in a task-supervised representation z_c alongside an environment-supervised auxiliary representation z_s, though the auxiliary representation's contribution remains unresolved.
AI.result: On Colored MNIST and Camelyon17-WILDS under distribution shift, increasing alpha lowers in-distribution validation accuracy while raising held-out test accuracy; on batch correction for 26 million Optical Pooled Screening images, z_c preserves biological signal while becoming less predictive of inter-well variation.
AI.conclusion: Purely supervised contrastive regularization with a single hyperparameter offers a simple mechanism to trade off in-distribution fit for environment invariance under distribution shift and large-scale batch correction.
